rule: The conformance requirement on the record row is what makes the component encodable: a nested record that declares `ISerializable`/`IDeserializable` supplies the members the synthesized bodies reach, and is then admissible as a serialized component.

title: a serialized rename colliding with another component's name is rejected
rule: The string must be a non-empty literal and must be unique among the serialized names of the type's components; a member's serialized name is its rename where one is declared and its declared identifier otherwise, so a rename equal to another member's identifier collides too. A collision is a compile error at the conformance declaration.

title: an enum is always serialization-eligible and admits a constant rename
rule: Enums are always serialization-eligible. The synthesized form writes the member's serialized name as a string — its `serialized "<name>"` rename where one is declared, its identifier otherwise.

title: a record with a requires-carrying constructor is constructor-only and declares fine
rule: A record type is constructor-only when it declares a constructor carrying a contract clause: a requires clause, an ensures clause, or both, on any constructor of the record, of any visibility, in any recorded tier.

title: default on a constructor-only record is rejected
rule: A constructor-only record is not defaultable; default(R) and every other site that supplies a default(T) are rejected.

title: a constructor-only record does not satisfy where T colon new()
rule: Port at a where T: new() substitution is also rejected.

title: an ordinary body record without a contract-clause constructor satisfies where T colon new()
rule: A value-type substitution satisfies the new() constraint exactly when it is defaultable; a record with no contract-clause constructor is not constructor-only and remains ordinary.

title: a constructor-only record is otherwise ordinary and remains auto-hashable
rule: In every other respect such a record is ordinary; a constructor is a member section 9.2 admits regardless of what its body does, so Port remains auto-hashable, hashable, and serialization-eligible.

title: default initialization of constructor-only-record storage is rejected
rule: A constructor-only record is not defaultable, so default initialization of `R`-typed storage is rejected: the field has no zero value to hold and no constructor behind one.

title: constructor-only-record storage initialized by a constructor call is admitted
rule: The remedy is a constructor or factory call: the property claims provenance — every value of a constructor-only record is produced by a call to one of that record's declared constructors — and a field initializer that calls one satisfies definite assignment.

title: a record declaring positional fields may not declare a contract-clause constructor
rule: A record declaring positional fields may not declare a constructor carrying a contract clause: a compile error at the record declaration. The auto-generated primary constructor carries no clause, so the combination would leave `new R(…)` outside every gate the declared constructor states.

title: default underlying values are assigned 0, 1, 2 in declaration order
rule: This declares constants `Priority.Low`, `Priority.Medium`, `Priority.High` of type `Priority`. The default underlying values are 0, 1, 2 — assigned in declaration order from zero.

title: same-valued constants denote one value under =
rule: Two or more constants of one enum may share an underlying value. Same-valued constants denote one value: `Legacy = Current` is `true`, and no construct can distinguish them at run time.

title: two case arms naming same-valued constants is rejected
rule: In a `case` over the enum, two arms — or two `|` alternatives — naming same-valued constants are a compile error, the later one being unreachable.

title: a case naming only one alias of a shared value is exhaustive and legal
rule: Exhaustiveness is over the set of distinct declared values, so an arm naming either alias covers both.

title: same-valued enum constants draw no diagnostic
rule: Two or more constants of one enum may share an underlying value ... Aliasing is legal and **draws no diagnostic**; exhaustiveness is over the set of distinct declared *values*, so an arm naming either alias covers both.

title: a colon-list head outside the eight integer types is read as an interface, and rejected as one
rule: The colon list is one list: if its first item resolves to one of the eight underlying-type keywords, that item is the underlying type; otherwise the underlying type is `int` and every item names an interface. `double` resolves to none of the eight, so it is read as an attempted interface — and is not one.

title: short is an admitted underlying type
rule: The underlying type must be one of `byte`, `sbyte`, `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`.

title: FromUnderlyingOrNull returns the declared constant matching the value
rule: `FromUnderlyingOrNull` returns the declared constant whose underlying value equals `value`, or `null` when there is none.

title: FromNameOrNull returns null for a digit string
rule: `FromNameOrNull(name)` returns the declared constant whose identifier equals `name`, or `null` when there is none; a digit string names no constant, since no identifier begins with a digit.

title: NameOf agrees with nameof for a written constant
rule: For a written constant `E.NameOf(E.A) = nameof(E.A)` — `NameOf` extends the compile-time operator to a runtime value over the same table.

title: NameOf yields the first-declared identifier for a shared value
rule: Under duplicate constant values, `NameOf` yields the first-declared constant's identifier for a shared value.

title: a user declaration cannot overload the compiler-provided FromNameOrNull
rule: Every enum carries three compiler-provided static members — `FromUnderlyingOrNull`, `FromNameOrNull`, `NameOf` — and no user declaration, a member or a declared constant, may override or overload any of them.

title: a distinctly named static method beside the compiler-provided tier is admitted
rule: Every enum carries three compiler-provided static members; a user declaration under a different name does not collide with them.

title: an enum's static owned readonly FrozenArray singleton is warning-free
rule: `FrozenArray<Priority>` declares the **immutable** statics-and-sharing fact, placing it in §22.12 rule 4's warning-suppression set — a `static owned readonly` of it is a warning-free, every-domain-readable singleton.

title: the same enum static at a mutable class type draws rule 4's sharing warning
rule: ... where the same field at `Array<Priority>` (a mutable class type outside the set) would draw rule 4's declaration-site sharing warning.

title: an enum cannot declare an instance field
rule: An enum may not declare instance fields (the runtime representation is the underlying integer).

title: a static readonly field is admitted where an instance field is not
rule: An enum may declare `static readonly` fields; instance fields are forbidden because the runtime representation is the underlying integer.

title: an enum cannot declare a block-form property
rule: An enum may declare exactly instance methods, expression-bodied read-only instance properties, static methods, `static readonly` fields, `const` members, and operator overloads — and no others; an enum may not declare block-form properties or properties with backing storage.

title: an enum may declare an expression-bodied read-only instance property
rule: An enum may declare exactly instance methods, expression-bodied read-only instance properties, static methods, `static readonly` fields, `const` members, and operator overloads.

title: override is rejected on an enum member outside the Object-virtual surface
rule: `override` is admitted only on the `Object`-virtual members — `Equals`, `GetHashCode`, `ToString` — and is rejected on every other enum member.

title: override is admitted on ToString
rule: An enum may declare — spelled `override` or plain — `Equals` taking the enum's own type, `GetHashCode(): int`, and `ToString(): string`; each replaces the compiler-generated default for every consumer.

title: overloading homogeneous = on an enum without Equals(T)/GetHashCode is rejected
rule: A record/enum/choice overloading homogeneous `=`/`<>` also declares `Equals(T)` and `GetHashCode` — on an enum, `override` or plain (the co-declaration rule).

title: overloading homogeneous = on an enum together with Equals(T) and GetHashCode is admitted
rule: A record/enum/choice overloading homogeneous `=`/`<>` also declares `Equals(T)` and `GetHashCode` — on an enum, `override` or plain (the co-declaration rule).

title: case matching an enum scrutinee admits the omitted prefix and selects the matching arm
rule: Inside a `case` whose scrutinee is an enum, the enum prefix may be omitted.

title: a primary constructor chains to the base via inheritance-clause args
rule: If the class has a base class that requires constructor arguments, the base's arguments appear in parentheses after the base class name in the inheritance list; this desugars to a primary constructor that chains to base(...) before executing field initializers.

title: two base classes on one class is rejected
rule: A class may declare at most one base class and any number of interfaces.

title: a convenience constructor that does not chain to the primary is rejected
rule: A class with a primary constructor may also declare additional constructors in its body using the constructor keyword; such constructors must chain to the primary constructor via this(...).

title: a class implements an interface implicitly by declaring matching public members
rule: A class implements an interface implicitly: by declaring matching public members.

title: an interface member may not carry a visibility keyword
rule: Interface members are implicitly public, have no body, and end with `;`.

title: an implementation may widen an interface parameter from T to T?
rule: An implementation may declare a parameter as T? where the interface requires T (the implementation accepts more inputs than the interface promises to pass).

title: an implementation may not narrow an interface parameter from T? to T
rule: The reverse -- interface T?, implementation T -- is rejected, because the implementation would refuse a null the interface promised to accept.

title: owned must match exactly between an interface parameter and its implementation
rule: An implementing method's signature and the interface method's signature must agree on owned as a parameter modifier. Interface declaring M(owned t: T) requires implementation to declare M(owned t: T).

title: a record may not implement an interface declaring a settable member
rule: A record may implement any number of interfaces that declare no settable property or indexer member -- a conformance naming an interface with one is rejected at the declaration (a value kind supplies no receiver-storing accessor).

title: two fields with the same name clash
rule: A type may not declare two members that are not distinguishable from each other. Two members clash when they have the same name... two fields, properties, or nested types with the same name.

title: two distinctly-named fields do not clash
rule: A type may not declare two members that are not distinguishable from each other -- distinctly-named members are unaffected.

title: a field and a property with the same name clash
rule: A non-overloadable member -- a field, property, or nested type -- additionally clashes with any other member of the type that shares its name, regardless of kind.

title: two methods with an identical signature clash
rule: Two members clash when they have the same name... two methods... with the same name that are not distinguishable as overloads.

title: methods distinguished by parameter type are legal overloads, not a clash
rule: Legal overloads -- members of the same name that are distinguishable per §22.6 -- are unaffected; this rule rejects only the duplicates that overloading does not admit.

title: an owned/plain parameter pair fails the declaration guard when it can collapse
rule: owned on an ordinary parameter distinguishes overloads exactly where §22.6's declaration guard admits the pair; a pair failing the guard clashes at the second declaration. where T: class does not qualify -- it admits string and function-type substitutions, at which the marker is erased and the pair collapses.

title: an owned/plain parameter pair is legal when the constraint excludes every collapsing substitution
rule: An interface bound qualifies exactly when the interface's conforming set excludes every value-kind and runtime-managed type as a matter of language rule -- where T: IDisposable qualifies, its closure guaranteed by §8.7.

title: owned on an out parameter never distinguishes overloads
rule: owned on an out parameter and scoped never distinguish overloads; two methods differing only in the owned qualifier on an out parameter are a compile error (§22.6).

title: the canonical modifier order is admitted on a static owned field
rule: visibility static (async|pure) (abstract|virtual|override|sealed override) (owned|scoped) readonly member-kind Name ... The combination static owned readonly is the canonical form for a static field that owns a long-lived resource.

title: readonly before owned is rejected
rule: The compiler rejects out-of-order modifiers. owned appears between the virtual-modifier slot and readonly.

title: owned before static is rejected
rule: visibility static (async|pure) (abstract|virtual|override|sealed override) (owned|scoped) readonly member-kind Name ... The compiler rejects out-of-order modifiers.

title: static before visibility is rejected
rule: visibility static (async|pure) (abstract|virtual|override|sealed override) (owned|scoped) readonly member-kind Name ... The compiler rejects out-of-order modifiers.

title: the canonical modifier order is admitted on an override
rule: visibility static (async|pure) (abstract|virtual|override|sealed override) (owned|scoped) readonly member-kind Name ...

title: visibility after override is rejected
rule: visibility static (async|pure) (abstract|virtual|override|sealed override) (owned|scoped) readonly member-kind Name ... The compiler rejects out-of-order modifiers.

title: virtual and override together are rejected as mutually exclusive
rule: abstract, virtual, override, and sealed override are mutually exclusive -- at most one may appear.

title: owned is rejected on a non-field member
rule: owned ... appears between the virtual-modifier slot and readonly. It applies only to fields; methods, properties, and other members do not carry owned.

title: a class body may declare nested types with required visibility
rule: A class body may declare nested classes, records, enums, and interfaces. Nested types may be public, internal, protected, or private, and the visibility keyword is required.

title: a nested type missing its visibility keyword is rejected
rule: A nested type is a class member, and §13.3's explicit-visibility rule applies with no exception for nested types -- omitting the keyword is a compile error, not a default.

title: a nested type's qualified name includes the enclosing path
rule: A nested type is referenced from outside as Outer.Nested, and the enclosing path is part of its qualified name wherever one is rendered.

title: a nested class may access the private members of an enclosing instance
rule: A nested class has access to all members (including private) of its enclosing class when it holds an instance of the enclosing class.

title: a static class may contain only static members
rule: A class declared static may contain only static members.

title: new on a static class is rejected
rule: A static class may not be instantiated: new on a static class is a compile error.

title: a static class may not declare an instance field
rule: A static class may not have instance fields, instance methods, instance properties, indexers, constructors (other than a static constructor), or destructors.

title: a static class may not be inherited from another class
rule: A static class may not be inherited from and does not implement interfaces.

title: sealed abstract is rejected, the diagnostic naming closed
rule: Combining `closed` with `abstract`, `sealed`, or `static` is a compile error; the modifier pair `sealed abstract` is rejected too, the diagnostic naming `closed`.

title: a closed class may declare abstract members and be subclassed within its own module
rule: A class declared with the closed modifier is a closed abstract class: a class that cannot be instantiated directly and cannot be inherited from outside the declaring module. A closed class may declare abstract members without carrying the abstract modifier.

title: closed combined with abstract is rejected
rule: Combining closed with abstract, sealed, or static is a compile error.

title: a static class may not declare an instance method
rule: A static class may not have instance fields, instance methods, instance properties, indexers, constructors (other than a static constructor), or destructors.

title: a static class may not declare an instance constructor
rule: A static class may not have instance fields, instance methods, instance properties, indexers, constructors (other than a static constructor), or destructors.

title: a static constructor is the one constructor a static class may declare
rule: A static class may not have constructors *other than a static constructor*; the static constructor runs after all static field initializers complete (§22.13).

title: a static owned readonly field on a static class is permitted
rule: Static `owned` fields are permitted: `static owned readonly` fields and static owning-inline-array fields participate in §22.13's program-exit disposal exactly as on any other type — that mechanism is runtime-driven and independent of instance `Dispose()`.

title: a static class may not declare a destructor
rule: A static class may not have instance fields, instance methods, instance properties, indexers, constructors (other than a static constructor), or destructors.

title: a static class may not implement an interface
rule: A static class may not be inherited from and does not implement interfaces.

title: abstract and static are mutually exclusive
rule: The `abstract` and `static` modifiers are mutually exclusive, and `sealed` and `static` are mutually exclusive; combining either pair is a compile error.

title: sealed and static are mutually exclusive
rule: The `abstract` and `static` modifiers are mutually exclusive, and `sealed` and `static` are mutually exclusive; combining either pair is a compile error.

title: a closed class may not be instantiated directly
rule: A class declared with the `closed` modifier is a closed abstract class: a class that cannot be instantiated directly and cannot be inherited from outside the declaring module.

title: a closed class may not be subclassed from another module
rule: Classes derived from a `closed` base must be declared in the same module; the compiler rejects subclasses in other modules.

title: a conforming type supplies static interface members with exact signatures
rule: An interface member may be declared static: a contract the conforming type -- not an instance -- must satisfy. A conforming type supplies the static members with exact signatures.

title: a static interface member may not declare a body
rule: Static interface members are abstract-only (no default bodies; the same diamond-avoidance posture as the declined default interface methods).

title: calling a static interface member through the interface name is rejected
rule: Static interface members contribute nothing to the instance surface... calling a static member on the interface name (INumber<int>.Zero()) is a compile error -- the interface declares no bodies to run.

title: an interface declaring static members may not mark a type parameter variant
rule: An interface that declares static members may not mark its type parameters variant (in/out) -- a compile error at the declaration.

title: T.Member(...) dispatches to the conforming type's static member
rule: In a generic body whose parameter T carries a static-interface constraint, T.Member(...) calls the conforming type's static member, and an operator applied to T-typed operands resolves through the constraint's static operators.

title: an override matching the base member exactly is admitted
rule: A method, property, or indexer is non-virtual unless marked virtual. To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member override.

title: an override with a mismatched parameter type is rejected
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly.

title: an override may widen a parameter from T to T?
rule: An override may declare a parameter as T? where the overridden member declares T -- the same contravariant nullability widening §11.2 grants interface implementations.

title: an override may not narrow a parameter from T? back to T
rule: The reverse direction (overridden T?, override T) is rejected, as in §11.2.

title: a virtual override runs through a base-typed reference
rule: A method, property, or indexer is non-virtual unless marked virtual. To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member override.

title: an extension member is resolved by the receiver's static type, not dispatched virtually
rule: A method, property, or indexer is non-virtual unless marked virtual -- an extension member has no override relationship at all, and §26.5 resolves it by the receiver's declared type.

title: a derived class may not redeclare a visible inherited member's name
rule: Declaring a member in a derived class with the same name as any inherited member visible at the derived class's declaration site is a compile error, unless the declaration is an override of a virtual member.

title: overriding a virtual base member is the sanctioned way to reuse its name
rule: Declaring a member in a derived class with the same name as any inherited member visible at the derived class's declaration site is a compile error, unless the declaration is an override of a virtual member with a matching signature.

title: an invisible private base member does not block the name in a derived class
rule: A private base member never blocks -- two same-named private fields in base and derived are distinct members and legal... When a base member was invisible at the derived declaration site, the derived declaration creates a distinct member.

title: base.Member bypasses virtual dispatch
rule: Inside a derived member, base.Name(...) calls the base class's implementation, bypassing virtual dispatch.

title: inheriting from a sealed class is rejected
rule: sealed on a class prevents inheritance from that class.

title: bare sealed on a member is rejected
rule: On a member, `sealed` appears only as the compound `sealed override`: a member declaration carrying `sealed` without `override` is a compile error, whatever the member's kind and whatever other dispatch modifier it carries.

title: virtual on a member of a sealed class is rejected
rule: A member of a `sealed` class may not be declared `virtual`: the class admits no subclass, so a new virtual slot on it can never be filled, and an inert modifier that reads as load-bearing misleads every reader of the declaration.

title: the same virtual member on a non-sealed class is admitted
rule: The rejection is keyed on the class being `sealed` — a class that admits subclasses may declare a new `virtual` slot, which is what §12.1's override-matching rule exists to fill.

title: new on an abstract class is rejected
rule: new on an abstract or closed class is a compile error.

title: a class with an abstract member must itself be abstract or closed
rule: A class containing one or more abstract members must itself be abstract (or closed, §11.7).

title: async abstract is rejected
rule: async abstract is a compile error. An abstract method whose implementations are expected to be asynchronous declares a Task or Task<T> return type without async.

title: is T narrows the tested variable to T in the true branch
rule: is T tests whether a value is an instance of T and produces bool. When the test succeeds and the tested expression is a simple variable, the variable is flow-narrowed to T within the controlled block.

title: a chain-extending store into a value-narrowed Object box is rejected
rule: A write whose store would land in the box is a compile error: an assignment, compound assignment, or ++/-- whose target is an lvalue chain extending the binding with a . or [...] hop.

title: a ref argument into a value-narrowed Object box is rejected
rule: A write whose store would land in the box is a compile error: such a chain passed as a ref or out argument, which §22.3's assignable-storage-location categories admit -- through which the callee's write reaches the payload.

title: a bare-binding compound assignment on a narrowed Object is not a box write
rule: What is not rejected is the bare-binding compound and ++/-- form: o += 1 and o++ are equivalent to o := o + 1, and that store targets the declared Object/interface location -- it boxes the result afresh.

title: a base(...) chain argument may read the constructor's own parameters and constants
rule: The only reads a base(...)/this(...) argument may make are of the constructor's own parameters, constants, and statics.

title: a chain argument may not read a field of this
rule: it may not read a field or auto-property of the object under construction -- nothing of this is assigned yet.

title: a chain argument may not read a primary-constructor parameter
rule: nor, in a class with a primary constructor, a primary-constructor parameter (§22.10; the field half is §22.7's ground: nothing of this is assigned yet).

title: the implicit base() insertion requires a parameterless base constructor
rule: If neither base(...) nor this(...) is written, the compiler inserts an implicit base() call (which requires the base class to have a parameterless constructor; otherwise the chain must be explicit).

title: a covariant type parameter used only in output position is admitted
rule: out requires T to appear only in output positions (return types, read-only property types, out parameters).

title: a covariant type parameter used in input position is rejected
rule: out requires T to appear only in output positions... The compiler enforces position constraints.

title: a variance marker on a generic class is rejected
rule: Classes, records, and concrete generic types are always invariant -- and the variance markers are interface-only syntax: in/out on a generic parameter of a class... is a compile error.

title: a variant assignment whose source has a value-type type argument is rejected
rule: What is rejected is the variant assignment of IEnumerable<int> to IEnumerable<Object>, which would require per-element boxing at every access. For value-typed T, the only legal assignment of IEnumerable<T> is to IEnumerable<T> itself or to Object.

title: a class naming itself as its own base is a cycle
rule: The simplest case is a type naming itself (class C: C).

title: a two-class inheritance cycle is rejected
rule: the general case is a chain (class A: B, class B: C, class C: A) and the mixed class/interface chains the relation admits.

title: an interface extending itself is a cycle
rule: An inheritance cycle is a compile error. A type may not, directly or transitively, list itself among its base types — neither as the base class of a class, nor as an extended interface of an interface.

title: a two-interface extension cycle is rejected
rule: The relation followed is the union of base-class edges and extended-interface edges; a cycle is any sequence of types where each lists the next as a base type and the sequence returns to its start.

title: a three-class inheritance chain that returns to its start is rejected
rule: The general case is a chain (`class A: B`, `class B: C`, `class C: A`); the compiler detects the cycle and reports an error naming the participating types.

title: an acyclic chain over both edge kinds is accepted and dispatches
rule: An inheritance cycle is a compile error only where the sequence returns to its start; a chain over base-class edges and extended-interface edges that never returns to its start is admitted.

title: a private member is not visible outside the declaring class
rule: `private` — Visible to the declaring class only.

title: a private member is visible within its own declaring class
rule: `private` — Visible to the declaring class only.

title: an internal member is not visible from another module
rule: `internal` — Visible to code in the same module. A module is the set of source files declaring the same module name presented to the module's one compilation; a separately-compiled importing module is not that set.

title: an internal member is visible from another class in the same module
rule: `internal` — Visible to code in the same module. Unlike `private`, an internal member is reachable from any class compiled as part of the same module, not only the declaring class.

title: a protected member is reachable from a derived class in another module
rule: `protected` — Visible to the declaring class and all classes derived from it. §13.1: a derived class in a different module sees `protected` even though it does not see `internal` — that is the whole point of the level.

title: a protected member is not reachable from an unrelated class in the same module
rule: `protected` — Visible to the declaring class and all classes derived from it. §13.1: an unrelated class in the same module sees `internal` but not `protected` — module membership alone does not confer access; only the inheritance relationship does.

title: internal does not extend to a derived class in another module
rule: `internal` and `protected` are incomparable — a derived class in a different module sees `protected` but not `internal`. Inheriting from a class in another module confers no access to that class's internal members.

title: a top-level type declared protected is rejected
rule: Top-level types may be `public` or `internal`. They may not be `protected` (no enclosing class) or `private` (no file-scope concept).

title: internal is an admitted top-level visibility
rule: Top-level types may be `public` or `internal`.

title: a field with no visibility keyword is rejected
rule: Every class member must declare its visibility explicitly, except the four exempted kinds. On every other member, omitting the visibility keyword is a compile error.

title: a field with an explicit visibility keyword is admitted
rule: Every class member must declare its visibility explicitly, except the four exempted kinds.

title: a destructor given an explicit visibility keyword is rejected
rule: A `destructor` is a member kind user code can never invoke or name at a use site — for such a member no visibility choice exists to spell, and it carries no visibility keyword.

title: a destructor with no visibility keyword is admitted
rule: A `destructor` carries no visibility keyword — for such a member no visibility choice exists to spell.

title: files in Foo get no special access to files in Foo.Bar
rule: The dotted form is a single name; files in `Foo` get no special access to files in `Foo.Bar`.

title: a dotted module name is an ordinary whole name for internal access
rule: A module is the set of all source files declaring the same `module Name.Path;`; the dotted form is a single name, so files sharing the whole dotted name share internal access exactly as an undotted name would.

title: files in Foo.Bar get no special access to files in Foo
rule: The dotted form is a single name; `Foo` and `Foo.Bar` are unrelated modules in both directions — neither gets special access to the other's internal members.

title: two modules under a common dotted prefix are unrelated siblings
rule: The dotted form is a single name; it does not establish nesting (§2.1). `Foo.Bar` and `Foo.Baz` share a prefix but are unrelated modules — neither gets access to the other's internal members.

title: protected internal is not a valid combined visibility
rule: Bezel does not provide combined forms (no `protected internal`, no `private protected`).

title: protected alone is a valid single visibility
rule: Bezel does not provide combined forms (no `protected internal`, no `private protected`); a single level is unaffected.

title: an accessor visibility less restrictive than the property is rejected
rule: A property's `get` or `set` may carry its own visibility, which must not be less restrictive than the property's overall visibility.

title: a more restrictive accessor visibility is admitted
rule: A property's `get` or `set` may carry its own visibility, which must not be less restrictive than the property's overall visibility; a more restrictive accessor is the useful form.

title: an internal field typed at a private nested class is rejected
rule: Every type appearing in a member's signature must be at least as visible as the member — `internal _x: NestedPrivate;` is an error when `NestedPrivate` is `private`: the field's type is not as visible as the field.

title: a private field typed at a private nested class is admitted
rule: Every type appearing in a member's signature must be at least as visible as the member — `private _y: NestedPrivate;` is fine: also private, matches `NestedPrivate`'s visibility.

title: a protected member with an internal-typed parameter is rejected
rule: Every type appearing in a member's signature must be at least as visible as the member. The rule applies at every visibility level: a `protected` member's signature types must be at least `protected` — `internal` and `protected` are incomparable (§13.1), so an `internal` type does not satisfy it.

title: a protected member with a protected-typed parameter is admitted
rule: Every type appearing in a member's signature must be at least as visible as the member; equal visibility satisfies the rule.

title: an override declaring a different visibility than the base member is rejected
rule: An override must declare the same visibility as the base member.

title: an override matching the base member's visibility is admitted
rule: An override must declare the same visibility as the base member.

title: a generic class parameterizes its members over a type parameter
rule: Classes, interfaces, records, and methods may be generic; type parameters use angle brackets (§14.1).

title: a class type satisfies where T: class
rule: `where T: class` accepts non-nullable reference types only — classes, interfaces, string, function types (§14.2).

title: a record fails where T: class
rule: `where T: class` accepts non-nullable reference types only; a value type is excluded (§14.2).

title: a record satisfies where T: value
rule: `where T: value` accepts non-nullable value types — records, enums, choices, primitives, inline arrays, the unit type (§14.2).

title: a class fails where T: value
rule: `where T: value` admits only non-nullable value types; a reference type is excluded (§14.2).

title: a non-nullable class satisfies where T: notnull
rule: `where T: notnull` accepts non-nullable types only, value or reference (§14.2).

title: a nullable class type fails where T: notnull
rule: `where T: notnull` excludes a nullable type, value or reference — a nullable type is excluded (§14.2).

title: a class implementing the named interface satisfies where T: IFoo
rule: `where T: IFoo` admits non-nullable types conforming to `IFoo`: classes implementing it, directly or by inheritance (§14.2).

title: a class not implementing the named interface fails where T: IFoo
rule: `where T: IFoo` admits only types conforming to `IFoo` per the interface-conformance rule; a non-conforming class is excluded (§14.2).

title: a class with a public parameterless constructor satisfies where T: new()
rule: For `where T: new()`, a class substitution satisfies the constraint exactly when the class declares a parameterless constructor that is `public`; inside the generic body `new T()` produces an owned reference via that constructor (§14.2).

title: a class without a public parameterless constructor fails where T: new()
rule: A class substitution satisfies `where T: new()` exactly when the class declares a parameterless constructor that is `public` — not merely accessible from some scope — or declares no instance constructor at all, in which case §22.7's implicit parameterless constructor, which is `public`, satisfies it on the same terms. A class declaring only a parameterized constructor satisfies neither arm (§14.2).

title: a defaultable record satisfies where T: new() and new T() is default(T)
rule: A value-type substitution satisfies `where T: new()` exactly when it is defaultable; inside the generic body, `new T()` for a value substitution is equivalent to `default(T)` (§14.2).

title: an interface never satisfies where T: new()
rule: Interface substitutions never satisfy `new()` — no constructor exists (§14.2).

title: a choice never satisfies where T: new()
rule: Choices never satisfy the value-type arm of `where T: new()` — a consequence of the property: no choice is defaultable (§14.2, §17.11).

title: contradictory constraints are a compile error at the declaration
rule: Contradictory constraint combinations (e.g. `class, value`) are compile errors (§14.2).

title: int satisfies where T: sendable
rule: `where T: sendable` admits types whose sendable derived type property holds; all primitives are sendable (§14.2, §30.14).

title: an interface type fails where T: sendable
rule: `where T: sendable` is decided by the §30.14 computation; interface types are never sendable (§14.2, §30.14).

title: int satisfies where T: hashable
rule: `where T: hashable` admits types whose hashable derived type property holds — every type except a non-auto-hashable record (or choice) with no user equality (§14.2, §3.6).

title: a record with an explicit field and no user equality fails where T: hashable
rule: `hashable` excludes a record that is neither auto-hashable nor declares user equality; an explicit field declaration makes a body record not auto-hashable (§14.2, §3.6, §9.2).

title: a member where clause naming the enclosing type parameter is rejected
rule: A `where` clause on a member declaration may constrain only that member's own type parameters; a clause whose constrained parameter is a type parameter of the enclosing declaration is a compile error naming the conditionally-admitted-members subsection (§14.2 rule 1, v0.277).

title: a member where clause constraining its own type parameter, bound to an enclosing one, is admitted
rule: A clause constraining the member's own parameter is unaffected, including where its bound names an enclosing parameter (`method M<U>() where U: T` on `class C<T>`) — the ordinary constraint form of §14.2 (§14.2 rule 1, v0.277).

title: owned does not propagate through a generic type argument
rule: `owned` does not propagate through generic type arguments — so `Array<owned T>` is not a type (§14.4).

title: OwningArray<T> is the sanctioned replacement for Array<owned T>
rule: The owning forms are separate named types with their own declarations: `OwningArray<T>` beside `Array<T>` (§14.4).

title: a value type element is rejected on OwningArray<T>
rule: Most standard-library owning types restrict their element type T to class and interface types; value types are rejected at the instantiation site (§14.4).

title: a nullable class type element is admitted on OwningArray<T>
rule: The owning-type instantiation rule checks the underlying type, not the nullable wrapper; a nullable class type is admitted (§14.4).

title: a value type argument is rejected on OwningTask<T>
rule: `OwningTask<T>` is a compile error when T's underlying (nullability-stripped) type is neither a class nor an interface type (§14.4, Appendix C.6).

title: a nullable class type argument is admitted on OwningTask<T>
rule: Nullable class types are admitted for the owning task family: the underlying type is checked, and the nullability of the result is independent of the disposal obligation (§14.4).

title: a partial explicit type-argument list is rejected
rule: An explicit type-argument list binds the declared type parameters in declaration order and must supply exactly as many arguments as the method declares type parameters; a shorter or longer list is a compile error — there are no partial lists (§14.5).

title: a full explicit type-argument list binds every type parameter
rule: An explicit type-argument list binds the declared type parameters in declaration order; when a full explicit list is supplied, no inference runs (§14.5).

title: argument-driven unification infers a type parameter from a bare-parameter position
rule: A parameter type that is a bare type parameter X binds X to the argument's static type (§14.5, phase 1).

title: conflicting bindings for one type parameter fail inference
rule: All bindings a type parameter receives must be the same type; two different bindings are an inference failure — the compiler computes no common supertype and no widened join (§14.5, *Agreement*).

title: an explicit type argument resolves an agreement failure
rule: A conflicting-inference failure is remedied with explicit type arguments: with an explicit list, the parameter type is fixed and each argument converts at the ordinary argument-conversion site (§14.5, *Agreement*).

title: a record's type arguments are never inferred from constructor arguments
rule: Class-, record-, and interface-level type arguments are never inferred from constructor arguments: `new Pair(1, "x")` against `record Pair<TF, TS>(First: TF, Second: TS)` is a compile error directing to explicit arguments (§14.5).

title: explicit type arguments construct a generic record
rule: The remedy for uninferred record-level type arguments is explicit arguments: `new Pair<int, string>(1, "x")` (§14.5).

title: a type parameter appearing only in the return type is unbindable without a target
rule: A type parameter still unbound after arguments and lambdas is bound from the call's target type where one exists; a type parameter that remains unbound — appearing in no self-determined argument position and no target context — is a compile error naming the parameter (§14.5).

title: self-referential recursion at the same bare type parameter is legal
rule: Recursion at the same arguments stays legal: an edge substituting a type parameter of its target with a bare type parameter in scope at the source declaration is within the bounded-instantiation-closure rule (§14.6).

title: an in-SCC edge that nests a type parameter inside a larger argument is rejected
rule: Any substitution on an in-SCC edge other than a bare in-scope type parameter or a closed type is a compile error at the declaration holding the edge, with a diagnostic naming the cycle and the growing argument (§14.6).

title: an inline array with a defaultable element type default-initializes to zero
rule: When the element type T is defaultable, an inline array declaration without an explicit initializer is filled with that element default per slot (§15.1).

title: an inline array's explicit initializer fills its slots in order
rule: The initializer is a comma-separated list of N expressions in brackets (§15.1).

title: an inline array initializer with too few elements is a compile error
rule: The list must contain exactly N elements; mismatch is a compile error (§15.1).

title: a zero-size inline array is a compile error
rule: N must be greater than zero; `[0]T` is a compile error (§15.1).

title: inline arrays of different sizes are distinct types
rule: The size N is part of the type; `[3]int` and `[4]int` are distinct types that do not interconvert (§15.1).

title: multi-dimensional inline arrays are not admitted
rule: Inline arrays may not be elements of inline arrays in the form `[N][M]T` — multi-dimensional inline arrays are deferred to a future revision (§15.1).

title: move arr[i] on an owning inline array transfers ownership and requires restoration
rule: The `move arr[i]` form is admitted on `[N owned]T` slots; for non-nullable slots, restoration requires assigning a fresh owned T (§15.1.1).

title: the owned slot marker is rejected on a value-typed element
rule: `[N owned]T` requires T to be a class or interface type; value types are not admitted with the `owned` marker (§15.1.1).

title: string fails the class-or-interface restriction of an owning inline array at instantiation
rule: When T is a generic type parameter, the class-or-interface restriction on `[N owned]T?` is checked at instantiation, so instantiating with T = `string` is a compile error at the instantiation site (§15.1.1).

title: an owning inline array of nullable slots defaults to all null
rule: Nullable owned slots default to all null, with no initializer required at declaration (§15.1.1).

title: an owning inline array local disposes its slots in reverse slot order at scope end
rule: When an owning inline array's lifetime ends, the array's auto-dispose pass disposes each non-null slot **in reverse slot order**; for locals this happens at scope end via the standard owned-local discharge.

title: an owning-inline-array instance field disposes its slots in reverse slot order
rule: For **instance** fields of owning-inline-array type, the enclosing class's compiler-generated `Dispose()` disposes each non-null slot — in the same reverse slot order as every other ending of the value — and no user-written `destructor` is required.

title: whole-value reassignment disposes the displaced slots in reverse slot order
rule: A third ending is **whole-value reassignment**: overwriting an owning-inline-array local or instance field disposes each live slot of the displaced value before the store, in this section's reverse slot order — §15.3's per-slot drop-on-overwrite, the same pass run at the overwrite point.

title: a static owning-inline-array field disposes its slots in reverse slot order at program exit
rule: A fourth ending is **program exit**, for a static field of owning-inline-array type: the exit pass disposes each non-null slot of each such field, in this section's reverse slot order, taking the fields themselves in reverse order of static initialization.

title: an inline array's Length is a compile-time constant N
rule: Every inline array `[N]T` exposes `arr.Length: int` — a compile-time constant N (§15.1.2).

title: an inline array cannot be passed where IEnumerable<T> is expected
rule: Passing an inline array to a method expecting `IEnumerable<T>` is rejected: inline arrays are not class types and declare no interface conformances (§15.1.2).

title: an inline array of FFI-compatible scalars is admitted as an extern parameter
rule: Inline arrays of FFI-compatible scalar elements may appear as `extern` method parameters under the by-address rule (§15.1.3).

title: a heap array used at fixed size keeps its literal-constructed Count
rule: Users who want fixed-size discipline simply do not call resizing methods; the array's `Count` matches its construction-time capacity throughout its lifetime (§15.2).

title: an owning heap array constructed via literal owns its elements
rule: `OwningArray<T>` is a class type allocated with `new` and requiring disposal via `using var`; a collection literal transfers ownership of each element into it (§15.2).

title: reading a moved-from move-only local is a compile error
rule: A move-only value type is a value type whose instances cannot be duplicated; assignment transfers the value, leaving the source moved-from, and reading from a moved-from location is a compile error (§15.3).

title: a move-only value type may not be a field of a record
rule: A move-only value may not be a field of a record — records support only copy semantics, not move semantics (§15.3).

title: a move-only value carrying no borrows may be a field of a class
rule: A move-only value carrying no borrows may be a field of a class; the class's destructor disposes the field's owned slots (§15.3).

title: whole-value reassignment of an owning inline array disposes the displaced live slot
rule: Whole-value reassignment on a move-only local is drop-on-overwrite applied per slot: the RHS is evaluated first, then each live slot of the displaced value is disposed, then the new value is stored; the replacement is itself auto-disposed at scope end (§15.3, §15.1.1).

title: a wholly moved-from move-only local is readable again after reassignment
rule: After the move, `x` is in moved-from state and may not be read until reassigned; the standard restoration mechanism is to assign a fresh owned value (§15.3).

title: moving a move-only local while a closure capture of it is live is rejected
rule: The consume-site freeze applies regardless: moving a move-only local while a live borrow of it exists — e.g. a closure capture — is a compile error (§15.3, §28.9).

title: reassigning a move-only local is frozen while a borrow of a slot's object is live
rule: The reassignment is a consume of the displaced value — at a local, frozen while a live local borrow of the displaced value exists, a borrow of any slot's object included, since the pass disposes it (§15.3).

title: a slot moved-from via move arr[i] and never reassigned is rejected at the exit edge
rule: The field-restoration rule applies to individual slots: any slot moved-from via `move arr[i]` must be reassigned before any exit edge, because auto-dispose on a moved-from slot is not defined (§15.3).

title: assigning a fresh owned value restores a slot moved-from via move arr[i]
rule: The standard restoration mechanisms apply: assign a fresh owned value to the slot moved-from via `move arr[i]` before any exit edge (§15.3, §15.1.1).

title: a move-only argument is moved-from after the call and may not be read
rule: A parameter declared `(x: V)` for a move-only V is by value-move (transfer ownership); the caller's argument expression is in moved-from state after the call (§15.3).

title: owned on a move-only value parameter is admitted as a redundant marker
rule: A parameter declared `(owned x: V)` is identical to plain `(x: V)` for a move-only V; the modifier is admitted for documentation but is redundant (§15.3; §28.1's type requirement, clause 1).

title: equality over move-only values compares slot-wise by borrow and leaves both operands readable
rule: Move-only values support equality via borrowing comparison (reads each slot without moving), provided their element types support equality (§15.3; operator operands bind borrows, §25.2). An owning inline array's equality is element-by-element (§3.6's table), so two arrays whose slots compare equal are equal and two whose slots differ are not.

title: using var on an owning inline array locks out reassignment
rule: For a move-only inline-array local `using var` has no disposal effect, and its only observable consequence is preventing reassignment — the spelling for "fixed at construction and may not be rebound" (§15.3, §28.10).

title: a whole-value move out of a move-only local creates no restoration obligation
rule: A whole-value move — a plain binding, a plain argument, a return — creates no restoration obligation on a local: it leaves the local holding no value rather than a hole, so no pass walks it (§15.3).

title: a collection literal with no determinable target type is a compile error
rule: A collection literal has no standalone type; it is well-typed only in a context that provides the target type. A collection literal in a position where no target type is determinable is a compile error (§15.4).

title: a sequence literal targeting an inline array type produces a value
rule: The target types that admit collection literals include inline arrays `[N]T`; the literal must have exactly N elements (§15.4).

title: a sequence literal targeting Array<T> stores elements in textual order
rule: For `Array<T>`, elements are stored in textual order; index 0 is the first literal element (§15.4).

title: a fresh collection literal returned through an owned return transfers to the caller
rule: A collection literal targeting a reference type produces an owned value that must reach an owned location; `return [...]` is admitted through an `owned` return, the container's obligation following the transfer (§15.4, Appendix C.1).

title: a fresh collection literal returned through a non-owned instance return is rejected
rule: A fresh literal returned through a non-`owned` instance return is rejected exactly as any freshly-produced owned value is (§15.4, §28.6).

title: a fresh non-trivial-dispose element in a borrowing-family literal is rejected at the literal site
rule: For borrowing-family targets, each element expression of non-trivial-dispose class type must be a borrow; a fresh producer of such a type is rejected at the literal site (§15.4).

title: binding the source first remedies the fresh-element literal rejection
rule: The remedy for a fresh non-trivial-dispose literal element is to name the source first: `using var c := new Connection("a"); var conns: Array<Connection> := [c];` (§15.4).

title: a Set<T> literal collapses duplicates, retaining the first occurrence
rule: For `Set<T>`, duplicate elements are silently collapsed; the first occurrence in textual order is retained (§15.4).

title: duplicate compile-time-constant dictionary keys are a compile error
rule: For `Dictionary<K, V>` and `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, duplicate keys are a compile error when all duplicate keys are compile-time constants (§15.4).

title: a literal mixing bare expressions and colon pairs is a compile error
rule: The sequence and dictionary literal forms are syntactically distinguished by whether the elements contain a top-level colon; a literal cannot mix bare expressions and colon pairs (doing so is a compile error) (§15.4).

title: a colon inside a literal element is a compile error at a non-dictionary target
rule: The key-value pair syntax is recognized only when the target type is `Dictionary<K, V>` or `OwningDictionary<K, V>`; in any other target context a colon inside a literal element is a compile error (§15.4).

title: the empty literal is always rejected for an inline-array target
rule: The empty literal `[]` is admitted for every collection target but is always rejected for inline arrays — a literal must supply exactly N >= 1 elements (§15.4, §15.1).

title: the empty literal is admitted for a heap-collection target
rule: The empty literal `[]` is admitted for every collection target listed in this section — every collection type has a well-defined empty value — the target type determining which empty collection it constructs (§15.4).

title: a user class conforming to ICollectionLiteralTarget is constructed by a sequence literal
rule: A class opts into sequence-literal construction by conforming to `ICollectionLiteralTarget<TSelf, T>`, supplying `FromCollectionLiteral`; usage is identical syntax to built-in collections (§15.4.1).

title: a matching FromCollectionLiteral without the conformance is rejected at the declaration
rule: A class that declares a `public static` method named `FromCollectionLiteral` whose signature matches either interface's member at `TSelf` = the class, but that conforms to neither interface, is a compile error at that declaration naming the missing conformance (§15.4.1).

title: a record may not conform to a sequence-literal target interface
rule: A value kind — record, choice, or enum — may not conform to either sequence-literal target interface: the literal's result is a fresh owned heap value, and the §11.8 erasure of the member's `owned` return at a value kind does not make one a target (a compile error at the declaration) (§15.4.1).

title: a sequence literal targeting a class that is not a sequence-literal target is rejected
rule: A sequence literal in a context targeting a type that is not a sequence-literal target is the usual "cannot infer target type" / "no applicable target" compile error (§15.4.1).

title: the empty literal targeting a user sequence-literal target is admitted
rule: The empty literal `[]` targeting a sequence-literal target is admitted: the borrowing form receives an empty `ReadOnlyArraySpan<U>`, and the factory is responsible for handling the empty case (§15.4.1).

title: a user owning-form target receives the literal's elements as an owned OwningArray
rule: For a class that owns its elements the conformance is `IOwningCollectionLiteralTarget<C<T>, T>` and the witness is `FromCollectionLiteral(owned elements: OwningArray<T>): owned C<T>`; the compiler materializes a temporary owned `OwningArray<U>`, transfers each element into it in textual order, and transfers the array into the call (§15.4.1).

title: fixed extent uses Length while resizable extent uses Count
rule: One rule assigns the member name: fixed extent uses `.Length`; resizable uses `.Count` (§15.5).

title: range slicing an Array<T> produces a fresh owned array
rule: Range slicing `arr[a..b]` is supported on `Array<T>`; the produced array is owned by the caller (§15.6).

title: slicing is not admitted on OwningArray<T>
rule: Slicing is not admitted on `OwningArray<T>` — the copy-returning semantics would manufacture a second owner for each owned element (§15.6).

title: slicing is not supported on inline arrays
rule: Slicing is not supported on inline arrays in this version — the result type `[K]T` would need to encode its length, and K is not a compile-time constant here (§15.6).

title: an inclusive range includes its upper bound
rule: `a..b` is inclusive on both ends — iterating `1..10` yields 10 as its last value.

title: a half-open range excludes its upper bound
rule: `a..<b` is inclusive on the lower bound, exclusive on the upper — iterating `0..<10` yields 9, never 10, as its last value.

title: mixing bitwise AND with a range operand requires explicit parenthesization
rule: Range (`..`, `..<`) with bitwise (`&`, `|`, `^`) is a mandatory- parenthesization mix: "`mask & 0..n` is a compile error; write `(mask & 0)..n` to disambiguate." The rule is syntactic — it reads the operators' categories and whether an operand is parenthesized, never the operands' types.

title: parenthesizing the bitwise operand admits the bitwise-then-range mix
rule: The smallest legal edit of s16_1_0003 — grouping the bitwise operation inside its own parentheses ("write `(mask & 0)..n`") resolves the mandatory- parenthesization category mix and the expression type-checks as `int..int`.

title: a range may omit either endpoint, or both, to construct an open-ended range
rule: A range may omit one endpoint, producing an open-ended range used for slicing and pattern matching — the four forms `a..b`, `..b`, `a..`, `..` are all admitted range expressions.

title: open-ended range patterns match "less than" and "at or above" the written bound
rule: In a pattern, `..<0` matches 'any value less than 0' and `31..` matches 'any value at or above 31.'

title: a Range<double> is rejected — the element type is restricted to the integer types and char
rule: `T` is restricted by the compiler to the integer types (`byte`, `sbyte`, `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`) and `char`. Other substitutions are rejected — at the range expression or the `Range<T>` annotation... `float`, `double`, and `decimal` conform [to `ISteppable<T>`] and are not admitted.

title: a closed range's Start and End are non-null, and the default Step is 1
rule: `Start` and `End` are nullable; a `null` endpoint indicates the range is open-ended on that side. For closed ranges (both endpoints present), both are non-null. ... "The default step is 1."

title: a byte-typed step silently terminates iteration on overshoot of the endpoint or of the type's range
rule: a range like `0..10 step 256` over `T = byte` constructs without error, but the enumerator advances by 256 ... and the first computed value past the start is `256`, which exceeds the upper endpoint, so the iteration yields only the start value and terminates. ... "Iteration over `200..255 step 100` for `T = byte` similarly yields `200`; the next computed value (300) overflows `byte`'s range, so iteration terminates."

title: iteration over Range<char> steps across the surrogate gap
rule: Iteration steps across the gap: the successor of U+D7FF is U+E000 and the predecessor of U+E000 is U+D7FF... `'ퟰ'..'' step 4` yields U+D7F0, U+D7F4, U+D7F8, U+D7FC, then U+E000 (the fourth successor of U+D7FC), then U+E004, U+E008, U+E00C, U+E010. No surrogate is ever yielded.

title: Contains agrees with the direction of iteration, not with unordered-interval membership
rule: an iteration-empty range contains nothing: `50 in 100..0` is `false` (matching Rust and Python), while `(100..0 step -1).Contains(50)` is `true` (descending and nonempty).

title: a constant-folded zero step is rejected at the range expression
rule: A step of zero is rejected at construction: a literal (or constant- folded) step of zero is a compile error at the range expression.

title: a runtime-computed step of zero raises OverflowException at the range expression
rule: evaluating a range expression whose computed step is zero raises `OverflowException` at the expression.

title: step may not be applied to an open-ended range
rule: `step` may not be applied to open-ended ranges.

title: step is not legal in case patterns
rule: `step` is not legal in `case` patterns (patterns test the written bounds; stride has no meaning). Confirmed by the grammar: `RangePattern ::= PatternBound (".." | "..<") PatternBound` carries no step clause (Appendix A).

title: a constant range whose direction disagrees with its step's sign warns that iteration is empty
rule: When the compiler can prove at compile time that a range's direction and step sign disagree (both endpoints and step are constants or constant after folding), it emits a warning: 'this range produces an empty iteration.'

title: an open-ended range literal directly in a for statement warns it cannot be iterated
rule: The compiler emits a warning when an open-ended range literal appears in an iteration context — `for var i in 10.. do ... end;  // WARNING: open-ended range cannot be iterated`.

title: iterating an open-ended range stored in a variable raises InvalidOperationException at runtime
rule: For ranges stored in variables, the check is deferred to runtime: `var r: Range<int> := (if someCondition then 1..10 else 10..); for var i in r do ... end; // InvalidOperationException if r is open-ended`.

title: an inclusive equal-bounds range yields exactly one value, regardless of the step's sign
rule: An inclusive equal-bounds range (`5..5`, `5..5 step 1`, `5..5 step -1`) yields exactly one value — the bound itself. The step's sign does not matter; the iteration produces the start, the next computed value (start ± step) is past the inclusive end, and iteration terminates.

title: a half-open equal-bounds range is empty for any step
rule: A half-open equal-bounds range (`5..<5`, `5..<5 step n`) is empty for any step. The lower bound equals the upper bound and the upper bound is excluded, so no value is in range.

title: a range pattern rejects a nullable scrutinee
rule: a range pattern rejects a nullable scrutinee — keyed on the pattern's kind, the open-ended and fully open forms with the closed ones ... range membership is an ordering test, and ordering admits no absent participant.

title: a constant reversed range pattern warns that it never matches
rule: Because a constant reversed range pattern can never match, the compiler emits a warning at the pattern ('this pattern never matches — bounds are reversed').

title: v in r over a nullable v is rejected for every range test
rule: `v in r` over a nullable `v` is rejected alike [as the range-pattern case], both for one reason: range membership is an ordering test, and ordering admits no absent participant... so `n in 1..5` over an `int?` is rejected.

title: multiplicative operators bind tighter than additive operators
rule: Precedence table: Multiplicative (`*` `/` `mod`) is level 3, Additive (`+` `-`) is level 4 — the lower-numbered level binds tighter, so `*` groups before `+`.

title: unary not binds tighter than logical and
rule: Precedence table: Unary (`not`, prefix) is level 2, Logical AND (`and`) is level 13 — the lower-numbered level binds tighter, so `not a and b` parses as `(not a) and b`, not `not (a and b)`.

title: shift binds tighter than range — worked example
rule: `1<<2..1<<10` parses as `(1<<2)..(1<<10)` — Range looser than Shift.

title: range binds tighter than relational in — worked example
rule: `score in 60..100` parses as `score in (60..100)` — Range tighter than Relational.

title: null-coalescing binds tighter than logical or
rule: `??` binds tighter than `and`/`or`, so `a ?? b or c` parses as `(a ?? b) or c`.

title: bitwise AND mixed with equality without parentheses is rejected
rule: Bitwise (`&`, `|`, `^`) with equality (`=`, `<>`) or relational (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) is non-associative across categories and requires explicit parenthesization when mixed; `a & 1 = 0` is a compile error.

title: bitwise AND mixed with equality, parenthesized, is admitted
rule: write `(a & 1) = 0` — the mandatory-parenthesization rule applies only across the listed categories; parenthesizing the bitwise operand disambiguates and is admitted.

title: bitwise AND mixed with logical and without parentheses is rejected
rule: Bitwise with logical (`and`, `or`) is non-associative across categories; `flags & MASK and ready` is a compile error.

title: bitwise AND mixed with logical and, parenthesized, is admitted
rule: write `(flags & MASK) <> 0 and ready` — parenthesizing the bitwise subexpression, and comparing it to `0` to yield a `bool`, disambiguates and is admitted.

title: shift mixed with additive without parentheses is rejected
rule: Shift (`<<`, `>>`) with arithmetic (`+`, `-`) is non-associative across categories; `a << 2 + 1` is a compile error.

title: shift mixed with additive, parenthesized, is admitted
rule: write `a << (2 + 1)` or `(a << 2) + 1` — parenthesizing either subexpression disambiguates a shift-additive mix and is admitted.

title: range mixed with bitwise AND without parentheses is rejected
rule: Range (`..`, `..<`) with bitwise (`&`, `|`, `^`) is non-associative across categories; `mask & 0..n` is a compile error.

title: range mixed with bitwise AND, parenthesized on the bitwise operand, is admitted
rule: write `(mask & 0)..n` to disambiguate — a parenthesization restores a parse, and the result is then subject to the ordinary operand rules; `(mask & 0)..n` is the one shown grouping, `&` being defined on the integer types and `Range<T>` declaring no operators.

title: a class cannot overload the = operator
rule: `=` and `<>` invoke `Equals` with a null-safe wrapper. For classes, `=` cannot be overloaded; for records and enums, it can. §25.2: "`=` and `<>` may **not** be overloaded on classes ... For classes, `=` always invokes `Equals`."

title: a record may overload the = operator
rule: `=` and `<>` invoke `Equals` with a null-safe wrapper. For classes, `=` cannot be overloaded; for records and enums, it can.

title: inline-array equality uses default structural equality and cannot be overloaded
rule: For inline arrays, `=` cannot be overloaded (inline arrays are neither classes, records, nor enums, and the §26.2 extension rules forbid extending them); the default structural equality of §8.3 is used.

title: not is is rejected — is not is a single two-token operator
rule: `is not` is a single operator with two-token spelling — the parser does not accept `not is`.

title: is not is admitted as the two-token operator
rule: `is not` is a single operator with two-token spelling.

title: as on a value-type target produces a nullable result
rule: When the target type is a value type, `x as T` produces `T?` ... So `someObj as int` has type `int?`.

title: an inline-array as target is rejected
rule: An **inline-array target** (any form) is a compile error naming this rule: §15.1 admits no nullable inline-array form, so the operator's contract is unsatisfiable.

title: the unit type as target is rejected
rule: The **unit type** is likewise a compile error as an `as` target: `()` has exactly one value, so the operation could never carry more information than `x is ()`.

title: is and as are non-destructive — the operand keeps its ownership state
rule: `is`, `is not`, and `as` are non-destructive on their operand: ... after `if x is T then ... end` — and after `var r := x as T` — `x` retains whatever ownership state it had before the test.

title: in evaluates to Contains on an Array
rule: `x in collection` evaluates to `true` if `collection.Contains(x)` is true. `in` produces `bool`.

title: a nullable left operand over a range test is rejected
rule: This covers every range test: stdlib §9.8 declares `Contains(value: T)` over the non-nullable `T` ... so `n in 1..5` over an `int?` is rejected.

title: a nullable left operand is admitted where the selected Contains parameter is itself nullable
rule: Where the selected `Contains` parameter is itself nullable — `Array<int?>`'s `Contains(item: int?)` ... — a nullable left operand is admitted: the test performed is the null-safe equality of §8.4.

title: not x in c parses as (not x) in c and is rejected for a non-bool x
rule: Negated membership is written `not (x in c)` — the parentheses are required because unary `not` binds tighter than the relational `in` (§17.1), so `not x in c` parses as `(not x) in c`, a type error for a non-`bool` `x`.

title: the Contains lookup is structural — a user type's own Contains satisfies in
rule: The `Contains` lookup is structural rather than interface-based: any accessible method named `Contains` taking one parameter of compatible type and returning `bool` qualifies, whether it is an instance member or an extension method.

title: postfix ++ used as an expression is rejected
rule: `++` and `--` are postfix-only. They are statements, not expressions ... `x := y++` is a compile error.

title: postfix ++ as a statement increments the operand by one
rule: `var c := 5; c++; // c is 6`

title: prefix ++ is a parse error — there is no prefix form
rule: `++c` is a parse error. There is no prefix form.

title: a nullable operand to ++ is rejected
rule: An operand whose static type is a nullable type is a compile error: the desugared `x + 1` has no meaning on a nullable operand (§7.11) ... write `x := (x ?? 0) + 1;`, `x := x! + 1;`, or narrow first.

title: an indexer-slot ++ desugars to a read-modify-write through the indexer
rule: For an indexer slot `expr[i]` ... `expr[i]++` desugars to a read-modify-write through the indexer ... `__coll[__idx] := __coll[__idx] + 1;`.

title: operator ++ is not user-overloadable
rule: `++`/`--` are not user-overloadable (§25.1), so a type spells advancement as `x := x + 1` under its own `operator +`, or as a named method.

title: ++ on a read-only property is rejected
rule: The operand must be an assignable lvalue (a local variable, a parameter, a writable field, an indexer slot, or a property with a setter) ... Read-only locations cannot be incremented.

title: ++ on a property with a setter increments through the accessors
rule: The operand must be an assignable lvalue (a local variable, a parameter, a writable field, an indexer slot, or a property with a setter) ... `x++` is equivalent to `x := x + 1`.

title: ++ on a record that declares operator + is rejected
rule: On an operand of any other type the statement is a compile error on a separate ground: `++`/`--` are not user-overloadable (§25.1), so a type spells advancement as `x := x + 1` under its own `operator +`, or as a named method.

title: ++ on a char target applies the code-point rules of the conversion
rule: For a `char` target the §5.2 code-point rules apply (`c++` is `c := char(c + 1)`).

title: ++ past a narrow integer target's range raises OverflowException
rule: `x++` is equivalent to `x := x + 1` ... under exactly §6.6's rules: the same overflow semantics as `+` and `-` (§6.1), §6.6's checked narrowing for a narrow integer target.

title: an indexer-slot ++ calls the getter once and the setter once
rule: Implementations may not deduplicate the getter+setter pair: every `arr[i]++` performs one logical read followed by one logical write through the indexer.

title: new on a class produces an owned reference, undischarged draws the must-use warning
rule: `new T(args)` constructs an instance of T. For classes, `new` produces an owned reference (§28). §28.3 K3.14: "the implicit drop of a plain-`var` local ... carries the must-use warning". The class declares a destructor so it is not trivial-dispose (§28.9), whose ceremony exemption would otherwise free it silently with no warning.

title: new is rejected on an inline array
rule: `new [3]int(0, 1, 2)` is rejected by the type checker — inline arrays do not declare constructors, and the `new` syntax has no meaning on them.

title: the new() shorthand is admitted at a typed field initializer
rule: A field initializer or typed local declaration may use the `new()` shorthand when the type is unambiguous: `private owned _items: Array<int> := new();`

title: the new() shorthand is admitted at a return statement under a declared return type
rule: The shorthand is permitted at the written-declared-type positions ... and the `return e;` statement of (v) above: field initializers, typed local-variable declarations, default parameter values, and return statements (when the method has a declared return type).

title: the new() shorthand is not admitted at an expression body
rule: It is **not** permitted at an expression body (`=> new()`) or at a lambda's ascribed return.

title: Guid declares no constructor and admits no new Guid(...)
rule: A builtin declaring **no** constructor — `Guid` ... — admits no `new T(...)` at any argument list; the diagnostic names the declared producers — for `Guid`: `Guid.Empty`, `Guid.NewGuid()`, or `default(Guid)`.

title: a builtin positional-only record rejects the undeclared new T()
rule: For a builtin record whose only declared constructor is its positional primary constructor (`ExceptionInfo` ...), the undeclared parameterless form `new T()` is rejected the same way — exactly as for an identically-shaped user record.

title: x! asserts non-null and yields the non-nullable form of the type
rule: `x!` asserts that `x` is non-null. The result type is the non-nullable form of the expression's type.

title: there is no prefix ! operator — boolean negation is not
rule: `!` is the only postfix `!` operator. There is no prefix `!`; boolean negation is `not`.

title: null-forgiving preserves ownership — a borrow stays a borrow
rule: The null-forgiving operator preserves ownership: ... if `x` is borrowed, `x!` is borrowed with the same source. The operator is purely a type-system assertion (with a runtime null check); it does not move, copy, or borrow beyond what reading `x` already does.

title: nameof of a local returns its source-level identifier
rule: `nameof(expr)` returns the source-level name of an identifier as a compile-time `string` constant. Example: `nameof(amount) // "amount"`.

title: nameof of a dotted expression returns the rightmost identifier
rule: For a dotted expression, the result is the rightmost identifier. Example: `nameof(BankAccount.Deposit) // "Deposit"`.

title: nameof of a method call is a compile error
rule: Method calls, indexings, arithmetic, and literals are compile errors: `nameof(Foo())`, `nameof(a + b)`, `nameof(arr[0])`, `nameof(42)`.

title: typeof of a user type returns its Type value with Name and FullName
rule: `typeof(TypeName)` returns the `Type` value for a statically named type: `var t: Type := typeof(BankAccount); Console.WriteLine(t.Name); // \BankAccount\"`."

title: typeof(int?) is rejected — nullable forms are not accepted
rule: Nullable forms are not accepted (`typeof(int?)` is a compile error).

title: typeof(this) is a compile error
rule: `typeof(this)` and `typeof(base)` are compile errors. `this` and `base` are values, not type names. To obtain the runtime type of the receiver, use `this.GetType()`.

title: typeof does not accept a variable or a literal
rule: `typeof` does not accept variables, method names, or literals — those are compile errors. For the runtime type of a *value*, use `value.GetType()`.

title: default(int) is the numeric zero value
rule: `default(T)` produces the zero value of type T ... Numeric types: `0`, `0.0`, `0m`, etc.

title: default of a nullable reference type is null
rule: Reference types: `null` if the location is nullable.

title: default of an enum with a zero-valued constant is that constant
rule: Enums: the value with underlying integer 0 — necessarily a declared constant, per the compile error below.

title: default of an inline array fills every slot with the element's zero value
rule: Inline arrays whose element type is defaultable ... `default([3]int)` is `[0, 0, 0]`.

title: default of a non-nullable reference type is rejected
rule: `default(T)` is a compile error for the non-defaultable types: ... A non-nullable reference type.

title: default of an enum with no zero-valued constant is rejected
rule: An enum type with no declared constant of underlying value 0. Every producer of an enum value yields a declared value, and `default` is no exception: for such an enum, `default(E)` ... [is] rejected.

title: default of a constructor-only record is rejected
rule: A **constructor-only** record (§9.9) — a record declaring a constructor carrying a contract clause. Every value of such a record is produced by a call to one of its declared constructors, and `default(T)` calls none.

title: default of a choice type is rejected
rule: **Choices: no choice type is defaultable — `default(C)` is a compile error for every choice type** — a sum yields no distinguished zero case, and electing one would make program meaning depend on declaration order.

title: default(T) under where T: class is rejected
rule: Under `where T: class` (or any type-bound constraint that implies non-null T per §14.2), `default(T)` is a compile error — the constraint guarantees T is non-nullable, and the null value `default(T)` would produce does not fit T's contract.

title: default of bool is false
rule: `default(T)` produces the zero value of type T ... `bool`: `false`.

title: default of a positional record sets every field to its zero value
rule: Records all of whose declared fields are defaultable and which are not constructor-only: the record value with each field at its zero value. For positional records, the positional fields are considered.

title: default of a record with a non-nullable reference field is rejected
rule: `default(T)` is a compile error for the non-defaultable types: ... A record any of whose declared fields is not defaultable — a non-nullable reference type, a choice, an enum with no zero-valued constant, or (recursively) a record or inline array with a non-defaultable component.

title: default of a record whose reference field is nullable yields null in that field
rule: Records all of whose declared fields are defaultable ... the record value with each field at its zero value ... Reference types: `null` if the location is nullable.

title: default of an inline array with a non-defaultable element type is rejected
