rule: An inline array whose element type is not defaultable. `default([3]Connection)` (non-nullable Connection elements) is a compile error; the user must supply explicit initializers.

title: a computed property does not affect a record's default eligibility
rule: Expression-bodied (computed) properties have no backing storage and do not affect `default` eligibility.

title: throw expr is valid in any expression position — a case arm
rule: `throw expr` raises the supplied exception ... Valid in any expression position. Worked example: an indexer's `case` arm ending `_ => throw new IndexOutOfRangeException()`.

title: bare throw re-raises the currently-handled exception
rule: `throw` (no operand) re-raises the currently-handled exception with its stack trace preserved. Valid only as an expression appearing inside a catch arm body.

title: bare throw outside a catch arm body is a compile error
rule: Bare `throw` outside a catch arm body is a compile error, with the same diagnostic as the statement form `throw;` outside a catch context.

title: throw has the bottom type — assignable to any expected type
rule: Both forms have the bottom type — assignable to any expected type — because control transfers to the matching handler before any value is produced.

title: out _ discards the out-parameter result
rule: As a positional argument with the `out` modifier, `_` discards the out-parameter result ... `if dict.TryGetValue(key, out _) then ...`

title: ref _ is a compile error
rule: The discard composes with `out` only: **`ref _` is a compile error** — a `ref` argument reads its operand, which a discard cannot supply; pass a named location.

title: out var _ is a compile error
rule: `out var _` is likewise a compile error — it would declare nothing; write `out _`, which already means exactly this.

title: an owned discard result is disposed at the end of the discard statement
rule: An owned result is disposed at the end of the discard statement... `_ := expression;` evaluates `expression` and discharges the disposal obligation once the statement completes.

title: a discard of a named owned binding leaves it explicitly-disposed — a later straight-line read warns
rule: `_ := x;` where `x` is a named owned binding is a marker-free consume ... `x` is thereafter treated exactly as explicitly disposed — the scope-end pass skips it; a later read falls under the use-after-dispose regime of §28.2.

title: a read after a conditionally-discarded binding is a compile error at the merge
rule: `_ := x;` ... `x` is thereafter treated exactly as explicitly disposed ... and a join with a still-owned path yields maybe-consumed. §28.2: "at a join of an explicitly-disposed path with a still-owned path the variable is **maybe-consumed** and a later use is a compile error."

title: a Task-family result may not be discarded with _ :=
rule: **Exception: a `Task`-family result may not be discarded.** ... The discard is a compile error ... Use `Task.FireAndForget(expression)` for supervised fire-and-forget, or a named `using var t := expression;`.

title: the anonymous owning binding using var _ is rejected over a Task-family value
rule: so is the anonymous binding `using var _ := expression;` (and `await using var _ := ...;`, below) over a `Task`-family value: nothing can await an unnamed binding, so it is the same abandonment one scope later.

title: a lambda parameter _ is a true ignore — several may coexist
rule: a **lambda parameter** ... the ignored slot still contributes to the function type, and because nothing is named several ignores may coexist (`lambda(_, _) => 0` is legal).

title: a for-loop variable _ iterates for effects with the element unbound
rule: a **`for` loop variable** — `for var _ in xs do ... end;` iterates for effects with the element unbound, §29.2's semantics unchanged.

title: var _ := e; is rejected — _ is a discard, not a declarable name
rule: `var _ := e;` and `const _ := e;` (`_` is a discard, not a declarable name — the diagnostic names both remedies, `_ := e;` for end-of-statement release or `using var _ := e;` for the anonymous scope-end hold).

title: a Task?-typed result may not be discarded with _ := (nullable twin of 0008)
rule: **The keying strips nullability** (v0.302), exactly as the [announcement table]'s Keying rule does for its own rows: a `Task?`, `Task<T>?` or `OwningTask<T>?` operand is a `Task`-family value here, and discarding it is the same compile error.

title: an undiscarded int-returning call draws the unused-result warning
rule: In every permitted form the discard also suppresses the §21.9 unused result warning **where the undiscarded expression statement would draw one**.

title: the discard statement suppresses the unused-result warning on a value result
rule: In every permitted form the discard also suppresses the §21.9 unused result warning ... `_ := ComputeChecksum();` — int: cosmetic — suppresses the unused-result warning.

title: discarding an owned result is a permitted form and draws no diagnostic
rule: An owned result is disposed at the end of the discard statement ... the explicit "I want this owned result disposed now" form, useful when an `owned`-returning method's result is not needed.

title: the anonymous owning binding is a permitted form and draws no diagnostic
rule: `using var _ := expression;` is the one `_` form that owns storage — it binds the value to an unnamed scope-bound local, with scope-end disposal and every other §28.10 rule of a named `using var`.

title: discarding a borrowed local is purely cosmetic and draws no diagnostic
rule: A discard whose operand is in **borrow state** disposes nothing: the discard is purely cosmetic (it silences the §21.9 unused-result warning where one would fire), and the value's owner keeps the obligation.

title: constant integer arithmetic over a primitive-wrapper constant folds
rule: `const H := int.MaxValue / 2;` // 1073741823 : int — a reference to a compiler-provided constant of a primitive wrapper type, combined with the constant binary arithmetic operators, is a constant expression.

title: a constant if expression with constant condition and branches folds
rule: the `if` expression `(if c then a else b)` whose condition and both branches are constant expressions [is a constant expression] ... `const Cap := (if Flags > 0 then 64 else 32);`

title: integer overflow at a constant expression is a compile error at the declaration
rule: An evaluation **fault** — integer or `decimal` overflow, division or `mod` by zero, a shift count outside the §6.5 domain — is a **compile error at the constant expression**, never a deferred runtime fault: `const B := 2147483647 + 1;` ... are rejected where they are written.

title: division by zero at a constant expression is a compile error at the declaration
rule: An evaluation fault ... division or `mod` by zero ... is a compile error at the constant expression, never a deferred runtime fault: ... `const D := 5 / 0;` ... rejected where they are written.

title: a shift count outside the domain at a constant expression is a compile error at the declaration
rule: a shift count outside the §6.5 domain — is a compile error at the constant expression ... `const F := 1 << 64;` ... rejected where they are written.

title: an interpolated string is not a constant expression
rule: Nothing else is constant. In particular: ... interpolated strings ... are not constant expressions. `const S := $\v{H}\";` [is a] compile error: interpolated strings are not constant." The constant-expression initializer condition "remain[s] mandatory for class-level and `static const` declarations" — at a *local* `const` a non-constant initializer is a runtime const instead (s17_14_0010).

title: default(T) is not a constant expression — rejected as a class-level const initializer
rule: Nothing else is constant. In particular: ... `default(T)` ... (declined-liftable ...) ... are not constant expressions. The type restriction on `const` — a constant-expression initializer — "remain[s] mandatory for class-level and `static const` declarations."

title: a local const with a non-constant-expression initializer is a runtime const, not an error
rule: A *local* `const` failing either condition is a **runtime const** rather than an error; a reference to a local `const` is a constant expression only when the declaration is compile-time-classified.

title: the binding atom binds a name and evaluates the body against it
rule: `(var name := initializer; body)` ... the body is one full expression, and the atom's value, type, and ownership classification are the body's. Worked example: `var area := (var w := bounds.Width(); w * w);`

title: multiple clauses chain, each terminated by ;
rule: `(var a := E1; var b := E2; body)` ... at least one clause is required; clauses chain.

title: a clause's own initializer does not see the binding it introduces
rule: A binding is in scope from the end of its own clause ... its own initializer does not [see it].

title: a borrow sourced from an atom binding may not escape the atom
rule: A borrow whose source is an atom binding may not escape the atom — in the body's value or any other holder — per K8.4: rejected, never lifetime-extended; bind at statement level (`using var`) when the value must outlive the expression.

title: an owned production undischarged in the atom is disposed at the atom boundary
rule: an owned production makes its binding a **named unbound owned temporary whose boundary is the atom itself**: if still undischarged when the atom completes, it is disposed there ... after the body's evaluation ... with no must-use warning.

title: the binding atom is admitted inside a contract clause
rule: In contract clauses (§22.16) the atom is admitted — it is the form's motivating position: clauses are expression-only and pure, so without the atom a clause using a subresult twice would have to recompute it.

title: digit separators are ignored and integer suffixes are case-insensitive
rule: `1_234_567` // digit separators allowed except at start/end and "Suffixes are case-insensitive: `L`/`l`, `U`/`u`, `F`/`f`, `M`/`m`."

title: an untyped integer literal that exceeds int's range without an L suffix is rejected
rule: The compiler does not silently promote integer literals: in an untyped context `3_000_000_000` is a compile error without an `L` suffix.

title: a suffix-less over-int literal is admitted at a written integer target whose range contains it
rule: The smallest legal edit of s18_1_0002 — ascribing the target type — is admitted: "(At a written integer target whose range contains it the literal is admitted at the target type — §4.2's target-typed integer constant.)"

title: the boolean literal true renders as the four-character text True
rule: `true`, `false`, `null`. are the boolean and null literals; the boolean's rendering is `bool.ToString()`, normative in stdlib §9.4: "public pure method ToString(): string; // 'True' or 'False'".

title: a full-code-point char escape resolves to its numeric code point
rule: `'\U0001F600'` // 8 hex digits, full code point range is an admitted char literal form; converting it to `int` yields the code point's decimal value (stdlib: "`I(c)` for `char` `c` ... converts the code-point value").

title: a char escape resolving to a surrogate code point is a compile error
rule: Escape sequences resolving to U+D800–U+DFFF are compile errors.

title: a non-verbatim string literal processes its escape sequences
rule: \Line 1\\nLine 2\"      // escapes processed"

title: a null interpolation hole renders the four characters null
rule: An interpolation hole renders `ToString()`; a null hole renders the four characters `null`.

title: a format spec on a double dispatches to ToString(format) with exact fixed-point rendering
the P1 format spec renders a percentage with one decimal
the X format spec renders an integer in uppercase hex
positive alignment right-aligns and negative alignment left-aligns in a field of the given width
rule: Alignment is an integer, optionally negated; positive right-aligns in a field of that width, negative left-aligns. Example: "`$\"|{name,20}|\"` // right-aligned in 20-character field".

title: alignment and a format spec compose as {expression,alignment:format}
rule: `{expression,alignment:format}` with example "`$\"{amount,12:F2}\"`" — the F2-formatted "1234.50" (7 characters) right-aligned in a 12-character field pads with 5 leading spaces.

title: a hole without a format spec dispatches to the value's ordinary ToString()
rule: A hole without a format spec formats via the value's ordinary `ToString()` (§8.5).

title: a format spec dispatches to ToString(format); a user type opts in via IFormattable
rule: A hole with a format spec dispatches to `ToString(format: string)`: ... a user type opts in by implementing the auto-imported interface `IFormattable`.

title: a format spec on a non-formattable, non-IFormattable operand is a compile error
rule: A format spec on an operand whose type is neither intrinsically formattable nor `IFormattable` is a compile error naming this rule.

title: a null nullable hole with a format spec renders the padded text null, without invoking the spec
rule: When the value is `null` at render time, the hole renders as the four-character text `null` ... A format spec on a nullable-typed hole is checked at compile time against the non-nullable form ... and the spec is simply not invoked when the value is null. The alignment applies to the rendered text `null` exactly as to any other rendered text. Worked example: `var x: double? := null; Console.WriteLine($"[{x,8:F2}]"); // prints: [    null]`.

title: a present nullable hole with a format spec dispatches ordinarily
rule: Continuing s18_5_0010's worked example: "`x := 3.0; Console.WriteLine($ \"[{x,8:F2}]\"); // prints: [    3.00] — present value: ordinary dispatch`."

title: an indexer inside a hole needs no parenthesization before a format spec
rule: the alignment `,` and the format-spec `:` are recognized only at the top nesting level of the hole ... Consequently `{d[k]:F2}` needs no parenthesization tricks (`[…]` nests its colon).

title: an unescaped closing brace that does not close a hole is a compile error
rule: An unescaped `}` that does not close a hole is a compile error; write `}}` for a literal closing brace.

title: a doubled brace in an interpolated string renders as a single literal brace
rule: In interpolated strings ... a doubled brace denotes a literal brace: `{{` produces `{`, `}}` produces `}`.

title: an unrecognized format specifier raises FormatException at runtime
rule: An unrecognized specifier at runtime raises `FormatException` (the defined-fault rule, stdlib §2.18).

title: a verbatim string suppresses escape processing — backslashes are literal
rule: A `@` prefix suppresses escape processing. Example: `var path := @"C:\Users\Bezel\Program.bzl";` — the backslashes are literal characters, not escape introducers.

title: a doubled quote inside a verbatim string produces a single embedded quote
rule: Inside a verbatim string, `\\"` produces a single `\"`."

title: an interpolated verbatim string combines suppressed escapes with interpolation holes
rule: `$@` combines both — escape suppression and interpolation. Example: `var documentPath := $@"C:\Users\{user}\Documents\report.pdf";` renders the backslashes literally and substitutes the hole.

title: the \x escape greedily consumes up to 4 hex digits as a single code point
rule: The `\\x` escape greedily consumes the maximum number of valid hexadecimal digits, up to 4. In the string `\\\x41BC\"`, the escape is `\\x41BC` (U+41BC), not `\\x41` followed by `BC`."

title: concatenation is the remedy to write a two-digit hex escape followed by literal characters
rule: To produce the two-digit escape `\\x41` followed by the literal characters `BC`, use concatenation (`\\\x41\" + \"BC\"`) or the `\\u` form."

title: a \u escape resolving to a surrogate code point in a string literal is a compile error
rule: Surrogate escapes (U+D800–U+DFFF) are compile errors. (distinct from s18_3_0002's char-literal instance of the same rule: here the escape occurs inside a string literal.)

title: a case with no scrutinee expression is a syntax error
rule: `case` always takes a scrutinee; a `case` written with no scrutinee expression is a syntax error — a ladder of conditions is an if/elif chain instead.

title: a case with no of delimiter is a syntax error
rule: The keyword `of` terminates the scrutinee and introduces the arms. A missing `of` is a syntax error at the first arm token; the diagnostic names the delimiter.

title: return inside an arm exits the enclosing callable, not the arm
rule: `return` inside an arm exits the enclosing callable, not the arm. `case` cannot be exited "early" via `return`; restructure into helper methods.

title: an arm result may not mark the scrutinee's own binding
rule: An arm result marking the scrutinee's own binding is always rejected by the consume-site freeze — the scrutinee borrow is live through the selected arm's completion.

title: a binding may not appear inside an alternative pattern list
rule: In an alternative list, every member must be binding-free — a constant, a payload-free choice case, a range, or a relational pattern — so a binding (`var c`) cannot appear inside an alternative list.

title: a binding-free alternative list matches any listed member
rule: `2 | 3 | 4 | 5` matches any of these — every member of an alternative list must be binding-free: a constant, a payload-free choice case, a range, or a relational pattern.

title: a relational pattern over a nullable scrutinee is rejected
rule: A nullable scrutinee — value or reference — is a compile error at a relational pattern: ordering admits no absent participant, and pattern position performs no narrowing.

title: a range pattern over a nullable scrutinee is rejected
rule: The nullable-scrutinee rejection at a relational pattern applies alike at a range pattern; the rejection is keyed on the kind of pattern, not on which bounds are written.

title: a relational pattern admits only the four ordering operators
rule: A relational pattern is `> 70`, `< 50`, `<= 100`, `>= 0` — these four operators only.

title: a destructuring slot list may not mix positional and named slots
rule: A slot list is either positional or named, never mixed in one pattern; mixing is a compile error naming the rule.

title: a named destructuring slot interrogates the member by name
rule: A named slot is `Identifier "=" Pattern`; the `=` is the interrogation reading of §8.4, not an assignment — "is `Width` 3?" — and a slot list may be written entirely by name.

title: range, relational, and constant patterns select by value in order
rule: A leading `-` on a numeric literal is part of the constant pattern; ranges are inclusive (`90..100`) or exclusive (`0..<60`), open-ended (`31..`, `..<0`), or fully open (`..`); a relational pattern compares under the scrutinee's ordering; arms are tried in textual order and the first match wins.

title: an unbound type pattern subtype-matches a reference-typed scrutinee
rule: Type patterns without binding — `string`, `int`, `Dog` — subtype match: a `Dog` value matches an `Animal` pattern. Subtype matching is a property of reference-typed scrutinees.

title: individual positions of a positional destructure may be discarded
rule: The type name followed by parenthesized bindings matches the type and binds positional fields by position; individual positions may be discarded with `_` — `Point(_, y)`.

title: an unconstrained var pattern matches any value and binds it
rule: **Var patterns:** `var t`. Matches any value, binds it.

title: a discard used as a top-level catch-all arm must be last
rule: When used as a top-level pattern (a catch-all arm), `_` must be the last arm; placing it earlier is a compile error.

title: a discard as the last arm is the idiomatic catch-all
rule: `_` is the idiomatic spelling of an arm that matches everything; when used as a top-level pattern it must be the last arm.

title: classes have no positional-destructuring surface
rule: Classes do not have a positional-destructuring surface, even when they declare a primary constructor: primary-constructor parameters are not auto-promoted to public properties, and the positional shape is not part of the class's pattern-match surface.

title: an unknown name in a named slot is a compile error
rule: An unknown name, a duplicate name in one slot list, a write-only property, an indexer, a static member, or a record method or non-public explicit field is a compile error at the pattern, each naming its rule.

title: arms are tried in order and the first true guard wins
rule: Arms are evaluated in textual order. The first arm whose pattern matches and whose guard is true is selected.

title: a typed binding pattern matches only non-null values
rule: A bare type pattern `T` matches only non-null values. A typed binding pattern `var n: T` also matches only non-null values — `null` is matched only by the explicit `null` pattern, an untyped `var x` pattern, or `_`.

title: a non-exhaustive expression-position case draws the exhaustiveness warning
rule: In expression position, an unmatched value raises `MatchFailureException` at runtime; the compiler warns when it cannot prove exhaustiveness statically.

title: an unmatched statement-position case with no wildcard falls through
rule: A `case` with no `_` arm is permitted. In statement position, an unmatched value falls through with no action.

title: an unmatched expression-position case raises MatchFailureException
rule: In expression position, an unmatched value raises `MatchFailureException` at runtime.

title: an enum case covering every declared constant needs no wildcard
rule: **Enum scrutinee:** every declared constant has a matching pattern — a constant pattern naming it directly, a var binding, or `_`. A statically exhaustive enum case cannot raise MatchFailureException.

title: a choice case covering every declared case needs no wildcard
rule: **Choice scrutinee:** every declared case is covered by an unguarded arm — a payload-free case by a constant-style pattern; a payload-carrying case by a positional destructuring pattern whose every slot is irrefutable. When every case is covered, no `_` arm is required.

title: a generic closed hierarchy's leaf coverage is not attempted
rule: When the closed hierarchy's root or any leaf is generic, leaf coverage is not attempted; such a case is completable only by an irrefutable arm and draws the non-exhaustiveness warning without one.

title: a wildcard arm that is not the last arm is rejected
rule: If `_` appears, it must be the last arm; placing it earlier is a compile error.

title: a wildcard arm placed last is admitted and selected only when no arm matches
rule: If `_` appears, it must be the last arm. Arms are evaluated in textual order; the first arm whose pattern matches is selected, and an unguarded `_` is the irrefutable arm that makes the match statically exhaustive.

title: a case whose every arm is guarded is never statically exhaustive
rule: An arm carrying a `when` guard contributes nothing to static exhaustiveness. A match whose every arm is guarded is therefore never statically exhaustive — in expression position it draws the warning and raises `MatchFailureException` if every guard declines at run time.

title: an all-slots-irrefutable destructure of a record scrutinee needs no wildcard
rule: Record scrutinee: the scrutinee's static type is a non-nullable record type and some unguarded arm matches every value of it — a positional destructuring pattern whose head names that type and every of whose slots is irrefutable. No `_` arm is required.

title: a refutable slot makes a record-destructure arm contribute nothing
rule: Coverage is one level deep with no per-slot value-space analysis — a refutable slot (a constant, `null`, range, relational, alternative list, type test, or nested destructuring) makes the arm contribute nothing; the compiler warns when it cannot prove exhaustiveness statically.

title: a total positional destructure over a non-nullable record needs no wildcard arm
rule: **Record scrutinee:** the scrutinee's static type is a non-nullable record type and some unguarded arm matches every value of it — a positional or named destructuring pattern whose head names that type and every of whose slots is irrefutable. A record has exactly one shape and is implicitly sealed, so covering that shape covers every value; no `_` arm is required.

title: an exact-type pattern over a non-nullable record scrutinee is itself total
rule: A `case` over a non-nullable record scrutinee is statically exhaustive with no `_` arm when some unguarded arm is a type pattern naming that exact type — §19.3: over a non-nullable value scrutinee a type pattern naming its exact type always matches.

title: a refutable slot leaves a record case non-exhaustive
rule: Record-scrutinee coverage is one level deep with **no per-slot value-space analysis** — a refutable slot (a constant, `null`, range, relational, alternative list, type test, or nested destructuring) makes the arm contribute nothing, exactly as a refutable choice-case slot does; the compiler then warns that it cannot prove exhaustiveness.

title: a statement-position case is closed with end case not end switch
rule: In statement position `case` is an end-terminated statement (`case … of … end case?;`); `end switch;` is a near-miss the closer rejects.

title: an expression-position case atom composes inside an interpolation hole
rule: The atom is self-delimited and composes inside any expression position, including inside string interpolations; it opens with `(case` and its closing parenthesis is the terminator — there is no `end`.

title: a case arm's do block closes with a bare end and no semicolon
rule: A `case` arm `do … end` block closes with a bare `end`, taking no `;` of its own — the arm is followed by the `,` separator (or nothing, if last), not a statement terminator.

title: a statement-position case closes correctly with end case
rule: In statement position `case` is an `end`-terminated statement: `case … of … end case;`.

title: an enum-typed scrutinee omits the enum prefix in patterns
rule: When the scrutinee has an enum type, the enum prefix may be omitted in patterns.

title: the if expression selects the branch of the first true condition
rule: The `if` expression selects between values, condition-first — example `var max := (if a > b then a else b);`.

title: an elif chain performs multi-way selection, stopping at the first true condition
rule: Multi-way selection chains with `elif`, in the statement form's word order — the spec's own grade example: score 85 selects the "B" branch.

title: the else branch of an if expression is mandatory
rule: the `else` branch is mandatory (an expression produces a value on every path).

title: only the selected branch is evaluated — an unselected throw branch's operand never runs
rule: each condition and branch is a full expression with no precedence restriction — in particular, a `throw` branch is admitted in any branch position together with "only the selected branch is evaluated." Since the `then` branch is selected here, the `else` branch's `new Probe()` — whose constructor is observable — never executes.

title: a selected throw branch propagates its exception out of the if expression
rule: a `throw` branch is admitted in any branch position and "the first `true` condition selects its branch, the `else` branch is selected when none holds" — here the condition is false, so the `throw` branch is selected and its exception propagates.

title: branches of a subclass and its base class compute a common type of the base class
rule: **The common type:** the common type of branch types A and B is whichever of the two the other implicitly converts into ... a subtype into its base class or implemented interface (a §5.1 reference conversion).

title: sibling classes with no reciprocal conversion have no common type — no LUB search
rule: If neither converts into the other, the expression is a compile error directing to an explicit conversion or upcast — there is no sibling-class least-upper-bound search. The smallest legal edit of s20_0006 — replacing the `Animal` branch with the sibling class `Cat` — loses the common type.

title: a bare null branch target-types to the nullable form of the other branch's type
rule: **Bare `null`.** A bare `null` branch likewise imposes no constraint of its own: it target-types to the nullable form of the other branches' common type.

title: an all-null arm set has no type and is a compile error
rule: an all-`null` arm set has no type and is a compile error.

title: a branch needing target-typing from context, like a collection literal, is rejected in an if
rule: **No branch-level target-typing** beyond the bare-`null` rule: a branch whose form requires a target type from context — a collection literal (§15.4) ... — is a compile error inside an `if` expression even when the whole expression occupies a target-typed position.

title: a bare case construction inside an if branch resolves ordinarily, not as case construction
rule: not to subexpression positions within a return operand — in `return (if c then Ok(v) else Error(e));` the branches are operands of the `(if …)` atom (§20) and resolve ordinarily; write two `return` statements, or the qualified form.

title: elif conditions are evaluated in textual order and only up to the first true one
rule: **Evaluation.** Conditions are evaluated in textual order; the first `true` condition selects its branch ... and only the selected branch is evaluated. The second condition is true, so the third is never evaluated.

title: mixing an owned (moved) arm with a borrowed arm is rejected
rule: **Ownership.** When the branches are class-typed, the expression's ownership is the arm-meet of §28.3's producers table: owned arms meet to owned, borrowed arms to borrowed with unioned source constraints, mixed arms are rejected; an unmarked read of a named owned binding written as a branch is a borrow arm, and the marked branch `move x` ... transfers.

title: two marked-move arms both meet to an owned result
rule: The smallest legal edit of s20_0013 — marking the second arm `move b` as well — makes both arms owned: "owned arms meet to owned ... the marked branch `move x` — `x` a local binding or `owned` parameter — transfers."

title: a defaultable local declared without an initializer holds that type's default
rule: A local of non-defaultable type must be assigned before it is read; a local of defaultable type declared without an initializer holds that type's default from its declaration — `var balance: decimal;` is `0m`.

title: a local cannot be named the discard
rule: A local cannot be named `_` — the bare underscore is the reserved discard token. `var _ := e;` is a compile error whose diagnostic names both sanctioned spellings.

title: a runtime const local may not be initialized from an owned production
rule: The initializer of a runtime `const` must not be an owned production — rejected, with a diagnostic naming this rule and the `using var` remedy: a fresh `new`.

title: an if condition must be bool
rule: The condition must be `bool`.

title: for over an inline array is a direct indexed loop over value copies
rule: `for` iterates any iterable source, including inline arrays `[N]T`, which support direct indexed iteration through a compiler intrinsic.

title: for over a range iterates its integer values in order
rule: `for` iterates any iterable source... and `Range<T>` values (which the compiler may optimize into counted loops).

title: a type ascription on the ignore for-loop variable is rejected
rule: A type ascription on the ignore is rejected (`for var _: T in …` — a bare ignore takes its type from context, never an annotation).

title: the loop variable is freshly bound each iteration
rule: The loop variable is freshly bound on each iteration; assigning to the loop variable inside the body affects only that iteration — it does not alter how many iterations run, nor the next iteration's value.

title: a labeled break exits the named enclosing loop from a nested loop
rule: `break name;` exits the enclosing loop labeled `name`. After `break name;`, execution continues at the first statement after the labeled loop.

title: a labeled loop rejects the keyword closer
rule: Because the construct now has a name, the introducing-keyword closer (`end for;`, `end while;`) applies only to unlabeled loops — once labeled, the keyword closer is rejected.

title: a labeled loop closes with its label or a bare end
rule: A labeled loop's `end` may repeat the loop label (`end scan;`), and bare `end;` remains valid everywhere.

title: a break inside a finally may not target a loop enclosing the finally
rule: Inside a `finally`, a `break` or `continue` — labeled or unlabeled — whose target loop lies outside the `finally` is a compile error.

title: a break targeting a loop wholly inside the finally is admitted
rule: Loops wholly inside the `finally`, and jumps among them, are unaffected by the finally/loop-jump restriction.

title: a local declared inside a do end block is out of scope after it ends
rule: Locals declared in a block are visible only until the matching `end`.

title: a method with a return type must return on every exit path
rule: A method or accessor with a return type must `return expression;` on every exit path.

title: a method with no return type uses return to exit early
rule: A method or accessor with no return type uses `return;` to exit early; falling off the end is implicit.

title: an exhaustive statement-case whose every arm exits grants totality
rule: A statement-position `case` counts as exiting on every path — so a callable may end with it, with no trailing `return` — when the match is proven statically exhaustive and every arm's body itself exits on every path.

title: return inside a finally block is a compile error
rule: `return` inside a `finally` block is a compile error.

title: a total record statement-case grants totality with no trailing return
rule: The statement-`case` totality grant is keyed to §19.6's closed-value-space registry, and that registry now carries the **record** bullet: a statement-`case` over a non-nullable record scrutinee whose unguarded arm is an all-slots-irrefutable destructure satisfies condition (i), so a callable may end with it and needs no trailing `return`.

title: throw expression as a statement raises and is caught
rule: `throw expression;` and the bare re-raise `throw;` are the statement spellings of the `throw` expression, equivalent to the expression form followed by `;`.

title: a bare re-raise outside a catch arm is a compile error
rule: The bare re-raise is valid only inside a catch arm body. Bare `throw` (either form) outside a catch arm body is a compile error.

title: a discarded non-unit expression statement result draws a warning
rule: An expression statement whose result is a non-`()` type is permitted but the compiler emits a warning: the result is silently discarded, which may indicate a bug.

title: the discard statement suppresses the unused-result warning
rule: To suppress the warning, use the discard form `_ := expression;`.

title: a bare Task-family statement result is a hard error, not a warning
rule: For `Task`, the warning is replaced by a hard error directing the caller to the discard `_ := expression;`, `using var _ := expression;`, an explicit `.Dispose()`, or `Task.FireAndForget` as appropriate.

title: a discarded string-returning call on a fluent receiver draws the unused-result warning
rule: An expression statement whose result is a non-`()` type is permitted but the compiler emits a warning: the result is silently discarded, which may indicate a bug.

title: the fluent-receiver discard draws no unused-result warning
rule: One exemption: the fluent-receiver discard. A discarded method-call result draws no warning when it is a §28.3 borrow whose source set lies within the statement's receiver chain and whose static type equals the receiver's static type — the `return this` fluent shape (`sb.Append(x);`).

title: a fluent method returning a base of the receiver's type stays warned
rule: A fluent method whose declared return is a *base* of the receiver's type stays warned — conservative by design; the exemption requires the result's static type to equal the receiver's static type.

title: a unit-returning call as a statement draws no unused-result warning
rule: Method calls returning `()` ... are the common cases; no warning is emitted for these.

title: awaiting a resultless Task as a statement draws no unused-result warning
rule: Method calls returning `()` and `await` expressions on `Task` (no result) are the common cases; no warning is emitted for these.

title: a bare-statement call returning a non-trivial-dispose class is a hard error
rule: For non-trivial-dispose class types ... the warning is replaced by a hard error directing the caller to the discard `_ := expression;` ... `OpenLog();` is rejected, and `_ := OpenLog();` is the remedy.

title: a local record is declared and used inside its enclosing body
rule: A `record` or `enum` may be declared as a statement, scoped to the enclosing body like a local variable. The local type is an ordinary nominal record.

title: a local record may not carry a visibility keyword
rule: The `Visibility?` slot must be empty — a local type has no access surface, so a visibility keyword is a compile error naming the rule.

title: a local record may not declare generic parameters
rule: The `GenericParams?` slot must be empty (v1) — a local type declares no type parameters of its own.

title: a local type must be declared before its first use
rule: The declaration must precede first use; local types are therefore order-significant.

title: a class may not be declared as a local type
rule: `class` and `interface` may not [be declared locally] — a class carries ownership, destructors, and the §28 disposal machinery, a body-scoped kernel surface for no recorded need.

title: an interface may not be declared as a local type
rule: `class` and `interface` may not [be declared locally] — … an interface is a contract for an outside a local has none of.

title: a choice may not be declared as a local type
rule: `choice` may **not** be declared locally (its payload-derived three-way classification, owning-match consume obligations, and coverage machinery are a heavier admission deserving its own study).

title: a local type may not appear in a member signature
rule: The name may not appear in any member signature of an ENCLOSING or SIBLING declaration — parameter, return, field/property/indexer, generic-constraint, or base/interface positions — which is a compile error naming that rule ("a method-local type may not appear in a member signature"), v0.301.

title: a local type may not reference an enclosing generic parameter
rule: A local type may not reference an enclosing generic parameter (an enclosing method's or class's `T`) — a compile error naming the rule.

title: a local type may not shadow a type visible at its declaration point
rule: The declared name may not shadow any type name visible at the declaration point (a local `NameAge` silently shadowing a module-level `NameAge` is a trap, not a convenience — the collision is an error).

title: a local type's name leaves scope at the end of its enclosing block
rule: A local type's name is in scope from its declaration statement to the end of the innermost enclosing statement block — exactly a local variable's scope.

title: a local enum is a §10 enum wholesale, prefix omission included
rule: A local `enum` is a §10 enum wholesale: constants, explicit values, underlying types, methods, interface conformances, and `case` matching with prefix omission (§10.6) and enum-scrutinee exhaustiveness (§19.6) inside the scope.

title: a local record gets §9.2 auto-equality like any other record
rule: The local type is an ordinary nominal record — every §9 rule applies unchanged; auto-equality (§9.2) is computed by its existing rules from the declaration.

title: a method declares a return type after the colon
rule: A method has a return type after `:`, or no `:` clause for a procedure (return type `()`).

title: a procedure omits the colon return-type clause entirely
rule: A method has a return type after `:`, or no `:` clause for a procedure (return type `()`).

title: an expression body replaces the block when the body is one expression
rule: When the body is a single expression, `=> expression` replaces the block.

title: a method with no declared return type may use an assignment as its arrow body
rule: A method with **no declared return type** may also use a single *assignment* as its arrow body, the same shape the accessor form `set => _x := value;` has always had.

title: the assignment arrow body is an error under a declared return type
rule: On a method with a declared return type the assignment form is an error (an assignment produces no value).

title: an expression body under a declared choice return type target-types a bare case
rule: An expression body under a declared return type is a declared-result position: a bare choice-case construction in it target-types against the declared type, exactly as a `return` operand does.

title: a ref local argument is a true alias, visible through the caller's location
rule: `ref` local and field targets alias: callee writes are visible through the caller's location immediately (the `Swap(ref a, ref b)` semantics presupposes this).

title: the caller must write ref at the call site
rule: `ref` — pass by reference. The caller writes `ref` at the call site.

title: the callee assigns every out parameter on every normal-completion path
rule: The callee must assign every `out` parameter on every normal-completion (return) path.

title: an out parameter left unassigned on some normal-completion path is rejected
rule: The callee must assign every `out` parameter on every normal-completion (return) path; failing to do so is a compile error.

title: omitting the move marker on a named owned binding argument is rejected
rule: Omitting the marker on a named owned binding is a compile error naming the fix ("this call consumes `x`; write `M(move x)`").

title: a named owned binding fed with the move marker reaches the owned parameter
rule: **Call-site marker:** when the argument is a named owned binding, the caller writes the transfer marker at the call site: `M(move x)`.

title: writing move on a fresh producer is rejected as redundant
rule: Writing [the move marker] on a borrow, a fresh producer, or a non-`owned` parameter position is likewise an error. A fresh producer — a `new` expression ... — stays unmarked: no live binding is invalidated, so there is nothing to announce.

title: a fresh producer stays unmarked at an owned parameter
rule: A fresh producer — a `new` expression, a call returning `owned T`, an operator result, or a `move obj._field` — stays unmarked: no live binding is invalidated, so there is nothing to announce.

title: writing move at a non-owned parameter position is rejected
rule: Writing [the move marker] ... on a non-`owned` parameter position is likewise an error (at a non-`owned` position the diagnostic names the borrow default — an owned expression may not feed a borrow slot).

title: a ref argument's static type must exactly match the referent type
rule: **Exact referent type.** The argument's static type must be **exactly** the parameter's referent type. Because the parameter aliases the caller's location, no implicit conversion is admitted — not even a widening one that an ordinary by-value argument would take.

title: a ref argument may not name a location of owned state
rule: A `ref` or `out` argument must be an assignable storage location, subject to two recorded v1 bounds (liftable): no location of owned state — an owned local or `owned` parameter, an `owned` field, an owning-collection or owning-inline-array slot.

title: out owned is the only modifier compound; others are mutually exclusive
rule: The combination `out owned` is the only modifier compound; the others are mutually exclusive.

title: out var name declares a new variable inline, typed from the parameter
rule: `out var name` declares a new variable inline. Its type is inferred from the method's `out` parameter declaration.

title: out var underscore is a compile error
rule: `out var _` is a compile error — it would declare nothing; write `out _`, which already means exactly this.

title: out underscore is the admitted discard spelling
rule: `out var _` is a compile error — it would declare nothing; write `out _`, which already means exactly this.

title: out using var is accepted against an out owned parameter
rule: For disposal-aware inline declarations against an `out owned` parameter, use `out using var`.

title: out using var against a plain out parameter is rejected
rule: A caller cannot write `out using var` against a plain `out` parameter (the result would have no owned source).

title: an explicit type annotation on the inline out form is not permitted
rule: An explicit type annotation is not permitted in the inline `out` form; the type is inferred from the method's `out` parameter declaration.

title: a short-circuited and-guard definitely assigns the inline out variable
rule: The analysis is required to honor the standard short-circuit facts (`A and Call(out var x)` assigns `x` when the whole expression is `true`) ... so the idiomatic guarded read stays accepted.

title: reading a non-nullable-reference out variable off the guarded path is rejected
rule: On a path where the call may not have run, a read of a **non-nullable-reference-typed** out variable is a compile error, exactly as for any other unassigned non-nullable local — an inline `out` variable counts as assigned only on paths where the introducing call was actually evaluated.

title: a pre-declared uninitialized local adopts owned against out owned
rule: A pre-declared local passed as plain `out x` is admitted against `out owned` exactly when it is in one of the two adoptable states — uninitialized or polymorphic-null — and adopts owned on every normal-return path of the call.

title: named arguments may appear in any order
rule: Named arguments may appear in any order after positional arguments.

title: a positional argument after a named argument is rejected
rule: Named arguments may appear in any order after positional arguments.

title: a ref or out argument has no named spelling
rule: A `ref`/`out`/`scoped` argument is positional-only: those modifiers inhabit the `ArgModifiers` alternative of `Argument`, which has no named form — `M(out var result := n)` has no reading and does not parse, the `:=` of the binding form and the `:=` of the named form being the same token.

title: a default value may be a literal or constant expression
rule: A default-value expression must be type-compatible with the parameter's declared type ... [it] may be a literal, constant, or `default(T)`.

title: a default value may not reference instance state
rule: A default-value expression may not reference instance state (`this`, instance fields, instance properties) — the default belongs to the method's signature, not to a particular receiver's frame.

title: a default value may read an earlier parameter, never a later one
rule: A default-value expression may "read other parameters appearing **earlier** in the same parameter list (e.g. `M(a: int, b: int := a + 1)` is permitted; later-parameter forward references are not)."

title: supplied arguments evaluate in call-site textual order regardless of naming
rule: A call's **supplied** argument expressions are evaluated in **call-site textual order** — left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike (`M(b := Next(), a := Next())` evaluates the `b` expression first).

title: two overloads indistinguishable by arity, types, modifiers clash
rule: A type may not declare two members indistinguishable under §22.6's rules — the clash rejected at the second declaration.

title: overloads distinguished by arity are admitted
rule: Overload resolution considers number, types, the `ref`/`out` modifiers, and the presence of `owned` on an ordinary parameter — overloads differing in any of these are distinguishable.

title: overloads distinguished by the ref modifier are admitted
rule: Overload resolution considers number, types, the `ref`/`out` modifiers ... — overloads differing in any of these are distinguishable.

title: example 1 -- exact match preferred over a widening conversion
rule: For a single argument position, one candidate is better than another when the better candidate requires no implicit conversion ... and the other requires an implicit conversion.

title: example 2 -- two equally-ranked conversions are ambiguous
rule: Two candidates that both require an implicit conversion at the same position are equally ranked there, regardless of which conversion each uses.

title: example 3 -- exact on one argument, conversion on the other, is unambiguous
rule: A candidate is unambiguously better than another when it is better-or-equal on every argument position and strictly better on at least one.

title: example 4 -- each candidate exact on a different argument is ambiguous
rule: If no candidate is unambiguously better — because each of two candidates is exact on a different argument ... the call is ambiguous and is a compile error.

title: example 5 -- no reachable candidate cites no candidates
rule: If no candidate is applicable at all ... the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable.

title: example 6 -- applicability filtering removes an inapplicable candidate
rule: byte→sbyte is NOT implicit ... ⇒ Process(sbyte) is not applicable. byte→ushort IS implicit ... ⇒ Process(ushort) is the only applicable candidate.

title: the defaulted-arity tie-break prefers the candidate that fills no default
rule: A candidate applicable **without filling any default** is preferred over a candidate that fills one or more ... `M(5)` against `M(n: int)` and `M(n: int, m: int := 0)` resolves to `M(int)`.

title: a non-generic candidate is preferred over a generic one on a tie
rule: When a non-generic candidate and a generic candidate are both applicable, and neither the ranking ... nor the defaulted-arity tie-break separates them, the non-generic candidate is selected ... `Show(x: int)` and `Show<T>(x: T)` on `Show(5)` resolve to the non-generic.

title: the defaulted-arity tie-break applies before the non-generic preference
rule: the defaulted-arity tie-break applies first: `M(n: int, m: int := 0)` and `M<T>(x: T)` on the call `M(5)` resolve to the *generic* candidate — it fills no default.

title: an unmarked borrow read selects the plain member of an owned-ordinary pair
rule: A borrow is applicable only to the plain candidate: an unmarked read of a named binding ... `r.Append(w)`; // borrow — the plain overload; w untouched.

title: a move-marked owned production selects the owned member of an owned-ordinary pair
rule: An owned production is applicable only to the `owned` candidate: a move-rooted argument (`move x` ...) ... `r.Append(move w);` // transfer — the owned overload.

title: owned on an out parameter never distinguishes overloads
rule: `owned` on an **`out` parameter** stays outside the distinguishability list: two methods differing only in the `owned` qualifier on an `out` parameter are a compile error.

title: scoped never distinguishes overloads
rule: `scoped` does not participate in overload resolution: two overloads differing only in `scoped` on a parameter ... are a compile error.

title: an owned/ordinary pair over a where-T-class constraint fails the declaration guard
rule: **`where T: class` does not qualify** — it admits `string` and function-type substitutions, at which §28.1 erases the marker and the pair collapses to identical signatures. At any failing position the pair clashes: the declaration-site error ..., reported at the second declaration.

title: an owned/ordinary pair over a where-T-IDisposable constraint passes the declaration guard
rule: A pair differing only by ordinary `owned` is declarable exactly when, at every differing position, the declared type ... is a class type, an interface type, or a type parameter whose constraints exclude every substitution at which the pair collapses ... `where T: IDisposable` qualifies, its closure guaranteed by §8.7.

title: a constructor may chain to another constructor of the same class with this
rule: Multiple constructors are permitted; chaining uses `this(...)` or `base(...)` in the chaining position before the body.

title: a derived constructor may chain to a base constructor with base
rule: Multiple constructors are permitted; chaining uses `this(...)` or `base(...)` in the chaining position before the body.

title: a this-chain argument may not read a field of the not-yet-constructed instance
rule: A `this(...)` argument may read neither a primary-constructor parameter nor any field of `this` — in the chaining position no field of the declaring type is yet assigned (§22.8's step-1-before-step-2 sequence, restated at §22.7's chaining-position clause).

title: a this-chain argument may read the delegating constructor's own parameter
rule: The only reads a chaining argument may make are of the constructor's own parameters, constants, and statics (§22.10); and "for a `this(...)` chain, the chained-to constructor runs to completion (its own steps of this sequence) before control returns here" (§22.8 step 1).

title: an instance method call on this in the chaining position is rejected
rule: A synchronous observation of `this` — an instance method ... invocation with receiver `this` ... is admitted only at points where every field ... is definitely assigned on every reaching path. In the chaining position ... any observation of `this` there is a compile error.

title: a virtual call on this from a non-sealed class's constructor body is rejected
rule: No virtual dispatch from constructor bodies of non-sealed classes. A call from a constructor body to a `virtual`, `override`, or `abstract` member with receiver `this` ... is a compile error unless the declaring class is `sealed` and not `abstract`.

title: a caught exception inside a static constructor does not fail the type
rule: An exception caught inside the static constructor's body does not transition the type to the failed state — the constructor completes normally and static initialization is considered successful.

title: a dispatching call on this from a sealed non-abstract constructor body is admitted
rule: A call from a constructor body to a `virtual`, `override`, or `abstract` member with receiver `this` — any dispatching call not through `base.` — is a compile error unless the declaring class is `sealed` and not `abstract`. In a sealed, non-abstract class the dispatch target is statically bounded and the call is admitted under rule 1's gate.

title: a class declaring no instance constructor has an implicit public parameterless one
rule: A class that declares **no instance constructor** and no primary-constructor parameter list has an implicit parameterless constructor: `public`, no parameters, an empty body, chaining implicitly per §12.8 — and it satisfies `where T: new()` on the same terms a declared public parameterless one does (§14.2), which is what `new T()` reaches at such a substitution.

title: a primary-constructor parameter list suppresses the implicit parameterless constructor
rule: Declaring **any** instance constructor suppresses the implicit parameterless constructor, a primary-constructor parameter list included.

title: a static constructor does not suppress the implicit parameterless constructor
rule: A `static constructor` does not suppress the implicit parameterless constructor (it is never a chaining or `new` target); it runs once before the type's first use.

title: a standard-library builtin gets no implicit parameterless constructor
rule: A **standard-library builtin** type is excepted from the implicit parameterless constructor: its constructor surface is closed by §17.7, and `Subscription` declares none, so `new Subscription(...)` is a compile error at any argument list.

title: new C() reaches the implicit parameterless constructor directly
rule: A class that declares **no instance constructor** and no primary-constructor parameter list has an implicit parameterless constructor: `public`, no parameters, an empty body. It is what `new C()` reaches on such a class.

title: a field declared in a class may include an initializer
rule: A field declared in a class or record may include an initializer.

title: a readonly field assigned in an ordinary method is rejected
rule: A field declared `readonly` may be assigned only in a field initializer or in a constructor body; assignment anywhere else is a compile error.

title: a readonly field assigned once in the constructor body is admitted
rule: A field declared `readonly` may be assigned ... in a constructor body; the field is also assigned at most once.

title: a readonly field with an initializer assigned again in the constructor body is rejected
rule: A field initializer and a constructor-body assignment are therefore **two** assignments wherever both run, which is wherever the constructor's chaining position holds `base(...)` or the implicit `base()`.

title: a readonly field assigned in mutually exclusive branches is admitted
rule: Assignments in mutually exclusive branches are one assignment per path and are admitted.

title: a readonly assignment inside a loop body is rejected unconditionally
rule: An assignment lexically inside a loop body within the assignment window is rejected unconditionally: a loop could assign on more than one iteration.

title: a field initializer may not reference this or an instance member
rule: Field initializers may **not** reference: `this`, instance members, `base`, virtual methods, or any expression that would observe `this` indirectly.

title: a constructor may not assign another instance's readonly storage
rule: The context is per-instance, not per-type — an instance `readonly` field is assignable only through an lvalue chain rooted at `this`, so a constructor of the declaring type may not write another value's `readonly` storage held in a parameter, local, or field.

title: a constructor-body throw disposes the step-2 owned field, not the class's own destructor
rule: An exception in the constructor body (step 3) triggers disposal of every owned field assigned during initialization (step 2) and the base subobject. ... the throwing class's `destructor` body is **never** executed on these edges.

title: an exception in a field initializer disposes earlier-completed owned fields in reverse order
rule: An exception during a **field initializer** (step 2) triggers disposal of any earlier derived owned fields whose initializers completed, in reverse declaration order, followed by the base subobject's `Dispose()`.

title: an exception during the base constructor call leaves no derived state to clean up
rule: An exception during the **base or chained constructor call** (step 1) leaves no derived state to clean up ... The exception propagates to the derived ctor's caller; the derived instance is never observable.

title: a this-chaining body throw after the chain completes runs the normal dispose
rule: If the chaining constructor's **body** throws, the chained-to construction completed and the instance is at that point fully initialized: the runtime disposes it through the normal generated-`Dispose()` path ... before the exception propagates.

title: primary constructor parameters are in scope inside field initializers
rule: Primary-constructor parameters are in scope inside field initializers.

title: primary constructor parameters are in scope in the inheritance clause's base call
rule: Primary-constructor parameters are in scope inside the inheritance clause's base call; this replaces an explicit `base(...)` call.

title: a primary constructor parameter referenced in a body position is captured and readable from methods
rule: The parameters are in scope inside the body of any method, property, constructor, or destructor of the class. The compiler captures them as private fields automatically.

title: a convenience constructor's this(...) chaining position may not read a primary-constructor parameter
rule: Primary-constructor parameters are not in scope in a convenience constructor's chaining position: the arguments of a `this(...)` call run before the chained-to primary's capture step, so reading a primary-constructor parameter there is a compile error.

title: a convenience constructor's this(...) chaining position may read its own parameters
rule: The only reads a chaining argument may make are of the constructor's own parameters, constants, and statics.

title: ref is rejected on a primary constructor parameter
rule: A primary-constructor parameter list admits plain and `owned` parameters only; `ref` and `out` are rejected semantically.

title: out is rejected on a primary constructor parameter
rule: A primary-constructor parameter list admits plain and `owned` parameters only; `ref` and `out` are rejected semantically.

title: an owned primary-constructor parameter referenced only in an initializer is not captured
rule: Referenced only in field initializers (or the base call): not captured — the initializer consumes it.

title: an owned primary-constructor parameter referenced in a body position is captured as an owned field
rule: Referenced in a body position: captured as a compiler-generated owned private field, disposed by the generated `Dispose()` exactly like a declared owned field.

title: an owned primary parameter used in an initializer and a body position is rejected
rule: Referenced both in an owned-consuming initializer and in a body position: compile error — the body reference is a read of a moved-from value.

title: a class-typed scoped primary-constructor parameter is admitted and captured as a non-owned field
rule: A class- or interface-typed `scoped` primary-constructor parameter follows the same capture rule: referenced in a body position, it is captured as a compiler-generated non-owned private field — exactly the direct non-owned field of the bounding object that §28.14's callee side admits, the constructed object being the bounding object. At the call site the argument carries the marker — `new Box(scoped src)` — and is admitted under §28.14's bounding-object forms exactly as at a declared constructor: the holder is a `using var` local or `this`, the source is declared before the holder.

title: primary constructor parameters are not automatically promoted to public properties
rule: Primary-constructor parameters are not automatically promoted to public properties. To expose one, declare a property explicitly.

title: only the primary constructor may chain to base(...)
rule: A class with a primary constructor may declare additional convenience constructors. Each must chain to another constructor via `this(...)`; only the primary may chain to `base(...)`.

title: a convenience constructor chains to the primary via this(...)
rule: A class with a primary constructor may declare additional convenience constructors. Each must chain to another constructor via `this(...)`; only the primary may chain to `base(...)`.

title: a primary constructor's inheritance-clause base call replaces an explicit base(...)
rule: When a class with a primary constructor has a base class, the base call appears in the inheritance clause. This replaces an explicit `base(...)` call.

title: a fresh producer at a scoped primary-constructor argument is rejected
rule: At the call site the argument carries the marker and is admitted under §28.14's bounding-object forms exactly as at a declared constructor: a fresh producer is rejected — the unbound owned temporary dies at the end of the full expression (§9.7's no-temporary-source rule); bind the source first.

title: scoped on a value-typed primary-constructor parameter is rejected
rule: A primary-constructor parameter list admits plain, `owned`, and class- or interface-typed `scoped` parameters. `scoped` is valid on function-typed parameters and on class/interface-typed parameters; other parameter types are rejected semantically (Appendix A.4).

title: an unreferenced scoped primary parameter captures no field and its call site is still admitted
rule: The freeze is keyed on the signature, not on the capture: a `scoped` parameter referenced in no body and no initializer captures no field, and the call site freezes its source all the same, harmlessly.

title: the holder of a scoped primary-constructor borrow is disposed before its source
rule: At the call site the argument is admitted under §28.14's bounding-object forms exactly as at a declared constructor: the holder is a `using var` local, the source is declared before the holder, and the source is frozen until the holder's scope exits. With declared-before admission, the freeze, and reverse-declaration-order disposal (§21.6, §28.10), the source provably outlives the bounding object including its destructor.

title: a with expression over a class-typed source is rejected
rule: The object-initializer block does not exist: a `with` expression requires a record-typed source, and a class-typed source is a compile error.

title: with on a freshly-constructed record is unaffected by the retirement
rule: Record `with` on a freshly-constructed record (`new Point(1, 2) with(Y := 9)`) is unaffected.

title: named and optional constructor arguments replace the retired object-initializer block
rule: In its place, use named/optional constructor arguments — which run the constructor and respect its invariants.

title: binding the instance to a local and assigning members replaces the retired form
rule: In its place, ... bind the instance to a local and assign its members as ordinary statements, whose exception-path disposal is §28.3's general discharge of an owned local.

title: static methods, properties, fields, and constructors are declared with static
rule: Static methods, properties, fields, and constructors are declared with `static`.

title: a class-level const is implicitly static
rule: A class-level `const` is implicitly static; writing `static const` is redundant but permitted for clarity — both forms declare the same constant.

title: static const is the redundant-but-permitted spelling of a class-level const
rule: A class-level `const` is implicitly static; writing `static const` is redundant but permitted for clarity — both forms declare the same constant.

title: const requires a primitive value type or string
rule: `const` declarations require a compile-time-constant expression and a primitive value type or `string`.

title: const requires a compile-time-constant expression
rule: `const` declarations require a compile-time-constant expression and a primitive value type or `string`.

title: static readonly of immutable content is unrestricted
rule: `static readonly` of immutable content — value types of sendable-value category, `string`, enums — and `const` are unrestricted (shared-immutable).

title: a mutable static field of an ordinary class type is rejected
rule: any other class type — `owned` or not — takes: mutable: error † — a mutable static admitted by none of (i)-(iv) is a compile error naming this rule.

title: a mutable static field of a primitive value type warns
rule: A mutable static whose declared type is a primitive value type or an enum type ... warns (iii): the obligation is to confine every use of the storage to one domain, or take the synchronized spelling.

title: a static readonly field of a synchronized handle type is admitted warning-free
rule: declares synchronized, not displacement-unbounded — the form-(i) set — `static readonly`: ok — in the set.

title: a static readonly field of a class outside the warning-suppression set warns
rule: A `static readonly` (including `owned`) field or auto-property of class type is admitted with a declaration-site warning unless the class is in this rule's warning-suppression set.

title: a static readonly Channel field deliberately still warns
rule: A `static readonly Channel<T>` deliberately still warns (`Channel<T>` declares no facts) — the reminder that the channel is the single-consumer receiving end and must stay confined to one consuming domain.

title: a mutable static field of bare generic parameter type is rejected at the declaration
rule: A mutable static field or auto-property whose declared type is a bare generic parameter, or its nullable form, is admitted by no form above and is a compile error at the declaration site, whatever the parameter's constraints or eventual substitutions.

title: a Task-typed lazy cache static field is admitted
rule: Lazy task cache: a static whose declared type is `Task?` or `Task<T>?` — the admission is keyed to the declared type alone.

title: an OwningTask-typed static field is not admitted as a lazy task cache
rule: `OwningTask<T>?` — mutable: error — not (ii), †.

title: each distinct instantiation of a generic class has its own static state
rule: A static member of a generic class is accessed by supplying the type arguments on the type name in receiver position. Each distinct instantiation has its own static state.

title: a static owned readonly SharedEventSource field is the admitted warning-free publication point
rule: A process-global publication point is an ordinary static field of type `SharedEventSource<T>` — a form-(i) member, admitted warning-free in the recommended shape `private static owned readonly _e: SharedEventSource<T> := new();`.

title: a capturing handler passed to SharedEventSource.Subscribe is rejected
rule: Every call resolving to a subscribe position declared on `ISharedEvent<T>`/`SharedEventSource<T>` admits only capture-free handlers: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference.

title: a static owned readonly Mutex is in the warning-suppression set and is silent
rule: A `static readonly` (including `owned`) field of class type is admitted with a declaration-site warning **unless the class is in this rule's warning-suppression set** — every type declaring the **synchronized** or the **immutable** fact, `Mutex` among them.

title: the same static owned readonly field at a class outside the set warns
rule: A `static readonly` (including `owned`) field or auto-property of **class type** is admitted with a **declaration-site warning** unless the class is in this rule's warning-suppression set: confining its use to one domain is the programmer's obligation.

title: a static owned readonly CancellationTokenSource is silent under 4(a)
rule: The four members outside rule 2's form (i) — `Locked<T>`/`RwLocked<T>`, `FrozenArray<T>`, and `CancellationTokenSource`, the process-global shutdown source — are in the warning-suppression set; `owned` enrols the field in §22.13's program-exit disposal.

title: a static owned readonly FrozenArray is silent by its immutable fact
rule: The warning-suppression set is derived, not curated: every type declaring the **synchronized** or the **immutable** fact — `FrozenArray<T>` among them — so a `static owned readonly` of it is admitted warning-free.

title: static readonly is the warning-free spelling of a process-global primitive
rule: `static readonly` of **immutable content** — value types of sendable-value category, `string`, enums — is unrestricted (shared-immutable); it is the warning-free spelling where the value never changes after initialization.

title: dropping readonly from the same primitive static draws form (iii)'s warning
rule: **(iii) Warned value static:** a mutable static whose declared type is a primitive value type ... the obligation it names is to confine every read and write of the field to one domain, or to move to a synchronized spelling.

title: a static owned readonly Locked registry is the canonical warning-free process-global
rule: The four members outside rule 2's form (i) — the data-owning locks `Locked<T>`/`RwLocked<T>` (`static owned readonly` being the canonical process-global registry idiom) ... — are in rule 4's warning-suppression set, so the declaration is admitted warning-free.

title: static fields of a single type are initialized in textual declaration order
rule: Within a single type, static fields are initialized in textual declaration order.

title: a static readonly field may not read a static readonly field of the same type declared after it
rule: If the initializer expression for a `static readonly` field F reads a `static readonly` field G of the same type declared after F in the source — directly — the reference is rejected at compile time.

title: a forward read routed through a statically-resolvable call is rejected
rule: ...directly, or transitively through the bodies of statically-resolvable calls (static methods and static property getters reached by direct name within the compilation unit) — the reference is rejected at compile time.

title: a static constructor body may freely reference fields in any order
rule: A static constructor body may freely reference any of the type's static fields in any order; the constructor body runs after all field initializers have completed, so no forward-reference question arises there.

title: forward references between const declarations are not subject to the ordering rule
rule: Forward references between `const` declarations are not subject to this rule: a `const` initializer must be a compile-time-constant expression, so forward references between consts are either resolved at compile time or are themselves a compile error for non-constant operands.

title: a cyclic static-initialization dependency between two types is a compile error
rule: The compiler builds a static-initialization dependency graph over distinct types ... A cycle in this graph is a compile error naming the participating types.

title: TypeInitializationException carries the original exception as InnerException
rule: A touch of a type whose static initialization is in progress raises TypeInitializationException; more generally, every subsequent access to a static member of a permanently-failed type raises TypeInitializationException whose InnerException is the original exception.

title: every access to a permanently-failed type observes the same cached TypeInitializationException
rule: The instance constructed on first failure is the one cached and rethrown; the triggering access and every subsequent access see the same cached TypeInitializationException instance.

title: eager startup assignment of a Task cache avoids the check-then-store race
rule: Eager startup assignment of the task cache — assign the `Task<T>?` cache before any spawn or other first use; the check-then-store race never arises and the work runs exactly once.

title: await is rejected in a static field initializer
rule: `await` may not appear in static field initializers or static constructor bodies.

title: await is rejected in a static constructor body
rule: `await` may not appear in static field initializers or static constructor bodies.

title: static owned fields of one type are disposed at program exit in reverse declaration order
rule: Within a single type, multiple static `owned` fields are disposed in reverse declaration order, mirroring the instance-field disposal rule.

title: a static readonly class-typed field without owned is exempt from the ownership-discharge requirement
rule: A `static readonly` field of class type or interface type that is not marked `owned` is exempt from the ownership-discharge requirement: assigning a fresh owned value into such a field discharges the producer. The value lives for the duration of the program.

title: a static readonly field of a non-trivial-dispose class declared without owned warns
rule: The compiler warns (not errors) when a `static readonly` field of a class type whose `Dispose()` is non-trivial — a class with a user-defined destructor ... — is declared without `owned`.

title: a mutable static owning-inline-array field is admitted with a declaration-site warning
rule: A mutable static field of owning-inline-array type (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`) is admitted — with rule 4's declaration-site warning: the array's owned instances are reachable from every domain and its slots are mutable.

title: a variadic-style signature uses Array<T> with a collection literal at the call site
rule: There is no `params` keyword. A variadic-style signature uses `Array<T>` with a collection literal at the call site.

title: a pure method may call another pure member
rule: The compiler rejects, inside a pure body, any call whose statically resolved declaration is not pure — a call to a pure member is therefore admitted.

title: a pure body may not call a non-pure member
rule: The compiler rejects, inside a pure body, any call whose statically resolved declaration is not pure.

title: a pure member declares no ref parameter
rule: A pure member declares no `ref`, `out`, `out owned`, `owned`, or `scoped` parameters: `ref` is a writable alias of caller storage.

title: a pure member declares no out parameter
rule: A pure member declares no `ref`, `out`, `out owned`, `owned`, or `scoped` parameters: `out` obliges a caller-visible assignment channel.

title: a pure member declares no owned parameter
rule: A pure member declares no `ref`, `out`, `out owned`, `owned`, or `scoped` parameters: `owned` brings a disposal obligation into the frame whose discharge runs `Dispose` — user code at disposal time.

title: a pure member rejects a move-only value parameter
rule: A move-only value parameter — an owning-choice instantiation, or an owning inline array — is likewise rejected: the plain spelling is identical to the `owned` spelling for such a type.

title: an owned class-typed return is rejected on a pure member
rule: The return type is unrestricted except: an `owned` class-typed return is rejected.

title: a move-only value return is rejected on a pure member
rule: So is a move-only value return — an owning-choice instantiation, or an owning inline array — no pure body can produce an owned class instance or a value that carries one.

title: pure is rejected on an async member
rule: `pure` is rejected on async members and async lambdas: an `async` body interleaves with the domain's continuation queue and traffics in tasks; `pure` implies non-`async`.

title: pure is rejected on an iterator method
rule: `pure` is rejected on iterator methods (`yield`) — a pure-iterator form is deliberately left open, not designed.

title: pure is rejected on a destructor
rule: `pure` is rejected on destructors — disposal is the effect context purity fences off.

title: pure is rejected on an auto-property as redundant
rule: Fields and auto-properties as declarations: the auto-accessor classification is implicit; writing `pure` on an auto-property is rejected as redundant.

title: pure is rejected on a static constructor
rule: `pure` is rejected on static constructors — no call site exists to consume the fact.

title: a pure body may not store to an instance field outside a pure constructor's birth store
rule: Prohibited, as the closed list's contrapositive: any store whose target root is an instance field ... (stores to `this`'s fields outside pure constructors' birth stores included).

title: a pure body may not store to a static field
