rule: Prohibited, as the closed list's contrapositive: any store whose target root is an instance field, a static field, an indexer slot of a class instance, or whose access path dereferences a class-typed reference.

title: a pure body may mutate a record-typed parameter's fields as frame-private state
rule: Locals and frame-local mutation: assignment ... where the target's root is a local variable or by-value parameter of this body and the access path from that root traverses only value-typed storage (record fields, inline-array slots).

title: a pure body may not construct a class instance outside the throw carve-out
rule: Prohibited: class construction — `new C(…)` ... except the throw operand below (constructors and destructors run arbitrary user code, and an owned instance drags in the discharge machinery).

title: the throw carve-out admits a pure-constructed trivial-dispose exception operand
rule: Inside a pure body, `new E(args)` is admitted only as the immediate operand of a `throw` statement or `throw` expression, and only when the invoked constructor of E is pure-declared and E is a trivial-dispose class.

title: the throw carve-out is rejected when the exception class is not trivial-dispose
rule: `new E(args)` is admitted [in a throw operand] only when ... E is a trivial-dispose class.

title: a pure body may not invoke a function-typed value
rule: Prohibited: invoking function-typed values (the value's type carries no effect information).

title: a pure body's for loop over a concrete Array<T> source is the normative elision
rule: A source whose static type at this body's own check site is concretely `Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`, class-typed `OwningBuffer<T>`, or `string` — the admitted protocol elision is likewise the normative semantics inside a pure body.

title: a pure body's for loop over an interface-typed source is rejected
rule: A source whose static type is an interface (`IEnumerable<T>` included) or a generic type parameter remains rejected: the remedy is declaring the source at a concrete sequence type.

title: an override of a pure member must itself be declared pure
rule: Purity is never dropped. An override of a pure member must itself be declared `pure`, and a class member implementing a pure interface member must be declared `pure`; omission is a compile error at the override or implementation.

title: an override may strengthen purity where the base member is not pure
rule: Purity may be strengthened. An override or implementation may declare `pure` where the overridden or interface member is not.

title: purity is monotone down an override chain once a member becomes pure
rule: Monotone down the chain. An override matches against the nearest overridden declaration: once a chain member is pure, every further override is pure.

title: a pure constructor's birth-store rule admits assignment to this's fields
rule: A constructor may be declared `pure`. Its body is checked under the pure-body rules with one addition, the birth-store rule: assignments whose target root is a field of `this` are permitted — the instance under construction is unreachable from any other holder until the constructor returns.

title: pure is rejected on a set accessor
rule: Purity attaches to the getter; `pure` on `set` is always rejected.

title: a violated requires clause raises ContractViolationException in every build mode
rule: A `requires` clause is evaluated on every invocation, after argument binding and before any execution of the member; a clause evaluating `false` raises `ContractViolationException`, in every build mode.

title: a satisfied requires clause lets the member run normally
rule: A `requires` clause is evaluated on every invocation ...; a clause evaluating `false` raises `ContractViolationException`. (A clause evaluating `true` on every invocation lets the member proceed.)

title: a contract clause's expression must be of type bool
rule: The expression must be of type `bool` (§4.1 — no truthiness).

title: a contract clause may call only pure members
rule: Each clause's expression is of type `bool`, is admitted under the pure-body discipline of §22.15.

title: await is rejected in a contract clause, even on an async member
rule: `await` is rejected, on every member including `async` ones (a clause is not part of an async body's statement sequence and has no suspension semantics).

title: throw is rejected in a contract clause
rule: Three clause-specific amendments: `throw` is rejected (a clause states a proposition; the mechanism, message, and blame of a violation belong to this section's machinery).

title: result denotes the returned value in an ensures clause, read as a borrow
rule: Within an `ensures` clause of a member with a declared return type, `result` denotes the value being returned, typed as the declared return type, in a read-only borrow position.

title: result is a compile error in a unit-typed member's clauses
rule: `result` is a compile error in a unit-typed member's clauses, in a constructor's clauses, and in any `requires` or `invariant` clause.

title: result is a compile error in a requires clause
rule: `result` is a compile error ... in any `requires` or `invariant` clause.

title: result is a compile error in a constructor's clauses
rule: `result` is a compile error in a unit-typed member's clauses, in a constructor's clauses, and in any `requires` or `invariant` clause.

title: old is a compile error in a requires clause
rule: `old` is a compile error in `requires` clauses, in `invariant` members, in constructor clauses, and outside clauses entirely.

title: old is a compile error in an invariant member
rule: `old` is a compile error in `requires` clauses, in `invariant` members, in constructor clauses, and outside clauses entirely.

title: old is a compile error in a constructor's clauses
rule: `old` is a compile error in `requires` clauses, in `invariant` members, in constructor clauses, and outside clauses entirely (fields sit at §22.7's null watermark — no prestate exists).

title: old(old(E)) is a compile error
rule: `old(old(E))` is a compile error.

title: a move-only value operand is a compile error at old
rule: A move-only value operand is a compile error at the contract clause: a copy is the operation move-only-ness forbids, and the literal desugaring would not copy but consume.

title: an override may not declare requires clauses
rule: An override or implementation may not declare `requires` clauses. Strengthening a precondition breaks every caller dispatching through the base contract.

title: an override may add ensures clauses, conjoined with the inherited ones
rule: An override or implementation may add `ensures` clauses, conjoined with the inherited ones at its return edges — strengthening the postcondition, always sound for callers.

title: an undischargeable static requires clause is a compile error at the declaration
rule: The `static` clause qualifier demands the proven tier: a `static` clause the implementation cannot discharge statically is a compile error.

title: a static requires clause may mention only state its call sites can see
rule: A `static requires` clause may mention only state its call sites can see (the member's parameters, and members visible to every caller); a `static requires` over non-public state is a compile error at the declaration.

title: a static clause that is a constant expression folding to true is proven
rule: The current prover floor: exactly two things inhabit the proven tier: a clause whose expression (after call-site substitution, for `requires`) is a constant expression folding to `true`.

title: an invariant member given a visibility keyword is rejected
rule: `invariant(E);` declares no visibility choice to spell; it carries no visibility keyword (§13.3's principle).

title: an invariant member with no visibility keyword is admitted
rule: `invariant(E);` carries no visibility keyword — for such a member no visibility choice exists to spell.

title: an invariant in a static class is a compile error
rule: Out of scope in this revision, each recorded: ... static-class and static-state invariants (an `invariant` in a static class is a compile error — no instance boundary exists).

title: a constructor's requires clause may not observe this
rule: A constructor's `requires` may not observe `this` in any of §22.7's senses (no field of the declaring type is assigned at clause time) — it reads parameters and statics only.

title: requires clauses evaluate in declaration order and stop at the first false
rule: In declaration order, stopping at the first clause producing `false` — clause granularity is semantic: the clause is the unit of ... evaluation order (stop at first failure).

title: clauses never distinguish overloads; two members differing only in clauses clash
rule: Clauses never distinguish overloads and are not part of §22.6 resolution; two members differing only in clauses are the same signature and clash.

title: the four auto-property forms are admitted
rule: An auto-property is read-write, read-write with a restricted setter (`private set`), read-only (`readonly`), or read-only with an initializer; the compiler generates the backing field.

title: a readonly auto-property may not be assigned from an ordinary method
rule: A `readonly` auto-property may be assigned only in a field initializer or in a constructor, under §22.8's per-instance assignable context.

title: a constructor may not write another instance's readonly auto-property
rule: The assignment is admitted only through `this` for an instance auto-property — the assignable context is per-instance, so a constructor may not write another value's readonly storage.

title: readonly on an expression-bodied property is rejected
rule: On every body-bearing form read-onlyness is already expressed by the shape, and writing `readonly` there is a compile error.

title: an expression-bodied property without readonly is admitted
rule: An expression-bodied property's body is checked against the declared type; the shape expresses read-onlyness, so no `readonly` is written.

title: readonly on a get-only block-form property is rejected
rule: A get-only block form expresses read-onlyness by its shape; `readonly` there is a compile error.

title: readonly on a block form declaring a setter is rejected
rule: On a block form declaring a setter `readonly` is contradictory and is likewise an error.

title: a block-form property names its setter parameter value implicitly
rule: The implicit setter parameter is `value`. Each accessor uses `=> expression` or `=> do ... end`.

title: a block-form setter body runs on assignment through the property
rule: A property's accessors are member bodies: a store through the property invokes the setter, and a read invokes the getter.

title: an expression-bodied indexer is admitted
rule: An indexer is a property whose name is replaced by a parameter list in square brackets.

title: a block-form indexer closes with a bare end
rule: A block-form indexer's `end` clause has no name to reference; it is plain `end;`.

title: a block-form indexer closed with an identifier label is rejected
rule: An `end`-label that is supplied must match the construct it closes; an indexer has no name to reference, so a supplied identifier is a mismatch.

title: an indexer may take several parameters
rule: An indexer is a property whose name is replaced by `[parameters]`; the list may hold more than one parameter.

title: indexers overload by parameter type list
rule: Indexers may be overloaded by parameter type list.

title: an enum may not declare an indexer
rule: Enums may not declare indexers.

title: a static indexer is rejected
rule: Static indexers are not supported.

title: a ref parameter in an indexer parameter list is rejected
rule: `ref` and `out` parameters are not allowed in indexer parameter lists.

title: a named argument at an index position is rejected
rule: Index arguments are positional-only; the named-argument form (`Identifier :=`) is not admitted at an index position — a compile error naming this rule.

title: an enum may overload an operator
rule: Records, enums, choices, and classes may overload operators; an enum body admits operator overloads among the members it may declare (§10.4), and public static is the required spelling.

title: unary and binary operator overloads are admitted on a record
rule: Records, enums, choices and classes may overload operators; operators are declared as `public static` methods using the `operator` keyword. The unary set is `+`, `-`, `~` and the binary set includes `+`, `-`, `*`.

title: not is not user-overloadable
rule: `not` is not user-overloadable. It is the boolean-negation operator and applies only to `bool`; a domain-specific inversion is a named method.

title: the null-coalescing operator is not overloadable
rule: The null-forgiving `!`, the null-coalescing `??`, and the type-test operators have null-aware or type-system semantics fixed by the language; user types do not customize them.

title: an operator overload declared without public is rejected
rule: `public` is required: an operator invoked through `a + b` syntax has no call-site spelling that could name a restricted member, so any other visibility is a compile error.

title: an operator overload declared without static is rejected
rule: Operators are declared as `public static` methods using the `operator` keyword.

title: equality may not be overloaded on a class
rule: `=` and `<>` may not be overloaded on classes or on inline arrays. For classes, `=` always invokes `Equals`.

title: a homogeneous equality overload with Equals and GetHashCode beside it
rule: A record, enum or choice that overloads `=`/`<>` with both operands of the declaring type must also declare `Equals(T)` and `GetHashCode`.

title: a homogeneous equality overload without Equals and GetHashCode is rejected
rule: The co-declaration rule is compiler-enforced: the three surfaces (`=`, `Equals`, hashing) can otherwise silently diverge exactly where it hurts — `a = b` true while a `Set<T>` treats them as distinct.

title: a lone relational overload is rejected as an incomplete group
rule: Comparison operators must be overloaded as a complete group: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` together; `=` and `<>` together.

title: the four relational operators declared together are admitted
rule: Comparison operators must be overloaded as a complete group: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` together.

title: a ref modifier on an operator parameter is rejected
rule: Operator parameters admit no parameter modifiers: `ref`, `out`, `owned` and `scoped` on an operator's parameter list are rejected semantically.

title: an owned modifier on an operator parameter is rejected
rule: Operands are received as plain borrows (or value copies) under their type kinds; the return slot's optional `owned` is the sole ownership annotation on operators.

title: an operator whose parameters never mention the declaring type is rejected
rule: At least one parameter of an operator overload must be the declaring type; an operator whose parameters never mention it would be unreachable by the resolution rule.

title: a binary overload may carry the declaring type in either position
rule: A binary overload may pair the declaring type with any other type in either position.

title: operands are matched in order, with no automatic commutation
rule: Parameters match operands in order — there is no automatic commutation (`4 - v` is not matched against `operator -(v: V, n: int)`).

title: a block-bodied operator closes with end operator and its token
rule: When an operator overload is block-bodied, the optional name in the closing `end` is written as `end operator OpToken;`.

title: a block-bodied operator closed with the wrong token is rejected
rule: An `end`-label that is supplied must match the construct it closes; for a keyword-labelled construct the operator token is part of the label.

title: an overloaded operator is invoked by the operator syntax
rule: For `a <op> b` on non-primitive operands the candidate set is drawn from the operator overloads declared on the static types of both operands.

title: there is no user-defined conversion between record types
rule: User-defined types cannot declare implicit or explicit conversion operators; the explicit-cast expression `T(value)` applies only to the built-in conversions enumerated in §5.

title: a named factory method is the sanctioned conversion between user types
rule: To express a conversion between user types, define a named factory or instance method.

title: an extension block adds a method and a computed property
rule: An extension block is declared at module level and adds methods and computed read-only properties to a type; inside the block `this` refers to the receiver.

title: an extension block may close with end extension
rule: The block ends with `end;` or `end extension;`.

title: a primitive type may be extended
rule: Classes, interfaces, records, enums and built-in primitive types may be extended.

title: a nullable type may not be extended directly
rule: Nullable types may not be extended directly (`extension int?`); extend the non-nullable form and let callers handle nullability at the call site.

title: a choice may not be extended
rule: The extendable list is closed against the choice kind: choices cannot be extended.

title: an extension block may not declare a field
rule: An extension block declares only methods and computed read-only properties: no fields, auto-properties, constructors, destructors, or `owned` fields.

title: an extension property must be expression-bodied
rule: An extension property is expression-bodied only; the block-accessor form is not admitted — multi-statement logic goes in a method.

title: an extension block may not declare an operator overload
rule: An extension block declares no operator overloads.

title: an extension block may not declare an indexer
rule: An extension block declares no indexers.

title: a static member inside an extension block is rejected
rule: An extension block adds receiver-directed members only: a `static` modifier inside an extension block is a compile error.

title: an extension member may not be private
rule: Extension members must be declared `public` or `internal`; `protected` and `private` are compile errors — an extension block has no declaring class and no inheritance, so §13.1's definitions for those levels do not apply.

title: an extension member may not be virtual
rule: An extension block declares no `virtual`, `override`, `abstract` or `sealed` members — extensions are statically dispatched.

title: a bare identifier in the extended type's argument position binds a parameter
rule: In the extended type's argument positions, each bare single-segment non-nullable identifier introduces a fresh block-level type parameter.

title: a nullable-marked identifier in an argument position is rejected
rule: A nullable-marked identifier in an argument position (`extension Array<T?>`) binds nothing and is a compile error naming this rule — only the bare non-nullable identifier introduces a parameter.

title: a concrete instantiation is a legal extension head
rule: A concrete instantiation is written with keyword/primitive types, qualified names, or generic instantiations — none of which are bare single-segment identifiers, so none binds a parameter.

title: an instance member wins over a same-named extension member
rule: Instance members win — by name. If the receiver's declared type declares any instance member of that name, instance resolution is committed and extension blocks are never consulted for that name on that receiver.

title: a failed instance lookup does not fall back to an extension
rule: If the committed instance lookup fails — no applicable overload — the call is a compile error citing the instance members; it does not fall back to an extension.

title: an extension member is reached when the type declares no such name
rule: If the receiver's type declares no instance member of that name, the compiler searches the current module and all imported modules for extension blocks on the receiver's type, base types, or implemented interfaces.

title: an extension block declared in an imported module reaches the receiver
rule: If the receiver's type declares no instance member of that name, the compiler searches the current module and all imported modules for extension blocks on the receiver's type. `Doubled` is declared in `Lib`, not in `App`, and is reached because `App` imports `Lib`.

title: an extension's own module must be imported even when its type is only used
rule: Extension members are the one exception to use-without-import: they are candidates only from the current module and imported modules (§2.8.3 rule 2). `Widget` reaches `App` transitively through `Factory` with no import needed to *use* it, but `Doubled` lives in `Lib`, which `App` never imports, so it is not a candidate.

title: importing an extension's own module makes it reachable
rule: Extension members are candidates only from the current module and imported modules. Once `App` also imports `Lib`, `Doubled` is a candidate for the `Widget` receiver.

title: a default-internal extension block is invisible from an importing module
rule: The compiler considers only extension members visible at the call site (§26.3's effective-visibility rule); an extension block is `public` or `internal`, default `internal` (§26.1). `Lib`'s block carries no `public` keyword, so it is internal to `Lib` and not a candidate for `App`'s call, even though `App` imports `Lib`.

title: a public extension block is visible from an importing module
rule: The compiler considers only extension members visible at the call site. Marking the block `public` makes its member a candidate for any importing module.

title: two equally-specific extensions from different imported modules are ambiguous
rule: If two equally-specific extensions match, the call is a compile error (rule 4). Nothing in the same module can conflict this way (§26.6 merges same-module blocks and rejects duplicate *signatures*); the ambiguity here comes from two distinct imported modules each declaring the same substituted head and name.

title: narrowing the import to one candidate module resolves the ambiguity
rule: The remedies for extension ambiguity are the mechanisms that exist: remove or narrow a conflicting import. Importing only `ExtA` leaves one candidate, so the call resolves.

title: specificity ordering picks the more specific extension across two imported modules
rule: Extensions on the most specific type are preferred (rule 3, §26.5.1). `ExtCircle`'s block on `Circle` is more specific than `ExtShape`'s block on `Shape`, and the ordering holds even though the two candidates come from two different imported modules, neither importing the other.

title: instance members win over a same-named extension imported from another module
rule: Instance members win — by name. If the receiver's declared type declares any instance member of that name, instance resolution is committed and extension blocks are never consulted — regardless of which module declares the conflicting extension.

title: a failed instance lookup does not fall back to an extension from another module
rule: If the committed instance lookup fails — no applicable overload — the call is a compile error citing the instance members; it does not fall back to an extension, even one visible from an imported module.

title: the current module's own extension conflicts with an imported one
rule: The compiler searches the current module and all imported modules for extension blocks. `App`'s own block on `Shape` and the imported `ExtShape` block are equally specific (identical substituted heads), so the call is ambiguous (rule 4) exactly as if both candidates were imported.

title: an extension on a class outranks one on an interface it implements
rule: An extension on E1 is more specific than one on E2 when E1 is a subtype of E2 and E2 is not a subtype of E1. Class beats interface implemented by that class: for a receiver of type `Array<int>`, `extension Array<T>` is more specific than `extension IEnumerable<T>`.

title: an extension on a derived interface outranks one on the interface it extends
rule: An extension on E1 is more specific than one on E2 when E1 is a subtype of E2 and E2 is not a subtype of E1. Derived interface beats extended interface: `IReadOnlyCollection<T>` extends `IEnumerable<T>` (stdlib §4.1), and `Array<int>` implements both.

title: identical substituted heads never auto-rank, even with a where clause on one side
rule: Candidates with identical substituted heads never auto-rank: neither a more-concrete-looking declared head nor a stronger `where` clause on the same head makes one candidate more specific than the other. A `where` clause is an applicability filter, never a ranking signal. `extension IEnumerable<T> where T: value` and `extension IEnumerable<int>` both substitute to `IEnumerable<int>` for an `Array<int>` receiver.

title: distinct names remove an identical-substituted-heads ambiguity
rule: Candidates with identical substituted heads never auto-rank and are rejected as ambiguous (rule 4, §26.5); the recorded remedy for colliding blocks under the author's control is distinct names, which removes the collision entirely.

title: multiple extension blocks on the same type are merged
rule: Multiple `extension` blocks targeting the same type may appear across files in the same module. The compiler merges them.

title: duplicate signatures across merged blocks are a compile error
rule: Multiple `extension` blocks targeting the same type may appear; the compiler merges them. Duplicate signatures are a compile error.

title: merged blocks may contribute distinct overloads of the same name
rule: Multiple `extension` blocks targeting the same type are merged; duplicate *signatures* are a compile error, but two blocks contributing different overloads of one name are not duplicates.

title: an extension cannot return this as owned
rule: The receiver is always a borrow; extensions cannot store `this`, return it as `owned`, or dispose it.

title: an extension may return this as an ordinary receiver-sourced borrow
rule: The receiver is always a borrow; extensions cannot return it as `owned` — but an ordinary (non-owned) borrow return of the receiver remains legal, the same receiver-sourced borrow return every instance or extension method may make.

title: extensions may return owned values
rule: Extensions may return `owned` values.

title: a value-kind extension body cannot store into the receiver's own storage
rule: For a value-kind receiver, §9.4's value-receiver rule applies in the extension body exactly as in a declared member body: a store landing in the receiver's own storage is a compile error.

title: a value-kind extension body may read the receiver's own storage
rule: For a value-kind receiver, §9.4's value-receiver rule applies in the extension body exactly as in a declared member body — only a *store* landing in the receiver's own storage is rejected; a bare read of the same storage is ordinary member access and is legal.

title: other parameters may be owned in an extension, following normal method rules
rule: Other parameters may be `owned`, following normal method rules.

title: a two-parameter function type mirrors a two-parameter method declaration
rule: A function type is written `(params) -> returnType`; `method Foo(x: int, y: int): int` parallels `(int, int) -> int`.

title: a method with no return type has function type returning the unit type
rule: A method without a return type has function type returning `()`; `method Foo()` parallels `() -> ()`.

title: an owned-parameter function type is distinct from the unmarked form
rule: Function types may include the parameter modifier `owned`; `method Foo(owned t: T)` parallels `(owned T) -> ()`, and the modifier is part of the type.

title: the out-owned modifier compound forms its own function type
rule: Function types may include the modifier combination `out owned`; `method Foo(out owned r: T)` parallels `(out owned T) -> ()`.

title: named parameters in a function type are documentation, calls are positional
rule: Function types may include parameter names; names are documentation only and do not affect type identity — `(int, int, int) -> bool` and the named form are the same type, and calls are positional.

title: a named-argument call through a function-typed value is rejected
rule: A call through a function-typed value admits no named argument (v0.295): the named form at an invocation whose callee is a function-typed value is a compile error naming this rule.

title: a call through a function-typed value takes positional arguments
rule: A call through a function-typed value admits no named argument (v0.295); calls through a function-typed value are positional.

title: a wider-parameter function value is usable where a narrower one is expected
rule: Parameter slots of class or interface type are contravariant — the target's parameter type must implicitly reference-convert to the value's; a `(Animal) -> ()` value is usable where `(Dog) -> ()` is expected.

title: a narrower-parameter function value is not usable where a wider one is expected
rule: Parameter slots of class or interface type are contravariant — the target's parameter type must implicitly reference-convert to the value's; a `(Dog) -> ()` value is not usable where `(Animal) -> ()` is expected.

title: a narrower-return function value is usable where a wider return is expected
rule: The return slot, when of class or interface type, is covariant — the value's return type must implicitly reference-convert to the target's; a `() -> Dog` value is usable as `() -> Animal`.

title: a wider-return function value is not usable where a narrower return is expected
rule: The return slot, when of class or interface type, is covariant — the value's return type must implicitly reference-convert to the target's; a `() -> Animal` value is not usable as `() -> Dog`.

title: a function value is never usable at a function type with a different parameter count
rule: Every rule of function-type assignability is slot-wise over equal parameter counts — a value is never usable at a function type with a different number of parameter slots, whatever the slots' types (v0.296).

title: modifier slots must match exactly between two function-typed values
rule: Modifier slots (`owned`/`ref`/`out`/`out owned`/`scoped`) must match exactly (§27.1); there is no conversion between a modified and an unmodified parameter slot.

title: parentheses around a function type are required before a trailing question mark
rule: The parentheses around the function type are required before `?`; `((int) -> bool)?` is a nullable function returning bool, callable with the null-conditional call form.

title: a null-conditional call on a null function value is a no-op yielding null
rule: `((int) -> bool)?` is a nullable function returning bool; the null-conditional call result is nullable, and a null hole renders the four characters `null` (§18.5).

title: a non-null function returning a nullable value is a distinct type from a nullable function
rule: Without the parentheses, the `?` attaches to the return type — `(int) -> bool?` is a non-null function returning a nullable bool, a different type from `((int) -> bool)?`, and modifier/nullability slots follow the standard §7 rules under assignability (§27.1.1).

title: a lambda's parameter types are inferred from the target type
rule: When the lambda's target type is known from context, parameter type annotations may be omitted; the compiler infers them from the target.

title: a zero-parameter lambda spells the empty parameter list, never omits it
rule: A lambda expression's parenthesized parameter list is the empty pair for zero parameters; there is no paren-free form.

title: a return-type ascription is a written integer target for a target-typed constant
rule: The return-type ascription behaves exactly as a method's declared return type; it is a written integer target for §4.2's target-typed integer constant — `lambda(): long => 3_000_000_000` is admitted by §5.1's constant narrowing.

title: a block-bodied lambda where one path returns a value and another does not is rejected
rule: A body where one path returns a value and another exits without one is a compile error, the same totality rule as for methods.

title: a value-returning lambda does not convert to a procedure function type
rule: A target type, when present, is checked against the procedure-lambda classification — a procedure-bodied lambda does not convert to a value-returning function type, nor the reverse.

title: a lambda literal at a target-typed non-call position admits an implicit widening body
rule: A lambda literal at a position that supplies a function-typed target other than a call argument is admitted under the argument-position rule (v0.292); its inferred return type must equal the target's return slot or implicitly convert to it — `var f: (int) -> long := lambda(x) => x * 2;` is admitted, the `int` body widening to `long`.

title: an ascription narrows what a target-typed non-call position admits
rule: An ascribed lambda's ascription must agree with the target, judged as a value's return type under §27.1.1 — so an ascription narrows what the position admits: `var g: (int) -> long := lambda(x): int => x * 2;` is rejected where the unascribed form is admitted.

title: several ignore parameters may coexist in one lambda's parameter list
rule: A parameter slot may be the ignore `_`; because nothing is named, several ignores may coexist — `lambda(_, _) => 0` is legal.

title: no parameter modifier composes with the bare ignore
rule: No parameter modifier and no type annotation compose with the bare ignore — `FuncParamMods` with `_` is rejected, because a `ref` parameter reads and writes through its operand, which an ignore cannot supply.

title: a top-level lambda with no target type must specify parameter types
rule: In top-level contexts with no target type (`var f := lambda(x) => x * 2;`), parameter types must be specified.

title: an explicit parameter type admits a top-level lambda with no target type
rule: In top-level contexts with no target type, parameter types must be specified; an explicitly typed parameter satisfies the requirement.

title: a positional-record destructuring parameter binds each field by desugaring
rule: A lambda parameter may be a positional record destructuring; `lambda(Entry(k, v)) => ...` behaves as a lambda over the record type with each slot bound to the corresponding positional field.

title: a destructuring parameter slot may be the discard
rule: Each slot of a lambda-parameter destructuring is a naked identifier binding, a discard `_`, or a nested destructuring meeting the same rules.

title: a destructuring parameter's head must exactly name the target's parameter type
rule: The head of a lambda-parameter destructuring must name a positional record type, and it must be exactly the parameter's type: when a target type supplies the parameter type, a head naming any other type is a compile error.

title: a constant is a refutable element and is rejected inside a destructuring parameter
rule: Constants, ranges, relationals, type tests, `var`-form bindings, and alternatives are compile errors in destructuring parameter position — they are refutable, and a parameter list is not a `case`.

title: a captured local is shared, not copied, between a closure and its enclosing scope
rule: A lambda may reference variables from its enclosing scope; captured variables are heap-allocated in a closure object, and modifications to a captured variable inside the lambda are visible outside, and vice versa.

title: each for-loop iteration produces a fresh binding a captured lambda sees
rule: For `for` loop variables, each iteration produces a fresh binding; a lambda captured inside the body sees that iteration's value.

title: a closure may not assign to a captured owned binding
rule: For a captured owned binding the sharing is read-only in the ownership sense — the lambda may not assign to it, transfer from it, or dispose it (§28.3).

title: a closure may not move a captured owned binding
rule: `move` is an error inside a closure over a captured owned binding — captured owned bindings are uniformly in borrow state, so a closure cannot consume, reassign, or dispose one (§28.3).

title: a closure may not discard a captured owned binding
rule: For a captured owned binding, an explicit `Dispose()` or discard of it is a compile error — a closure cannot consume, reassign, or dispose a captured owned binding (§28.3).

title: a closure may not be stored in a field while it captures a borrow
rule: A closure is a borrow-carrying value whose source set is the union of its captures' sources; while it captures anything, it may not be stored in a field or a collection (§28.3, v0.298).

title: a closure may not be returned from the method while it captures a borrow
rule: While a closure captures anything, it may not be returned from the method — a function type announces no source set, so no caller could bound it (§28.3, v0.298).

title: a closure that captures a borrow may be passed to a plain function-typed parameter
rule: A capture-bearing closure may be passed as an argument to a function-typed parameter — a plain parameter is call-bounded, and the callee's use is bounded by the call (§28.3, v0.298).

title: reassigning a plain function-typed local from a capturing closure is legal
rule: Reassigning a plain function-typed local is fine — each assignment is checked on its own (§28.3, v0.298).

title: using var on a function-typed local forbids reassignment
rule: A closure value may be bound to a local, plain `var` or `using var` alike, whose scope does not strictly enclose any source's scope, `using var` adding only non-reassignability (§28.3, v0.298).

title: a static method reference is usable directly as a function value
rule: When a lambda's body is just a call to an existing method, the method reference may be used directly; method references work for static methods.

title: a property reference produces the getter, typed (Receiver) -> PropertyType
rule: Method references work for properties; a property reference produces the getter, and its type is `(Receiver) -> PropertyType` for instance properties.

title: a bound instance method reference captures the receiver at formation
rule: Method references work for instance methods — the instance is captured at formation, by reference for class-typed receivers.

title: a reference to an overloaded method with no target type is ambiguous
rule: When no target type is available (e.g. `var f := Math.Abs;` with no annotation), the reference is ambiguous and the compiler reports an error pointing to the candidate overloads.

title: a type annotation disambiguates a reference to an overloaded method
rule: The user disambiguates an ambiguous method reference by adding a type annotation: `var f: (int) -> int := Math.Abs;`.

title: an exact-match overload is preferred over a converting one when forming a reference
rule: Among unifying candidates, one whose parameter types and return type match the target's exactly is preferred; candidates that unify only through conversion are co-equal and lose to the exact candidate.

title: a function-typed value is called with ordinary call syntax
rule: A function-typed value is called with ordinary call syntax: `var sum := add(2, 3);`.

title: a null-conditional call on a null function value is a no-op
rule: `maybeHandler?(42);` is a null-conditional call — a no-op when the function value is null.

title: the result of a null-conditional call through a present function value is nullable
rule: The null-conditional call result is nullable.

title: two separately-constructed lambdas with identical source text are not equal
rule: A lambda (closure) value equals only itself — reference equality on the closure instance. Two separately-constructed lambdas with identical source text are not equal, even if they capture the same variables.

title: repeated evaluations of a method reference on the same receiver are guaranteed equal
rule: A method reference equals another method reference iff both denote the same method and, for instance references, are bound to the same receiver — repeated evaluations of `obj.Method` on the same class-typed `obj` are therefore guaranteed equal.

title: a lambda never equals a method reference
rule: A lambda never equals a method reference.

title: a type alias is a pure synonym interchangeable with the aliased type
rule: A type alias is a pure synonym — it does not create a new type; `UserId` and `int` are interchangeable.

title: a generic type alias may not reference itself
rule: A generic alias may not reference itself (no recursive aliases) and must resolve to a concrete type after substitution.

title: an interface-typed value may be discarded and is disposed by dispatch at end of statement
rule: The discard form `_ := expr;` disposes the value at the end of the discard statement for any class or interface type; at an interface-typed location the discard is permitted and disposes via runtime dispatch, so a future non-trivial implementation poses no cross-module hazard (§28's summary of disposal obligations by type kind).

title: a record local carries no disposal obligation and draws no discharge diagnostic
rule: Records, enums, and primitives need no disposal — their memory is reclaimed when their containing scope exits; the chapter's summary table records "Disposal required? No" for each, with no mechanism to announce (§28).

title: owned on a method parameter of class type is admitted
rule: The `owned` modifier is admissible on method parameter declarations: `method M(owned p: T)` takes ownership of the value at the call site.

title: owned on a method parameter of primitive type is rejected
rule: The declared type of an `owned` parameter, nullability stripped, must be a class type, an interface type, or a bare type parameter; a primitive is a compile error.

title: owned on a return type of class type is admitted
rule: The `owned` modifier is admissible on return type declarations: `method Acquire(): owned Connection` transfers responsibility for disposal to the caller.

title: owned on a return type of enum type is rejected
rule: On a primitive, `string`, a function type, an ordinary record, an enum, or the unit type, `owned` is a compile error: such values carry no disposal obligation to transfer.

title: owned on an out parameter of class type is admitted
rule: The `owned` modifier is admissible on `out` parameter declarations: `out owned p: T` produces an owned reference for the caller to take.

title: owned on a function-type parameter slot is admitted and consumes at the call
rule: The parameter slot of a function type may carry `owned`: `(owned T) -> ()` — the modifier is part of the function type's identity, and an invocation through the slot consumes the argument.

title: owned choice payload field is admitted
rule: The `owned` modifier is admissible on choice payload fields: `Fetched(owned response: Response)` takes ownership at construction.

title: owned inline-array slot marker is admitted
rule: The `owned` keyword placed between the size and the closing bracket (`[N owned]T?`) marks the inline array's slots as owned.

title: owned on a bare unconstrained type parameter is admitted
rule: `owned` requires the declared type, nullability stripped, to be a class type, an interface type, or a bare type parameter; at a bare type parameter the generic body type-checks under the class-or-interface assumption.

title: owned on a bare type parameter constrained to value is rejected at the declaration
rule: A declaration whose constraints exclude class and interface substitutions outright (`where T: value`) rejects the `owned` marker at the declaration — it could never be more than redundant.

title: Dispose is idempotent at run time: a second explicit call performs no second disposal
rule: `Dispose()` on any class instance is idempotent: the first call performs the disposal; subsequent calls are no-ops. That no-op carve-out states the **runtime** contract of a repeated call and suppresses no diagnostic — a second `Dispose()` on the same binding is a use of it and draws §28.2's use-after-dispose warning.

title: Dispose through a record receiver has no such member
rule: `Dispose()` is not on `Object`; it is class-only. Records, enums, primitives, and inline arrays do not implement `IDisposable`.

title: a straight-line read after an explicit Dispose raises the use-after-dispose warning
rule: The compiler must emit a warning when a local variable is used after an explicit `Dispose()` call on the same variable that dominates the use site on every path.

title: a straight-line read after a discard raises the same mandatory warning
rule: The compiler must emit a warning when a local variable is used after a discard of the binding that dominates the use site on every path.

title: a conditional dispose joins to maybe-consumed and a later read is rejected
rule: A conditional kill is treated more strictly: at a join of an explicitly- disposed path with a still-owned path the variable is maybe-consumed and a later use is a compile error.

title: every class implicitly implements IDisposable via a generated Dispose
rule: Every class implicitly implements `IDisposable` via a compiler-generated `Dispose()`; user code declares no `Dispose` member, and the generated one is callable on an instance the caller owns.

title: a class member named Dispose is rejected at a non-empty parameter list
rule: Declaring a member named `Dispose` on a class or a record is a compile error at that declaration, whatever its parameter list; the rule is keyed on the name, and at an optional-parameter declaration `Dispose(mode: int := 0)` it is additionally ambiguous against the compiler-generated `Dispose()` at every zero-argument call.

title: a record member named Dispose is rejected
rule: Declaring a member named `Dispose` on a class or a **record** is a compile error at that declaration, whatever its parameter list; on a record the name promises a disposal contract the kind does not have (§9.7 — records do not implement `IDisposable`).

title: the same member under any other name is admitted, optional parameter included
rule: The rule is keyed on the **name** `Dispose`, not on the shape of the declaration: a class member with the identical parameter list under any other name collides with no compiler-generated member and is admitted, callable at zero arguments through §22.5's optional parameter.

title: an interface may declare a member named Dispose
rule: Interfaces are unaffected by the class-and-record rejection of a member named `Dispose` — `IDisposable` declares `method Dispose();` and interfaces extend it.

title: the default build is checked: a read through a surviving borrow after Dispose faults
rule: Checked mode — any instance member access on a logically-disposed instance — an instance method call, a property or indexer accessor invocation, or a field access through the reference — raises `DisposedAccessException`. This is the default: a build that selects neither mode is a checked build.

title: the same program under the explicitly selected unchecked relaxation is accepted only
rule: Unchecked (release) mode — use of a disposed instance is undefined behavior; a build selects it explicitly. A program that would raise `DisposedAccessException` in checked mode has undefined behavior in unchecked mode: unchecked mode is the release-build relaxation of the default checked semantics, not a different language.

title: a static method returning a plain class type is rejected at the declaration
rule: A static method whose declared return type (nullability stripped) is a class or interface type must announce its classification in the signature — `owned`, a mint-announcing type, or a bare type parameter with a non-empty source set. Any other such signature is a compile error at the declaration.

title: an undischarged plain-var owned local raises the must-use warning
rule: The compiler emits a warning at the implicit-drop site of a plain-`var` owned local, to surface a drop that may have been unintended; the exception edge does not carry it.

title: an unmarked read of an owned binding is always a borrow
rule: The no-silent-consume rule: an unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes; `var b := a;` is always a borrow of `a`.

title: an owned argument fed without move is rejected
rule: Omitting `move` is a compile error when a named owned binding feeds an `owned` argument: write `M(move x)`.

title: an owned argument fed with move is admitted
rule: `move x` is the required spelling for a named owned binding feeding an `owned` argument.

title: assigning a borrow into an owned-state local is rejected
rule: State match on reassignment: an owned-state LHS requires an owned RHS; assigning a borrow to an owned-state LHS is rejected.

title: assigning a marked transfer into an owned-state local is admitted
rule: An owned-state LHS accepts a named owned binding under the explicit transfer marker: `x := move y;`, disposing the displaced value.

title: an if-expression merging an owned arm with an unmarked owned-binding arm is rejected
rule: owned meets borrowed at an if-expression merge is rejected; an unmarked read of a named owned binding is a borrow arm.

title: marking the if-expression arm transfer equalizes the merge
rule: The marked arm transfer `move x` as an if-expression branch is an owned producer, equalizing a merge with another owned arm.

title: move on a return operand under an owned return is rejected as redundant
rule: The transfer marker is rejected as redundant at a marker-free position: `return x;` under an owned return, never `return move x;`.

title: a return operand under an owned return carries no marker
rule: `return` under an `owned` return type is marker-free: the declared return type already announces the transfer.

title: move on a throw operand is rejected as redundant
rule: The transfer marker is rejected as redundant on a `throw` operand: `throw x;`, never `throw move x;`.

title: a throw operand carries no marker
rule: The `throw` keyword itself announces the consume; no marker is written at the operand.

title: move on a discard right-hand side is rejected as redundant
rule: The transfer marker is rejected as redundant on a discard right-hand side: `_ := x;`, never `_ := move x;`.

title: a discard right-hand side carries no marker
rule: The discard itself is the announcement; a named owned binding discards unmarked.

title: move on a store into an owned field is rejected as redundant
rule: The transfer marker is rejected as redundant on a store into an `owned` field: `sink._f := x;`, never `sink._f := move x;`.

title: a store into an owned field carries no marker
rule: The declared `owned` field already announces the transfer; the store is marker-free.

title: move on an owning iterator's yield return is rejected as redundant
rule: The transfer marker is rejected as redundant on an owning iterator's `yield return`: the declared owning interface already announces.

title: an owning iterator's yield return carries no marker
rule: The owning iterator's declared return type is the announcement; `yield return x;` is marker-free.

title: move on a borrow is rejected
rule: `move` is also an error on a borrow: the marker asserts a transfer, and a plain parameter carries no obligation to transfer.

title: using var y := move x is the adoption spelling
rule: `using var y := move x;` is the standard way to turn an owned local's obligation into scope-bound disposal: the value is disposed at the end of the adopting block.

title: using var y := x, unmarked, is a borrow-pin that assumes no obligation
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` over a named owned binding does not adopt: no obligation is assumed, `x` keeps it and stays readable, and the pin extends `x`'s required liveness to the block's end.

title: a using var local is not reassignable
rule: `using var` is a scope pin: non-reassignable.

title: a using var local can never be moved out of
rule: `using var` is never movable out of: `using var fresh := new Buffer(); return fresh;` is a compile error; a factory uses plain `var`.

title: a borrow assigned to a local whose scope strictly encloses its source is rejected at the assignment
rule: A borrow may not be assigned to a local whose scope strictly encloses its source's scope; rejected at the assignment, not at the later use.

title: the back-reference idiom admits a parameter-sourced borrow stored in a field
rule: A borrow whose source outlives the object is admissible: the back-reference idiom binds a constructor parameter into a non-owned class-typed field.

title: a borrow of a scope-bound local stored in a field is rejected
rule: A borrowed scope-bound local never satisfies the field-store rule: it is disposed at the end of its scope, which a field of the object outlives.

title: a borrow of an owned parameter stored in a field is rejected
rule: An `owned` parameter is scope-bound: the method disposes its undischarged value at its own end, so a borrow of it is rejected in a field store exactly as a borrow of a scope-bound local is.

title: a fresh owned value returned through a plain class-typed return is rejected
rule: An instance method whose declared return type is a plain concrete class type may return only a receiver-sourced borrow; a fresh owned value is rejected — declare `owned`.

title: returning a receiver-sourced borrow is admitted
rule: A receiver-sourced borrow from an instance method — a bare field read — is an admissible borrow return.

title: a merge of an owned branch with a borrowed branch is rejected
rule: At a control-flow merge, owned meets borrowed is rejected: the program must equalize the branches before the merge; the compiler never equalizes for it.

title: equalizing both branches to owned admits the merge
rule: Producing an owned value on both branches equalizes the merge to owned.

title: reading a variable that is owned on one path and moved-from on another is rejected
rule: owned meets moved-from is maybe-consumed at the join; a later use is a compile error.

title: consuming an owned binding while a live local borrow of it exists is rejected
rule: The consume-site freeze: consuming an owned binding while a live local borrow of its current value exists is a compile error.

title: transfer first, then re-borrow from the new owner, is the freeze's mechanical rewrite
rule: The mechanical rewrite for the frozen case is transfer first, then re-borrow from the new owner.

title: an explicit Dispose while a borrow is live is not frozen
rule: Site-announced kills are unfrozen: an explicit `Dispose()` is permitted while a live local borrow of the value exists — a borrow is live when some path from the consume site reaches a later use of it.

title: a discard while a borrow is live is not frozen
rule: Site-announced kills are unfrozen: the discard `_ := x;` is permitted while borrows of the value live.

title: a static method returning owned T announces its classification and is admitted
rule: Every admissible static signature is type-announced: `owned` on the declared return type admits a fresh or owned value.

title: an instance method that creates a fresh value through a non-owned return is rejected
rule: An instance method that produces a fresh value must declare `owned`; a freshly-produced owned value returned through a non-owned return is rejected.

title: declaring owned on the return admits the freshly-produced value
rule: An instance method that creates something must say `owned`; the declared `owned` return admits the fresh value.

title: a property getter returning a fresh owned value is rejected
rule: A property or indexer getter may never return a fresh owned value; getters lend only.

title: a property getter returning a receiver-sourced borrow is admitted
rule: A getter may lend a receiver-sourced borrow; expose a factory as a method returning `owned T` instead for a fresh value.

title: an unbound owned temporary is disposed at the end of the full expression
rule: An unbound owned temporary is disposed at the end of the full expression in which it is produced, after every borrowing use within that expression.

title: a binding atom disposes its owned temporary at the atom's completion
rule: A binding atom's clause whose initializer is an owned production is a named unbound owned temporary bounded by the atom, disposed at the atom's completion if undischarged.

title: a borrow of a binding atom's own owned binding may not escape the atom
rule: A borrow sourced by an atom binding may not escape the atom, not in the body's value; it is rejected, never lifetime-extended.

title: a case scrutinee's unbound owned temporary survives the selected arm
rule: A `case` scrutinee extends the disposal boundary to the whole `case` construct, so pattern bindings survive the selected arm.

title: an uninitialized local adopts the ownership state of its first assignment
rule: A local holding no classified value adopts the classification of the first assignment reaching it on each path; two owned-producing branches adopt owned on both.

title: an owned local live across an exception edge is disposed during unwinding
rule: Edge parity: owned locals live when an exception propagates out of their enclosing block are disposed implicitly during stack unwinding, exactly as on the normal edge.

title: a do end block disposes a using var early, before the outer scope continues
rule: A `using var` local is owned and additionally subject to scope-based disposal at the end of the enclosing block; a `do … end` block is such a block, so the value is disposed at its end, not at the method's.

title: an undischarged plain-var owned local in a library method draws the must-use warning
rule: The compiler emits a warning at the implicit-drop site of a plain-`var` owned local that is not trivial-dispose under §28.9's ceremony exemption, to surface a drop that may have been unintended.

title: using var suppresses the must-use warning on an owned local
rule: The warning is **suppressed** when the local is declared `using var` (the scope-bound intent is then explicit).

title: an explicit Dispose suppresses the must-use warning on an owned local
rule: The warning is **suppressed** ... when it is explicitly disposed or discarded.

title: a discard suppresses the must-use warning on an owned local
rule: The warning is **suppressed** ... when it is explicitly disposed or discarded — `_ := …` (§17.13).

title: a move into an owned argument suppresses the must-use warning
rule: The warning is **suppressed** ... when it is moved or returned (no implicit drop occurs).

title: returning an owned local under an owned return suppresses the must-use warning
rule: The warning is **suppressed** ... when it is moved or returned (no implicit drop occurs); a `return` operand under an `owned` return is a marker-free position.

title: the null-conditional dispose spelling suppresses the must-use warning
rule: The warning is **suppressed** ... when it is explicitly disposed or discarded — including through the null-conditional and null-forgiving spellings `x?.Dispose()` / `x!.Dispose()`, required for nullable owned locals.

title: the null-forgiving dispose spelling suppresses the must-use warning
rule: The warning is **suppressed** ... when it is explicitly disposed or discarded — including through the null-conditional and null-forgiving spellings `x?.Dispose()` / `x!.Dispose()`, required for nullable owned locals.

title: an undischarged owned parameter draws the must-use warning at its declaration
rule: The rule is uniform across body kinds: the must-use warning attaches at the implicit-drop site of a plain-`var` owned local **or `owned` parameter** that is not trivial-dispose.

title: the using var move adoption suppresses the owned-parameter must-use warning
rule: The adoption idiom `using var r := move reader;` suppresses the must-use warning on an `owned` parameter exactly as `using var` suppresses the local form.

title: under the report mode, a plain constructor parameter stored into a non-owned field reports
rule: In the trust-admission report mode, at every site where the compiler makes an admission that rests on a K4.3-recorded trust clause — a parameter-, receiver- or field-path-sourced borrow stored into a non-`owned` class- or interface-typed field — the compiler emits a warning naming the rule and its clause.

title: under the trust-admission report mode, a scoped construction reports nothing
rule: A class- or interface-typed `scoped` parameter upgrades the residual-trust back-reference admission to a static bound with no residual trust (spec §28.14); the trust-admission report mode reports only admissions that rest on a K4.3-recorded trust clause.

title: under the trust-admission report mode, a keys-based store reports nothing
rule: A compilation unit that emits no report under the trust-admission report mode carries no recorded trust clause: a SlotHandle stored in a field or a collection is a value, not a borrow, and no K4.3 clause attaches to it.

title: under the report mode, a parameter borrow added to a borrowing collection field reports
rule: In the trust-admission report mode, a parameter-, receiver- or field-path-sourced borrow stored into a borrowing-family collection (spec §28.11's store rule) is an admission resting on a K4.3-recorded trust clause, and the compiler emits a warning naming the rule and its clause.

title: outside the trust-admission report mode, an admitted collection-held borrow draws no diagnostic
rule: The trust-admission report is informative: it changes no verdict and no generated code, and outside the mode it is not emitted.

title: under the trust-admission report mode, abandoning a task minted over a borrowed receiver reports
rule: In the trust-admission report mode, a borrow held by a pending frame past the call that minted it — a task passed to Task.FireAndForget — is an admission resting on a K4.3-recorded trust clause (spec §30.1's settlement obligation), and the compiler emits a warning naming the rule and its clause.

title: under the trust-admission report mode, awaiting the task in its sources' scope reports nothing
rule: The settlement obligation of a frame holding a borrowed receiver is discharged by awaiting the task before any source's scope exits (spec §30.1); the trust-admission report mode reports only admissions that rest on a K4.3-recorded trust clause, and an awaited frame carries none.

title: the generated Dispose runs the destructor body, then owned fields, then the base chain
rule: The compiler generates a public, idempotent `Dispose()` that (1) runs the destructor body, (2) disposes all owned-bearing fields in reverse declaration order, (3) chains to the base class's `Dispose()`.

title: destructors run in subclass-to-base order across three levels
rule: Destructors run in subclass-to-base order.

title: Dispose cannot be overridden
rule: `Dispose()` cannot be overridden; the customization point is `destructor`.

title: an owning-inline-array field disposes only its non-null slots
rule: Disposing all owned-bearing fields covers fields of owning-inline-array type (`[N owned]T?`): each non-null slot's `Dispose()` is called, and a null slot disposes nothing.

title: the destructor body runs exactly once, the first time Dispose is called
rule: A class may declare at most one destructor. Its body runs exactly once, the first time `Dispose()` is called.

title: a class may declare at most one destructor
rule: A class may declare at most one destructor.

title: a throwing disposer does not skip the remaining disposals in the same cleanup pass
rule: In a multi-value cleanup pass, a throwing disposer does not skip the remaining values: every remaining disposal still runs, and the exception then propagates from the disposal point.

title: the destructor body runs on disposal, never on construction unwind
rule: A constructor that throws unwinds instead: owned fields assigned before the throwing statement are disposed, and the throwing class's own destructor body is not run.

title: an owned field of class type is admitted and auto-disposed with its container
rule: Owned fields are restricted to class- or interface-typed fields; a class holding one needs no destructor, the field being disposed with its container.

title: owned on a string field is rejected
rule: The declared type of an `owned` slot, nullability stripped, must be a class type, an interface type, or a bare type parameter. On `string` — a runtime-managed type — `owned` is a compile error.

title: an owned field of interface type is admitted and disposes via dynamic dispatch
rule: Only fields whose type is a class type or an interface type may be `owned`. Interface-typed owned fields are admitted because runtime dispatch resolves disposal to the underlying class's `Dispose()`.

title: owned on a function-typed field is rejected
rule: Function-typed fields may not be `owned`. Function values are runtime-managed.

title: owned on a class-typed field is admitted (function-typed field twin)
rule: Only fields whose type is a class type or an interface type may be `owned`; a class type is admitted where a function type is not.

title: owned on an inline-array field without the owned slot marker is rejected
rule: Inline-array fields (`[N]T`, `[N]T?`) without the `owned` slot marker may not be `owned`. The array's slots hold borrows; there is no per-slot ownership to manage.

title: an inline-array field without the owned slot marker is admitted unmarked
rule: Inline-array fields (`[N]T`, `[N]T?`) without the `owned` slot marker may not be `owned`; declared without the field modifier, the field is ordinary borrow-holding storage.

title: an owning-inline-array field needs no owned field modifier
rule: Inline-array fields with the `owned` slot marker (`[N owned]T`, `[N owned]T?`) are admissible as class fields without a separate `owned` modifier on the field; the inline array's own slot marker already signals that the class's generated `Dispose()` disposes each non-null slot (§28.4 step 2), and no user-written destructor is required.

title: double-marking an owning-inline-array field owned is rejected
rule: Writing `private owned slots: [16 owned]Connection?;` is rejected as a double-marking error — the field modifier is omitted because the type-level marker already conveys the obligation.

title: an owned field on a record is rejected
rule: Records may not have `owned` fields (records support only copy semantics, not move semantics).

title: a plain (non-owned) class-typed field on a record is admitted
rule: Records may not have `owned` fields; a plain reference-typed field (a borrow) is ordinary record storage — reference-typed fields in records are always borrows.

title: an owning-inline-array field on a record is rejected
rule: Records also cannot have inline-array fields whose slots carry the `owned` marker (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`); such fields are move-only value types, and records support only copy semantics.

title: a plain inline-array field (no owned slot marker) on a record is admitted
rule: Records cannot have inline-array fields whose slots carry the `owned` marker; an inline-array field without that marker holds per-slot borrows or value-typed copies, which a record may hold.

title: a generic owned field instantiated at a runtime-managed type is rejected
rule: When a generic class declares `private owned _slot: T`, the restriction "only fields of class or interface types may be `owned`" is checked at instantiation. Instantiating with a type that satisfies `where T: class` but is neither a class nor an interface (`string`, function types) is a compile error at the instantiation site.

title: a generic owned field instantiated at a class type is admitted
rule: A generic class's `owned` field is checked per instantiation; a class-typed instantiation of `where T: class` is admissible.

title: owned fields are disposed in reverse declaration order
rule: The `owned` modifier auto-disposes the field when the containing object is disposed, in reverse declaration order.

title: owned fields are disposed after the destructor body runs
rule: The `owned` modifier auto-disposes the field when the containing object is disposed, after the destructor body runs.

title: a null owned field disposes nothing
rule: A nullable owned field is null-checked before disposal, and a null field disposes nothing.

title: a bare read of an owned field returns as a receiver-sourced borrow
rule: A bare read of an owned field lends and may be returned through a non-`owned` return type as a borrow of the field — its source is the receiver.

title: a freshly-produced owned value stored into a non-owned field is rejected
rule: A freshly-produced owned value — a `new` expression, a call returning `owned T`, a `move` expression, or an owned operator result — stored into a non-`owned` (borrow) field is an error.

title: a freshly-produced owned value stored into an owned field is admitted
rule: A freshly-produced owned value stored into a non-`owned` field is an error; declaring the field `owned` gives the containing object a place to hold and dispose it.

title: a property getter returning a fresh owned value is rejected
rule: A property or indexer getter may not return a freshly-produced owned value. A getter is a borrow-producing position, and a fresh owned value returned through it would escape with no owner and leak.

title: a factory method returning owned is the remedy for a minting getter
rule: A property or indexer getter may not return a freshly-produced owned value; expose the factory as a method returning `owned T` instead, which can hand the caller ownership.

title: an unmarked mint-announcing method may not lend a stored frame field
rule: A mint-announcing-typed field is not returnable through an unmarked mint-announcing method return, that return type being container-ownership-transferring; a stored frame is instead re-exposed through a property, field, or collection slot.

title: a stored mint-announcing view is re-exposed through a property
rule: A mint-announcing-typed field is not returnable through an unmarked mint-announcing method return; a stored frame is instead re-exposed through a property, field, or collection slot.

title: a moved owned field is returned through an owned return via take-restore-return
rule: Transferring an owned field's value out to the caller is only admissible through an `owned` return type, in the take-restore-return shape: build the replacement, take the field, restore it, then return the taken value.

title: Dispose through a borrowed parameter is rejected
rule: `Dispose()` through a borrow is a compile error. The borrow receivers include a borrowed local or parameter.

title: Dispose through an owned parameter is admitted
rule: Explicit disposal requires a receiver the disposer owns: an owned local or `owned` parameter, among the admitted receivers.

title: an object may not dispose itself through this
rule: The borrow receivers include a borrowed local or parameter — including `this`: an object may not dispose itself out from under its owner.

title: disposing an owned field from within its declaring class is admitted
rule: Explicit disposal requires an owned receiver; an `owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type is such a receiver — unlike `this`, which an object may never dispose out from under its owner.

title: disposing an owned field read from outside its declaring class is rejected
rule: The borrow receivers for `Dispose()` include an owned-field read outside the declaring class — that read is a borrow, and disposing through it is rejected with no exception.

title: disposing another instance's owned field is admitted from the same declaring class
rule: The field admission is by declaring type, matching §13.1's levels: code of class C may dispose an owned field of any C instance it can reach — the same access symmetry as any private-member touch.

title: disposing a caught exception binding is rejected
rule: The borrow receivers for `Dispose()` include a `catch`-arm binding.

title: reading a caught exception binding without disposing it is admitted
rule: A `catch`-arm binding is a borrow; reading it (without disposing it) is ordinary borrow use.

title: disposing a case pattern binding is rejected
rule: The borrow receivers for `Dispose()` include a pattern binding.

title: using a case pattern binding without disposing it is admitted
rule: A pattern binding is a borrow of the scrutinee; ordinary borrow use (without disposal) is admitted.

title: disposing a captured owned binding inside a closure is rejected
rule: The borrow receivers for `Dispose()` include a captured owned binding inside a closure.

title: reading a captured owned binding inside a closure is admitted
rule: Inside a closure a captured owned binding is uniformly in borrow state: reads borrow, while assignment, a marked transfer, an explicit `Dispose()` or a discard of it are compile errors.

title: disposing a default-iteration element borrow is rejected
rule: No element-borrow disposal. An element borrow obtained from a borrowing-family collection — a default-iteration variable — is a borrow like any other: disposing it is a compile error, with no exception.

title: reading default-iteration elements without disposing them is admitted
rule: A default-iteration variable over a borrowing-family collection is a borrow of the slot; ordinary borrow use (without disposal) is admitted.

title: disposing a borrowed owning collection's container is rejected
rule: A borrow of an owning collection may not be disposed: the borrower does not own the container, and the actual owner disposes the container and cascades to its elements at scope/destructor end.

title: adding to a borrowed owning collection (pass-and-fill) is admitted
rule: Every operation but `Dispose` remains available on a borrowed owning collection — the idiomatic pass-and-fill pattern `method Fill(a: OwningArray<T>) a.Add(...)` takes a borrowed `OwningArray<T>` and adds to it.

title: a method returning this under an owned return type is rejected
rule: A method that returns `this` returns a borrow of the receiver. The returned borrow may not be assigned to an `owned` field or returned as `owned` — it is the receiver under a different name.

title: a method returning this without owned is admitted
rule: A method that returns `this` returns a borrow of the receiver — the return type is the class type, not `owned`. This enables method chaining.

title: an owned field passed as a plain argument may be stored as a back-reference borrow
rule: Passing an owned field as a plain argument is permitted; the callee receives a parameter-sourced borrow and may store the borrow into a non-owned class-typed field only where the borrowed-field store rule admits it (the back-reference idiom).

title: a freshly-produced owning value through a non-owned return escapes
rule: A freshly-produced owning value (`return new OwningArray<T>(...)`) returned through a **non-`owned`** return type is an error: the value would escape with no owner and leak. Expose the factory as a method returning `owned T` instead.

title: the same fresh owning value through an owned return transfers to the caller
rule: Handing a freshly-produced owning value to the caller is admissible through an `owned` return type — the caller assumes responsibility for its disposal — which is the remedy the non-`owned`-return rejection names.

title: reassigning an owned field evaluates the RHS before disposing the displaced value
rule: Assignment to an owned field disposes the displaced value; the right-hand side is evaluated first, then the previous live value is disposed, then the new value is stored.

title: reassigning a plain-var owned local disposes the displaced value
rule: Assignment to an owned field or owned local disposes the displaced value; the scope of this rule covers `owned` fields and plain-`var` owned locals alike.

title: reassigning a moved-from field stores without disposal
rule: The disposal is null-guarded and dynamically dispatched; a moved-from or null location therefore stores without disposal, which is how the move-then-reassign idiom stays single-disposal.

title: an explicit Dispose before reassignment composes with drop-on-overwrite as a no-op
rule: An explicit `field.Dispose();` before the assignment remains legal and behavior-preserving — Dispose is idempotent, so the implicit disposal of an already-disposed value is a no-op.

title: reassigning an owned field while a live borrow of the displaced value exists is admitted
rule: Reassigning an owned field or collection slot is not statically frozen — a borrow of the displaced value is invalidated at the overwrite, caught as DisposedAccessException in checked disposal mode and undefined unchecked, not rejected at compile time.

title: reassigning an owned local while a live local borrow of it exists is rejected
rule: Reassigning a plain-var owned local while a live local borrow of its current value exists is rejected by the consume-site freeze — the implicit disposal would silently invalidate the borrow.

title: whole-value reassignment of an owning inline array disposes live slots in reverse order
rule: An owning inline array takes drop-on-overwrite per live slot, in reverse slot order (v0.260) — the RHS is evaluated first, then each live slot of the displaced value is disposed, then the new value is stored.

title: reassigning an owning-inline-array static field is a plain store, never drop-on-overwrite
rule: A static owning-inline-array field stays a plain store — statics never take drop-on-overwrite for any type; whole-field reassignment never auto-disposes displaced slots.

title: a throwing RHS leaves the field untouched and still owned
rule: A throwing RHS leaves the field/local untouched and still-owned — the implicit path has no exception-unsafe window.

title: an owned parameter transfers ownership and may be stored into an owned field directly
rule: When a parameter is `owned`, the caller relinquishes ownership; the owned-field assignment drop-on-overwrites the displaced value, so a replacement method needs no explicit dispose-first step.

title: implicit boxing produces no disposal obligation and draws no discharge diagnostic
rule: Implicit boxing is not subject to the discharge rule of this section — when a value type is boxed to be used where `Object` is expected, the boxed wrapper is a runtime-managed value, not an owned `new`-result; the boxing itself is not a `new` expression and produces no disposal obligation.

title: the caller may not use an argument it transferred to an owned parameter
rule: When a parameter is `owned`, the caller relinquishes ownership and may not use the argument after the call (§28.8, K3.3).

title: the take-restore-return idiom hands an owned field's contents to the caller
rule: Moving an owned field's contents out uses the `move` expression form: the field is left moved-from and must be reassigned on every path to the method's exit, so the pattern for "atomically take this field's contents and return them as owned" builds the replacement first, takes, restores, then returns the taken value (§28.8, §28.8.1).

title: move on a field takes it out and a restoring assignment on every exit path satisfies the rule
