rule: The field-restoration rule: every control-flow path from the move site to the method's exit must execute a restoring assignment `x.f := value;` between the move and the exit.

title: a terminal move is rejected even under an owned return
rule: There is no terminal-move dispensation — a terminal move (`return move x.f;`, or any return whose operand evaluation performs the move with no restoring assignment before the exit) is rejected, the return edge being itself an unrestored exit.

title: a field moved on one branch and not reassigned on the other is rejected
rule: The rule applies to every reachable exit; the compiler rejects a move whose restoring assignment is missing on some path to the method's exit.

title: scoping the move to the branch where reassignment is mandatory satisfies the rule
rule: The fix is to scope the move to the branch where reassignment is reachable, so every path that performs the move also restores the field before the method's exit.

title: a throwable construction between the move and the restoration is an unrestored exception edge
rule: A throwable expression between the move and the reassignment introduces an exit path on which the reassignment has not run — the exception edge is an unrestored exit.

title: building the replacement before the move leaves no throwable edge between move and restoration
rule: Build before take — perform any throwable construction before the move, leaving only non-throwable assignments and the return between the move and the exits.

title: a loop that may execute zero times does not satisfy the field-restoration rule
rule: Loops that may execute zero times do not satisfy the rule — the analysis reuses the definite-assignment dominance machinery, so a restoration reachable only through a conditionally-taken loop body does not dominate the exit.

title: restructuring so the reassignment dominates the exits satisfies the loop case
rule: The fix is the same as the conditional case — restructure so the reassignment dominates the exits, moving the move after the loop.

title: moving a field before its first constructor assignment is a definite-assignment violation
rule: Inside a constructor body, the field has no value to move until it has been assigned; a `move x.f` before the field's first assignment is a definite-assignment violation, the same rule as for any other read of an unassigned non-nullable slot.

title: move on a field is permitted after its first constructor assignment
rule: After the first assignment, `move` is permitted, with the same field-restoration rule applying to constructor exit paths.

title: a move inside a destructor body needs no restoration and is discharged like any other owned value
rule: Inside a destructor body, the field-restoration rule does not require reassignment (K9.3 — teardown, no future read); the taken value must still be discharged, for example with `using var`.

title: using var u := move x.f is the canonical take-and-consume pattern
rule: `using var u := move x.f;` is the canonical pattern for 'take the field's value out and consume it scope-bound.' The using var discharges the moved value at scope end; the field-restoration rule still applies at the surrounding method's exits.

title: detaching via a nullable field moves the contents out and restores to null
rule: A class that wants "take the resource away and leave the field empty" declares the field nullable and assigns `null` after the move — the reassignment to null satisfies the field-restoration rule.

title: an argument-position move whose restoration follows a throwable call is rejected
rule: A method call is throwable, so an argument-position move whose restoration follows the call is rejected on the call's exception edge.

title: restoring the field before the call that may throw fixes the argument-position hazard
rule: The fix is to construct the replacement and reassign before the call — the same "build then take then restore" discipline, with the call moved to after the restore.

title: a new expression's argument expressions classify on their own between the move and the restoration
rule: The exclusion covers the construction only — a `new` expression's argument expressions classify on their own, so `_r := new Res(Fetch());` still puts Fetch()'s exception edge between the move and the restoration.

title: a getter returning a freshly-computed string needs no owned announcement
rule: Runtime-managed types are exempt from the ceremony this chapter states for class-typed values; a getter body whose result is a fresh runtime-managed production (an interpolation, a concatenation) remains admissible with no `owned` announcement.

title: a closure that would outlive its captured local borrow's source is rejected
rule: Runtime management relaxes nothing about the values a closure captures — a captured borrowed class reference is subject to §28.3's borrow-escape rules, so a function value that outlives the captured borrow's source is rejected.

title: a function value carrying no captured borrow may be returned from its method
rule: Runtime management governs the function value itself, and the compiler tracks captured borrows separately from the function value's own lifetime — a function value that captures no borrow has an empty source set, so nothing it carries can be outlived and it is admitted at the escaping sinks a capture-bearing one is not.

title: a closure may not dispose an owned local it captures
rule: Capturing an owned class-typed local does not transfer ownership into the closure — the closure may not assign to, transfer from, or dispose the captured binding.

title: a closure may read a captured owned local while the original binding retains the obligation
rule: The capture is a borrow whose source is the local's enclosing scope, borrow-state throughout, and the original `using var` (or other owned location) retains the disposal obligation.

title: move through a closure's captured borrow of a move-only local is rejected
rule: Capturing a move-only local follows the same rule — the closure captures a borrow whose source is the local's enclosing scope; reads of slots through the captured borrow are admitted, `move arr[i]` through it is not, because the closure does not own the array.

title: reading a slot through a closure's captured borrow of a move-only local is admitted
rule: Reads of slots through the captured borrow are admitted — the closure captures a borrow whose source is the local's enclosing scope.

title: using var on a function-typed local still forbids reassignment, though disposal there is a no-op
rule: A `using var` local of function type is nonetheless permitted (disposal at scope end is a no-op) and serves only the non-reassignability role — a plain `var` of function type scopes its captures identically.

title: an undischarged plain-var local of a trivial-dispose class draws no must-use warning
rule: No must-use / auto-drop diagnostic attaches to a trivial-dispose value: the §28.3 must-use warning is not emitted at the implicit-drop site of a plain-`var` owned local whose type is trivial-dispose — a class with no destructor and no `owned` fields of non-trivial-dispose type (§28.9).

title: adding a destructor makes the same undischarged local draw the must-use warning
rule: The ceremony exemption's boundary is exactly the runs-no-user-code line: a class that declares a destructor is not trivial-dispose, so the §28.3 must-use warning is emitted at the implicit-drop site of its plain-`var` owned local (§28.9, §28.3).

title: a trivial-dispose declared type over a destructor-bearing production is not exempt
rule: The exemption's classification is read from the produced type where the drop site's value has a statically-known producer: a trivial-dispose declared type standing over a destructor-bearing production — `var b: Base := new Derived();` at a trivial-dispose `Base` — is not exempt (§28.9).

title: an owned field of trivial-dispose type leaves the holder trivial-dispose
rule: The trivial-dispose check is recursive: an `owned` field whose declared type is itself trivial-dispose does not disqualify the holder — the synthesized disposal cascade over such fields frees memory and runs no user code, so the holder keeps the ceremony exemption (§28.9).

title: an owning collection is not trivial-dispose at any instantiation
rule: The owned-element variants of the standard collection types are not trivial-dispose at any instantiation: they own their elements, disposal cascades through to them, and their storage primitive declares a destructor — so the ordinary discharge obligations apply and the ceremony exemption does not (§28.9).

title: a borrowing collection is trivial-dispose even at a non-trivial element type
rule: The rule does not require the type arguments to be themselves trivial-dispose: `Array<MyClass>` is trivial-dispose even if `MyClass` is not — the elements are owned elsewhere and the array's free does not dispose them — so its undischarged local draws no must-use warning (§28.9).

title: owned over the Type token is inadmissible
rule: `Type` is runtime-managed: no `Type` expression is an owned production, none lends a borrow, and no holder carries an obligation for one — `owned` over `Type` is inadmissible (§28.9, v0.300; §28.1's type requirement names a class type other than `Type`).

title: an interface-typed owned binding is never exempt from the must-use warning
rule: An interface-typed binding is never exempt from the must-use warning, its conformance set being open across modules (§28.9's possibly-non-trivial-dispose reading), whatever the concrete class behind it does (§28.9, §28.3).

title: an undischarged owned parameter of trivial-dispose type draws no must-use warning
rule: The exemption covers **every holder form the warning attaches to**: the must-use warning is not emitted at the implicit-drop site of an undischarged `owned` parameter — a method's, an iterator's, or an async method's — whose type is trivial-dispose; the auto-drop itself is unconditional at every one of them.

title: a Type value is runtime-managed and its holder carries no obligation
rule: `Type` is runtime-managed: the runtime holds exactly one instance per type for the life of the process and user code never allocates one, so no `Type` expression is an owned production, none lends a borrow, and no holder carries an obligation for one — the compiler neither warns about an undisposed one nor requires it to appear in a `using var`.

title: a using var declared inside a loop body is disposed on a break exit
rule: Disposal happens on every exit path — normal completion, break, return, or exception.

title: a using var established inside a try's protected block is disposed before the try's own finally
rule: A try statement's own finally is established at entry to the protected block; an owned local or using var declared inside the protected block, established later, is disposed before the finally runs, in reverse establishment order.

title: using var admits an if expression whose two arms are both owned producers
rule: An expression whose arm-meet is owned — an if expression over fresh producers — is an owned producer for using var's admission.

title: the anonymous using var _ adopts a moved named owned binding exactly as the named form would
rule: Adoption composes — `using var _ := move x;` consumes `x` into the anonymous binding exactly as the named form would.

title: a using var initialized from a borrow does not assume a disposal obligation
rule: When the right-hand side of a using var declaration is a borrow rather than an owned value — a method call without an owned return, an indexer access, a field read, or an unmarked read of a class- or interface-typed named owned binding — the using var does not assume a disposal obligation: at scope end no Dispose() is called, because the value is not owned by this scope. An unmarked read of a move-only value binding moves instead and is an owned right-hand side.

title: an explicit Dispose of a borrow-pin's source is a site-announced kill the pin leaves unfrozen
rule: The using var still pins the borrow's source for the duration of the scope — the borrow stays live until the using-var's scope ends and the consume-site freeze then governs every consume of the source in that range: the frozen kills (a move, a transfer, a reassignment of the binding) are compile errors, and the site-announced kills stay unfrozen under their flag backstop — an explicit `Dispose()` of the source is permitted, and a read through the pinned binding afterwards raises `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode.

title: using var accepts a runtime-managed right-hand side, where disposal at scope end is a no-op
rule: using var accepts a value-type or runtime-managed right-hand side; for ordinary value types and runtime-managed types the disposal at scope end is a no-op, and the only effect is the reassignability restriction.

title: reassigning a using var of runtime-managed type is still a compile error
rule: using var is a scope pin — it is implicitly non-reassignable, whatever the right-hand side's type kind; reassigning a using var variable is a compile error.

title: moving a borrow-pin's source is a frozen kill the pin still rejects
rule: The using var still pins the borrow's source for the duration of the scope — the borrow stays live until the using-var's scope ends, and the consume-site freeze then governs every consume of the source in that range: the frozen kills — a move, a transfer, a reassignment of the binding — are compile errors.

title: an unmarked using var over a move-only local adopts rather than pins
rule: Where `x` is a local of **move-only value type**, the unmarked `using var y := x;` **adopts**: a move-only binding has no borrow reading to disambiguate, so the plain read moves, `y` carries the value's owned slots to the end of *its* block, and `x` is left moved-from.

title: the source of an unmarked using var adoption is left moved-from
rule: Under the unmarked move-only adoption, `x` is left **moved-from** — the plain read moved the value — and reading from a moved-from location is a compile error (§15.3). The whole-value move leaves the local holding no value rather than a hole, so it owes no restoration.

title: a read through a borrow-pin after the source's explicit Dispose faults in checked mode
rule: The site-announced kills stay unfrozen under their flag backstop: an explicit `Dispose()` of a borrow-pin's source is permitted, and a read through the pinned binding afterwards raises `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode.

title: storing a parameter-sourced borrow into a field-held borrowing collection is admitted
rule: Storing a class-typed borrow into a borrowing collection follows the same shape as §28.3's borrowed-field rule — parameter-sourced and receiver-sourced borrows are admitted at the store site.

title: storing a scope-bound local's borrow into an outliving field-held collection is rejected
rule: A borrow of a scope-bound binding — an owned parameter included — stored into a collection that provably outlives that scope — the collection is a field, is reachable from one, escapes the method, or is a local of strictly wider scope — is rejected at the store site.

title: move on a borrowing collection slot is rejected — there is no ownership to transfer
rule: Array<T>, Dictionary<K, V>, and the other borrowing collections do not admit move coll[i] — their slots hold borrows, not owned values; there is no ownership to transfer.

title: Array<T> and OwningArray<T> are distinct, unrelated types with no implicit conversion
rule: There is no implicit conversion between the two families; an OwningArray<Connection> is not an Array<Connection> and vice versa.

title: an OwningDictionary owns its values while its keys are classified as ordinary borrows
rule: For dictionaries the classification applies independently to the key slots and the value slots — an owning dictionary owns its values; its keys are value-like and classified per the borrowing column.

title: an owning collection over Type is rejected at instantiation
rule: In the element-category table, a runtime-managed reference element type — `string`, a function type, `Type` (§28.9) — is *rejected at instantiation* in the owning-family column: no holder acquires an obligation for such a value, so an owned element slot has nothing to own.

title: the same owning collection over a class element type is admitted
rule: The owning-family column admits a **class** element type: the slot owns its element and the container's `Dispose()` cascades to it, which is the family's defining behaviour.

title: an element borrow used after a dominating RemoveAt at its index draws the use-after-removal warning
rule: The compiler must warn when a local holding such a borrow is used after a call on the same collection binding that disposes the borrowed element and dominates the use on every path — `RemoveAt(i)` where the borrow was taken as `coll[i]` with the same index expression, and no structural operation on the same collection binding between the borrow and the kill.

title: using an element borrow after a dominating Clear on the same collection draws the warning
rule: The compiler must warn when a local holding such a borrow is used after a call on the same collection binding that disposes the borrowed element and dominates the use on every path — `Clear()`, which disposes every element.

title: an element borrow re-taken after the mutation is clean
rule: A borrow re-taken after the mutation is clean, and a use before the mutation, or on a path the kill does not dominate, draws nothing.

title: an element-level indexer write on the collection does not draw the element-borrow warning
rule: An element-level write — an indexer-set — does not draw this warning: it is not a §29.12 structural operation, and the two warnings share one operation vocabulary.

title: a RemoveAt at the borrow's index after an intervening Insert draws no warning
rule: `RemoveAt(i)` where the borrow was taken as `coll[i]` with the same index expression, and no structural operation of §29.12's list on the same collection binding between the borrow and the kill: a reposition or removal ahead of the slot would change which element the index names.

title: await using invokes DisposeAsync and the destructor body is not also run
rule: For await using, the awaited DisposeAsync() performs whatever asynchronous cleanup the class defines; the destructor body (if any) is not also run, because DisposeAsync supersedes it.

title: plain using runs the destructor synchronously and never invokes DisposeAsync
rule: For plain using (or a synchronous Dispose() call) on a class that implements both, the destructor body runs synchronously and DisposeAsync is not invoked — the class's two cleanup paths are alternatives, not a sequence.

title: a class implementing IAsyncDisposable without a destructor draws a compiler warning
rule: The compiler emits a warning when a class implements IAsyncDisposable without a destructor -- "synchronous Dispose() will skip async cleanup."

title: implicit discharge always takes the synchronous Dispose path, even inside an async body
rule: Implicit discharge is synchronous — the implicit disposal paths always take the synchronous Dispose() path, on every edge and in every context including async bodies; an implicit disposal point never awaits.

title: a direct DisposeAsync call awaited outside await using is legal and reclamation follows
rule: A direct DisposeAsync() call awaited outside await using is legal; the awaited task's completion is logical-disposal completion, and reclamation follows exactly as if await using had issued it.

title: a second call to DisposeAsync after the first has run is a no-op
rule: A second call to Dispose() or DisposeAsync() after either has run is a no-op — the runtime tracks completion at the granularity of the object, not per-method.

title: a Shared<T> handle is an ordinary owned binding requiring move at an owned-consuming call
rule: Handles are ordinary owned class instances. Every rule of this chapter applies to a handle unchanged — including the call-site `move` marker required when a named owned binding feeds an `owned` argument (§28.3).

title: marking the transfer with move discharges a Shared<T> handle like any owned binding
rule: Handles are ordinary owned class instances, discharged by `move` like any other owned binding (§28.3).

title: a Shared<T> handle may be stored in an owning collection like any class instance
rule: A handle may be stored in owning collections (`OwningArray<Shared<T>>`) like any class instance.

title: the compiler does not detect ownership cycles through Shared<T>
rule: Cycles leak. A value that (transitively, through owned fields) holds a `Shared<T>` handle participating in its own ownership keeps its count above zero forever. The compiler does not detect ownership cycles through `Shared<T>`.

title: Get()'s borrow does not outlive the handle that sourced it
rule: `Get(): T` produces a borrow of the underlying value whose source is the handle, valid while that handle lives. The borrow does not extend the value's lifetime; the handle does.

title: Get()'s borrow is fine to use within the sourcing handle's own scope
rule: `Get(): T` produces a borrow of the underlying value, valid while the handle lives; used within that scope it is an ordinary borrow.

title: a Weak<T> handle is an ordinary owned binding requiring move at an owned-consuming call
rule: Weak handles are themselves ordinary owned class instances and are disposed like any other — including the call-site `move` marker required when a named owned binding feeds an `owned` argument (§28.3).

title: marking the transfer with move discharges a Weak<T> handle like any owned binding
rule: Weak handles are themselves ordinary owned class instances, discharged by `move` like any other owned binding (§28.3).

title: a scoped callback parameter may be stored in a scoped field of the constructed bounding object
rule: The callee may store the callback, but only in scoped fields of the bounding object itself; a constructor call resolves the bounding object to the constructed object.

title: storing a scoped callback into a non-scoped field is rejected
rule: The callee may store the callback only in scoped fields of the bounding object itself — a plain (non-scoped) field is not an admitted store target.

title: a scoped callback may not be returned from the callee
rule: The callee may invoke the callback or store it in a scoped field; it may not return it, move it into non-scoped storage, or store it in any other object.

title: a scoped callback may be forwarded to another scoped parameter with the same bounding object
rule: The callee may forward the callback to another scoped parameter whose bounding object is the same object.

title: a plain function-typed parameter is call-bounded and any closure may be passed to it
rule: The caller side is correspondingly unrestricted — any closure, capture-bearing or not, may be passed to a call-bounded parameter, since every captured source trivially outlives the call.

title: a call-bounded callee may not store the callback in a field
rule: A function-typed parameter declared without scoped is call-bounded; the callback may not be stored in a field of any object.

title: a call-bounded callee may not return the callback
rule: Within the callee the call-bounded callback may not be returned, captured by a closure that itself escapes the callee, or forwarded into a scoped parameter position.

title: a call-bounded callee may not forward its callback into a scoped parameter
rule: The callee cannot see its argument's capture set, so it cannot vouch for the §28.14 admission — a callee that needs to register a callback it received must itself declare the parameter scoped.

title: a captured local declared before the using-var bounding object is admitted
rule: A closure argument capturing locals is admitted iff the bounding object resolves to a using var local L where every captured local source is declared before L in the same or an enclosing scope.

title: a captured local declared after the using-var bounding object is rejected
rule: Every captured local source must be declared before L in the same or an enclosing scope; a source declared after L fails the declared-before test.

title: self-capture of the bounding local itself is admitted
rule: Self-capture — a value whose borrow provably originates from L — is admitted: scope.Spawn(lambda() => Work(scope.Token)) is the sanctioned shape.

title: a captured local source may not be explicitly disposed while the bounding object lives
rule: Until L's scope exits, the captured local sources are frozen — they may not be moved from, reassigned, or disposed.

title: after the bounding local's scope exits the captured source is unfrozen
rule: After L's scope exits the sources are unfrozen, because L is disposed at that scope end — bounding L in a do ... end block is the sanctioned way to transfer a captured source out afterwards.

title: a scoped class-typed parameter may be stored in a direct non-owned field of the bounding object
rule: On a class- or interface-typed parameter the callee may store the borrow in a direct non-owned field of the bounding object; the call site writes M(scoped x), an argument modifier, and the argument's borrow source must satisfy the declared-before test against the bounding `using var` local the constructor call initializes.

title: a fresh producer argument at a scoped class-typed parameter position is rejected
rule: A fresh producer argument is rejected — the unbound owned temporary dies at the end of the full expression; bind the source first.

title: scoped on a static method with no owned return is a compile error
rule: A scoped parameter on a static method is admitted only when the method's return is owned; there is no receiver, no constructed object, and no instance to hold the stored value otherwise.

title: scoped on a static method with an owned return resolves the returned object as the bound
rule: A scoped parameter on a static method is admitted when the method's return is owned, so that a call site can resolve bounding form 2 or 3.

title: forming a method reference over a capture-free-register subscribe position is a compile error
rule: Register positions are stated at the callee, not marked in the parameter's function type, so forming a method reference over a capture-free-register position is a compile error, covering the shared-event subscribe positions.

title: a plain var holder resolves no admitted bounding object for a scoped borrow argument
rule: A class-typed `scoped` argument's borrow source is admitted, in place of a closure's capture set, iff the bounding object resolves to a `using var`/`await using var` local or to `this`; a bounding object that is none of the admitted resolutions admits no capture-bearing arguments.

title: a user-implemented IEnumerable/IEnumerator pair drives a for loop
rule: `for` operates on any value whose type implements `IEnumerable<T>`. Calling `GetEnumerator()` produces a fresh enumerator positioned just before the first element; `MoveNext()` advances the cursor; `Current` returns the element at the current position. An enumerator with no resources to release simply has an empty `Dispose` body; the compiler generates one if the implementor writes none.

title: a duck-typed enumerable with no IEnumerable conformance is rejected in a for loop
rule: `for` operates on any value whose type implements `IEnumerable<T>`. The protocol is interface-based; there is no duck-typing fallback.

title: a manually-obtained enumerator is bound with using var and discharged
rule: Code that calls `GetEnumerator()` manually — outside a loop form — obtains an owned enumerator subject to the standard §28.3 discharge rules; the `using var x := source.GetEnumerator();` shape is recommended (scope-bound disposal, no must-use warning).

title: a plain-var binding of a manually-obtained enumerator auto-drops with the must-use warning
rule: though a plain `var` binding is also legal and auto-drops at scope end with the must-use warning. The binding's producer is declared `owned IEnumerator<int>`, and §28.9's trivial-dispose ceremony exemption — over the obligation at every holder form, keyed on the produced type where the drop site has a statically-known producer — never reaches an interface-typed binding, whose conformance set is open across modules.

title: a class implementing both IEnumerable and IEnumerator may return this from GetEnumerator
rule: A class implementing both `IEnumerable<T>` and `IEnumerator<T>` may return `this` from `GetEnumerator()` — the one receiver return the announcement table's rows 2–3 admit (axiom A15); the disposal of a self-returned frame runs the object's `Dispose()` and does not reclaim it.

title: IEnumerator.Current is non-destructive across repeated reads
rule: `IEnumerator<T>.Current` is non-destructive: it returns a borrow of the most-recently-yielded value, which the enumerator continues to own. Multiple reads between `MoveNext` calls produce additional borrows of the same value.

title: the for variable over value-typed elements is a copy
rule: The `for` desugaring binds `var x := __enumerator.Current;`, and for a copy slot — a value-typed element of a borrowing collection — the element operation *indexer-get / default iteration* is "copy out" (§28.11's element slot policy), so writing to the loop variable does not reach the collection.

title: the for variable over string-typed elements is a shared reference
rule: The `for` desugaring binds `var x := __enumerator.Current;`, and for a shared-reference slot — a runtime-managed element type such as `string` — the element operation *indexer-get / default iteration* is "reference out" (§28.11's element slot policy); no ownership transfers.

title: the for variable over class-typed elements is a borrow of the slot
rule: For a borrow slot — a class-typed element of a borrowing collection — the element operation *indexer-get / default iteration* is "borrow out" (§28.11's element slot policy), so the loop variable names the same object the slot does and a mutation through it is visible in the collection.

title: an element borrow escaping the loop is admitted over a concrete collection type
rule: An iteration-variable borrow is admissible where its derived source chain reaches the collection under §29.2's desugaring: a collection-backed source re-borrows — the chain runs element slot → collection — so the reference stays valid past the loop while the collection lives.

title: an element borrow escaping the loop is rejected over an interface-typed source
rule: At an interface-typed enumeration source the backing is unprovable, so the iteration variable's source is conservatively the loop's implicit enumerator, a scope-bound local, and letting it escape the loop is rejected.

title: a fresh iterable-family for-loop source is disposed by the desugaring's hidden using var
rule: When `source` is a fresh class-typed expression ... the wrapping `using var` assumes the disposal obligation and ensures the iterable is disposed when the loop ends.

title: iterating a using-var collection pins it for the loop without taking ownership
rule: When `source` is itself an owned local — including a `using var` of class type — the desugaring is adjusted: `using var __source := source;` is replaced by a borrow that pins `source` for the loop's duration without assuming the disposal obligation.

title: default iteration over an OwningArray takes the borrowing path
rule: If `source`'s static type implements both `IEnumerable<T>` and `IOwningEnumerable<T>` (as `OwningArray<T>` does), the desugaring uses the `IEnumerable<T>` path — default iteration is borrowing.

title: iterating Drain() yields an owned element that the body discharges via move
rule: The iteration variable `x` is a plain owned local ... the user must be able to discharge `x` by moving it into another owned slot, e.g. `using var c := move x` for scope-bound adoption.

title: an undischarged owned Drain() iteration variable auto-drops with a per-iteration must-use warning
rule: The compiler applies the standard §28.3 owned-local discharge rule to the iteration variable on the loop body's every exit edge: on each normal-exit edge `x` is either discharged by the program or auto-dropped with the must-use warning, and the fall-through-to-the-next-iteration edge is checked the same way as the body's end.

title: for over a Dictionary yields DictionaryEntry
rule: The desugaring binds `var x := __enumerator.Current;`, so the iteration variable's type is the source's `IEnumerable<T>` element type. `Dictionary<K, V>` conforms as `ICollection<DictionaryEntry<K, V>>`, so iterating one yields `DictionaryEntry<K, V>` values, one per live entry, in insertion order (stdlib §4.8).

title: OwningDictionary has no default entry iteration
rule: `for` operates only on a value whose type implements `IEnumerable<T>`; `OwningDictionary<K, V>`'s interface conformance is `IDisposable` only, so default `for var entry in ownedDict do` iteration is not provided for it (stdlib §4.9).

title: iterating an OwningDictionary's Keys view is the borrowing remedy
rule: Where `OwningDictionary<K, V>` provides no default entry iteration, the borrowing remedy is the key-iteration pattern: `Keys` is an `IReadOnlyCollection<K>` view, which implements `IEnumerable<K>` and is therefore a legal `for` source (stdlib §4.9).

title: a named owned binding yielded from an owning iterator is a marker-free consume
rule: Under the marker discipline the operand read of a **named owned binding** is classified by the return type: in an iterator returning an **owning** enumeration interface the read is a marker-free owned-consuming position — the declared return type is the announcement (K3.13), exactly as for `return` under an `owned` return type — and the binding is moved-from when the yield resumes.

title: yielding a named owned binding twice from a borrowing iterator is an admitted re-borrow
rule: in an iterator returning a **borrowing** enumeration interface the unmarked read is a **borrow** (nothing announces a kill) ... An unmarked read of a named owned binding in the yield position of a *borrowing* iterator ... is a re-borrow: the binding stays owned in the frame.

title: an iterator method's body drives a for loop over its yielded values
rule: `yield return expression;` produces the next value and suspends. Falling off the end of the method has the same effect as `yield break`.

title: yield break terminates iteration early
rule: `yield break;` terminates iteration.

title: an iterator method may not declare a ref parameter
rule: An iterator method may not declare `ref` or `out` parameters: its arguments are captured into a heap state-machine frame that outlives the synchronous call, and a caller-stack-slot reference cannot be.

title: an iterator method with a plain parameter is admitted
rule: An iterator method may not declare `ref` or `out` parameters; `owned` parameters remain admitted (§29.8) — a plain parameter carries no such restriction.

title: an iterator method may not declare an out parameter
rule: An iterator method may not declare `ref` or `out` parameters: its arguments are captured into a heap state-machine frame that outlives the synchronous call, and a caller-stack-slot reference cannot be.

title: an IEnumerable<T>-returning iterator method reruns its body on each GetEnumerator call
rule: An iterator method's return type is `IEnumerable<T>` (re-iterable: each call to `GetEnumerator()` runs the body again from the start).

title: an iterator method's body does not run until MoveNext is first called
rule: An iterator method's body does not run when the method is called. Calling produces an `IEnumerable<T>` (or `IEnumerator<T>`); the body runs incrementally as the consumer calls `MoveNext()`.

title: an iterator's plain reference-typed parameter is held as a borrow across yields
rule: The returned state machine holds the factory's plain reference-typed arguments as borrows until it completes or is disposed.

title: a borrow-bearing record local crossing a yield must have a frame-resident source
rule: A borrow-bearing record local (§9.7) whose live range crosses a `yield return` is subject to the same frame-resident-source rule as §30.1's across-suspension rule: every borrow the local carries must have a source the frame itself owns — an owned local, a `using var`, or an `owned` parameter of the iterator body.

title: a borrow-bearing record local sourced from an owned iterator parameter is admitted across a yield
rule: every borrow the local carries must have a source the frame itself owns — an owned local, a `using var`, or an `owned` parameter of the iterator body ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters)).

title: plain return is not allowed inside an iterator method
rule: A method that uses `yield` cannot use plain `return`, including `return;`. Use `yield break` to exit early.

title: yield break is the correct early-exit spelling inside an iterator method
rule: A method that uses `yield` cannot use plain `return`, including `return;`. Use `yield break` to exit early.

title: plain return is barred in an async iterator too
rule: This rule applies equally to synchronous iterators (returning `IEnumerable<T>`) and async iterators (declared `async`, returning `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`). ... `yield` controls the flow, and `yield break` terminates it.

title: yield return inside a try block with a catch is rejected
rule: `yield return` or `yield break` inside a `try` block whose surrounding statement has a `catch`: forbidden.

title: yield return inside a try block with only a finally is admitted
rule: `yield return` or `yield break` inside a `try` block whose surrounding statement has only a `finally`: allowed. `using var` compiles to `try`/`finally` (no `catch`), so it is the preferred resource-management mechanism inside iterators.

title: yield is forbidden inside a catch arm's body
rule: `yield` inside a catch arm's body or a `finally` block: forbidden.

title: yield is forbidden inside a finally block
rule: `yield` inside a catch arm's body or a `finally` block: forbidden.

title: breaking out of a for loop early disposes the iterator's pending using var
rule: When a consumer stops iterating early — `break`, exception, or `using var` ending before exhaustion — the iterator is disposed. The state machine runs the pending cleanup actions active at the point of suspension.

title: partial-consumption disposal runs pending cleanups in reverse order of establishment
rule: Runs the pending cleanup actions active at the point of suspension — `using var` disposals ... and `finally` clauses — in reverse order of establishment, exactly as if the body had exited at the suspension point.

title: a second Dispose() on a partially-consumed iterator performs no second disposal
rule: The state machine runs the pending cleanup actions active at the point of suspension and transitions to a completed state — the machine's own bookkeeping, not a post-disposal guarantee to the consumer. A second `Dispose()` **is** observable and is a no-op: it is the single member §28.2's disposal contract keeps callable. The no-op is the runtime contract only: the second call is also a use of the binding and draws §28.2's use-after-dispose warning.

title: an iterator's owned parameter is discharged via using var move on entry
rule: The body may treat the `owned` parameter as it would in any other method. Using `using var … := move …` — the binding-position transfer marker — makes scope-bounded disposal explicit; the marked transfer moves ownership from the parameter to the local.

title: an undischarged owned iterator parameter carries the must-use warning
rule: If the body does not move ownership out, the state machine disposes the parameter at iterator disposal ... This implicit frame disposal carries the §28.3 must-use warning, attached at the parameter declaration.

title: iterator disposal disposes an owned parameter the body did not move out of
rule: When the iterator is disposed, the state machine disposes any `owned` parameter that has not been moved out of by the body.

title: multiple undischarged owned iterator parameters are disposed in reverse declaration order
rule: The order across multiple owned parameters is reverse declaration order, mirroring §28.4's destructor rule.

title: the using var move adoption is the iterator's warning-free spelling
rule: This implicit frame disposal carries the §28.3 must-use warning, attached at the parameter declaration ...; the `using var … := move …` adoption above is the warning-free spelling.

title: the same iterator without the adoption carries the must-use warning
rule: If the body does not move ownership out, the state machine disposes the parameter at iterator disposal ... This implicit frame disposal carries the §28.3 must-use warning, attached at the parameter declaration.

title: yield is a method-level construct and is barred inside a lambda
rule: `yield` is a method-level construct only.

title: an iterator method with only yield break is the canonical empty iterator
rule: An iterator method with only `yield break;` is the canonical empty iterator.

title: a body with no yield anywhere is an ordinary method, not an iterator
rule: An empty body (no `yield`) is not an iterator method.

title: iterating the same collection source twice with two for loops works as expected
rule: Each `GetEnumerator()` call produces an independent enumerator. Iterating the same source twice with two `for` loops works as expected for collection types.

title: a lazy query enumerated a second time is a compile error
rule: A lazy query ... is single-consumption. It may be enumerated at most once ... A second enumeration, or any other use after the first, is a compile error where the flow analysis can see it statically (the diagnostic points to `.ToArray()`).

title: materializing a lazy query first permits enumerating the result any number of times
rule: To enumerate the results more than once, materialize first: `using var ys := xs.Where(...).ToArray();` produces an owned `Array<T>`, which — like any collection — may be enumerated any number of times.

title: applying a further deferred operator spends the query's enumeration right
rule: Applying a further deferred operator: `var q2 := q.Select(f);` spends the binding `q`'s enumeration right — using `q` afterwards as a query is a static error where visible.

title: passing a lazy query as an IEnumerable argument transfers its single-enumeration right to the callee
rule: Passing the query as an `IEnumerable<T>` argument: the single-enumeration right transfers to the callee; the frame's disposal obligation stays with the caller, the plain argument being an ordinary borrow.

title: reusing a lazy query at the caller after passing it as an argument is a compile error
rule: Passing the query as an `IEnumerable<T>` argument: the single-enumeration right transfers to the callee.

title: a class-element terminal accessor over a minting same-unit iterator draws the provenance warning
rule: A call [to a class-element terminal accessor] must draw a warning iff the receiver's statically-tracked provenance ... roots at a directly-called iterator method, compiled in the same compilation unit, at least one of whose reachable `yield return` sites classifies as an enumerator-owned yield.

title: the terminal-accessor provenance warning traces through a materializer pass-through node
rule: At a class or interface element type the trace does not stop at a materializer result — `ToArray()`/`ToSet()`/`ToDictionary(…)` ... They are pass-through nodes, never roots: the verdict is always the root's.

title: a class-element terminal accessor over a concrete collection returns a live element borrow
rule: A **concrete collection value** as the root — a `new` collection, or a collection-typed parameter, field, or local bound to one — is a silent root of the terminal-accessor provenance predicate, and soundly so: the elements' owner is the collection, which outlives the accessor call, so the returned element borrow is live after the call returns.

title: a bound lazy query with no consumption point draws the must-use warning
rule: A bound lazy query whose enumeration right is never spent draws K3.14's must-use warning at its auto-drop (v0.301); the warning is suppressed where the binding's consumption point is statically visible. §28.9's ceremony exemption does not reach a compiler-synthesized frame, so the lint applies on §28.3's ordinary terms.

title: a statically visible consumption point suppresses the query's must-use warning
rule: A bound query is spelled `using var q := xs.Where(…);` where the frame is to be scope-disposed, and K3.14's must-use warning is **suppressed where the binding's consumption point is statically visible** (the value was used; the auto-drop still runs).

title: a terminal accessor over a concrete collection root stays silent
rule: Every other root stays **silent**, and this is the exhaustive list: a **concrete collection value** as the root — a `new` collection, or a collection-typed parameter, field, or local bound to one — must stay silent, the elements' owner being the collection, which outlives the accessor call.

title: a same-unit iterator with no enumerator-owned yield stays silent
rule: A **same-unit iterator none of whose reachable yields is enumerator-owned** — every yield a re-borrow of a parameter-, field-, or caller-sourced element — must stay silent: the elements' owner is the caller's.

title: making the same iterator's yield a fresh producer draws the provenance warning
rule: A call to a class-element terminal accessor **must draw a warning** iff the receiver's statically-tracked provenance roots at a directly-called iterator method, compiled in the same compilation unit, at least one of whose reachable `yield return` sites classifies as an enumerator-owned yield — minting, a fresh producer among them.

title: adding to a collection while iterating it raises InvalidOperationException on the next advance
rule: Modifying a collection while iterating it invalidates the active enumerator. Standard collections detect this and throw `InvalidOperationException` on the next `MoveNext()`. Structural modification invalidates: any operation that adds, removes, or repositions entries or reallocates storage — `Add` among them. The in-loop structural call on the iterated binding, from which the loop's next advance is reachable, also draws the mutation-during-iteration warning; the program stays accepted.

title: an indexer-set to an existing position does not invalidate the enumerator
rule: An element-level write that changes no structure does not invalidate: assigning through the indexer to an existing position (`arr[i] := v`) leaves the enumerator valid, and a later visit of that position observes the new value.

title: the two-loop remove-while-iterating idiom avoids structural modification during iteration
rule: The standard pattern for removing during iteration: collect matches in a first pass over the source, then remove them in a second pass over the matches.

title: direct-indexed loop elision still raises InvalidOperationException on modification
rule: The §29.2 protocol-elision optimization must preserve these faults: a `for` loop the compiler lowers to direct indexing still raises `InvalidOperationException` at the iteration boundary following a structural modification, exactly as the enumerator path would. The in-loop structural call on the iterated binding also draws the mutation-during-iteration warning; the program stays accepted.

title: a structural call on the iterated binding draws the mutation-during-iteration warning
rule: The compiler must warn at a call to a structural operation whose receiver is the same binding the enclosing `for` iterates, when the call sits in that loop's body and the loop's next advance is reachable from it; the call is warned whether or not it is conditional.

title: collect-then-remove mutates outside the iterating loop and draws no warning
rule: The warning names the remedies: collect the matches and modify after the loop — the standard pattern for removing during iteration. A structural call whose receiver is not the binding the enclosing loop iterates draws nothing.

title: a structural call followed on every path by an exit from the loop draws no warning
rule: A structural call followed on every path by an exit from the loop — `break`, `return`, a `throw` no `catch` within the loop body handles, or a labeled jump out of it — is exempt, no advance following it.

title: an element-level indexer write inside the iterating loop is not structural and draws no warning
rule: An element-level write that changes no structure does not invalidate: assigning through the indexer to an existing position leaves the enumerator valid. The mutation-during-iteration warning fires at a call to a structural operation of the list above only.

title: a structural call inside a lambda the loop body only defines draws no warning
rule: The call must sit in that loop's body — in the loop's own callable body, not inside a lambda literal or a local type declaration's member body that the loop body merely contains, whose invocation the loop does not sequence.

title: a dictionary indexer-set on an existing key does not invalidate the enumerator
rule: An element-level write that changes no structure does not invalidate: `dict[existingKey] := v` updating a present key leaves the enumerator valid. (The runtime's dict entry-for loop reads a key/value snapshot taken at loop entry, so a same-pass update is exercised here for its non-invalidation only, not for observing the new value on a later visit — that half of the sentence is demonstrated by the array arm, s29_12_0002.)

title: an async method may return Task<T> for a value-typed T
rule: The return type must be one of: `Task` — no result value; `Task<T>` for some type T admitted by §30.5's producer taxonomy — a result of type T, with no transferable ownership obligation on the awaiter.

title: falling off the end of a Task-returning async method is equivalent to return
rule: Falling off the end of a `Task`-returning async method is equivalent to `return;`.

title: an async method may return OwningTask<T> for a class-typed T
rule: `OwningTask<T>` for some class type T — a result whose ownership transfers to the awaiter (§30.5).

title: an async iterator may return IAsyncEnumerable<T>
rule: `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` — for re-iterable async iterators that contain `yield return` (§30.7). The yielded values are borrowed by the consumer.

title: an async method returning a plain value type is rejected
rule: A method declared `async` may use `await`. The return type must be one of `Task`, `Task<T>`, `OwningTask<T>`, or one of the async iterable interfaces — a plain `string` is none of these.

title: async is rejected on a constructor
rule: `async` may appear on instance methods, static methods, and lambdas. It may not appear on constructors, destructors, or property/indexer accessors.

title: async is rejected on a destructor
rule: `async` may appear on instance methods, static methods, and lambdas. It may not appear on constructors, destructors, or property/indexer accessors.

title: a ref parameter is rejected on an async method
rule: `ref` and `out` parameters are forbidden. An `async` method, `async` lambda, or iterator method may not declare a `ref` or `out` parameter; a compile error at the declaration.

title: an out parameter is rejected on an async method
rule: `ref` and `out` parameters are forbidden. An `async` method, `async` lambda, or iterator method may not declare a `ref` or `out` parameter; a compile error at the declaration.

title: a borrow-bearing record parameter is rejected on an async method
rule: Borrow-bearing parameters and results are forbidden. An `async` method, `async` lambda, or async iterator may not declare a parameter whose type is a borrow-bearing record (§9.7).

title: CancellationToken is the sole admitted borrow-bearing async parameter
rule: The one exception is a borrow-bearing record the standard library certifies with a normatively-stated source-outlives-task obligation — currently only `CancellationToken`.

title: a choice that holds borrows is rejected as an async parameter
rule: An `async` method ... may not declare a parameter whose type is a borrow-bearing record — or a choice that **holds borrows** (§35.4's holds-borrows property), whatever its classification.

title: a borrow-bearing record result type is rejected on an async method
rule: An `async` method ... may not declare ... a result/element type that is such a record or choice.

title: an undischarged owned async parameter carries the must-use warning
rule: An `owned` parameter never discharged by the body carries the §28.3 must-use warning at its declaration; `using var c := move conn;` on entry is the warning-free way to declare frame-lifetime intent. The class declares a destructor so it is not trivial-dispose (§28.9), whose ceremony exemption is over the obligation at every holder form — an undischarged `owned` async parameter among them — and would otherwise free it silently with no warning.

title: ensures is not admitted on an async method
rule: `requires` clauses on an `async` method evaluate in the synchronous prefix ...; `ensures` on `async` methods is not admitted in this revision (§22.16).

title: a borrow-bearing local with a caller-side source may not cross a suspension point
rule: A local of borrow-bearing record type ... is admitted across the suspension iff every borrow it carries has a frame-resident source ... A borrow whose source is caller-side — a plain parameter, `this`, a field reached through `this` — does not qualify.

title: a borrow-bearing local with a frame-resident source may cross a suspension point
rule: A local of borrow-bearing record type ... is admitted across the suspension iff every borrow it carries has a frame-resident source: an owned local, a `using var`/`await using var`, or an `owned` parameter of the same async body.

title: await on a value-typed Task<T> produces the result directly
rule: `await` suspends the current async method until a task completes. The shape `var result := await someTask;` is appropriate when `someTask` returns a value type, `string`, or `Task` (no value).

title: await outside an async method or lambda is rejected
rule: `await` is valid only inside an `async` method or `async` lambda.

title: Result is a legal blocking read outside any domain
rule: `Wait()` and `Result` are synchronous escape hatches for code running outside any domain — in practice, the synchronous portion of program startup: a non-`async` `Main`, and code it calls directly on the main thread.

title: Wait() lexically inside an async method is rejected
rule: The compiler rejects `Wait()` and `Result` lexically inside `async` methods and `async` lambdas (there, `await` is strictly superior and always available).

title: Result lexically inside an async method is rejected
rule: The compiler rejects `Wait()` and `Result` lexically inside `async` methods and `async` lambdas (there, `await` is strictly superior and always available).

title: IsCompleted reads True on an already-completed task
rule: `public class Task { public readonly property IsCompleted: bool; ... }` — a task produced by `Task.FromResult` is already completed.

title: OwningTask<T>.Result on a completed task transfers ownership
rule: `OwningTask<T>` exposes `Result`: reading it on a **completed** task in an owned-consuming position transfers ownership of the result to the reader exactly as `await` does.

title: a Task<T> may be awaited from multiple places
rule: A `Task` or `Task<T>` may be awaited from multiple places, sequentially or concurrently. Every awaiter sees the same eventual state. The underlying computation runs once.

title: a second await of an OwningTask<T> raises InvalidOperationException
rule: A `OwningTask<T>` is single-consumer per the Pattern B rules: the first await spends the task regardless of outcome, and a second await raises `InvalidOperationException` on the second await even when the first await completed successfully.

title: using var may not bind the borrow produced by awaiting a Pattern A Task<T>
rule: The borrow may not flow to a `using var` binding: `using var r := await task;` is rejected — a borrow cannot assume the disposal obligation the spelling would announce.

title: a plain var binds the borrow produced by awaiting a Pattern A Task<T>
rule: The borrow produced by `await task` may flow to a `var` binding: `var r := await task;` — `r` is a non-owned local with the same source as `task`.

title: using var is the canonical binding for a Pattern B await result
rule: The owned binding forms are `using var x := await ...` (the canonical form ...) and `var x := await ...`, which introduces an owned local of class type T under the standard discharge rules.

title: move is rejected on a Pattern B await operand
rule: The position is **marker-free** — the transfer marker is not admitted where the target already announces the consume; Pattern B await therefore deliberately joins no consume-site freeze list and takes no operand marker.

title: discarding a Task with the bare discard statement is rejected
rule: The only discards that remain errors are `Task`/`Task<T>` (use `Task.FireAndForget`, since disposing a task abandons a running operation — a semantic, not a leak, concern).

title: Task.FireAndForget is the supervised remedy for discarding a task
rule: The two legal patterns for "I don't want to await this task" are `Task.FireAndForget(call())` (supervised: exceptions thrown by the task are logged) and a **named** `using var t := call();`.

title: a named using var is the unsupervised remedy for discarding a task
rule: The two legal patterns for "I don't want to await this task" are `Task.FireAndForget(call())` and a **named** `using var t := call();` — unsupervised.

title: the scoped await-bind admits a fresh var declaration over an unbound producer await
rule: In a local declaration `var x := await E;` ... where `E` is an unbound owned temporary of static type `Task<T>` for class T, no unbound temporary arises at all: the compiler binds it to a hidden scope-pinned slot, and `x` is an ordinary borrowed local.

title: Task<T> over a move-only value T is a compile error at the declaration
rule: A **move-only value T** ... is admitted by **no row**: declaring `Task<T>` or `OwningTask<T>` over such a T is a **compile error at the declaration**.

title: Task.FromResult with a class-typed T is rejected
rule: The factory `Task.FromResult<T>(value: T)` ... is restricted to non-class T ...; calling it with a class-typed T is a compile error.

title: Task.FromOwnedResult produces a Pattern B task for a class-typed T
rule: For class T, use `Task.FromOwnedResult<T>(owned value: T): OwningTask<T>` instead. The caller transfers ownership of `value` to the task; the produced task is Pattern B.

title: a bare expression-statement Pattern B await is rejected
rule: For a `OwningTask<T>` not awaited in an owned-consuming context — a bare expression-statement `await t;`, whose minted result would be dropped silently — the await is a compile error.

title: the explicit discard is an owned-consuming context for a Pattern B await
rule: The explicit discard `_ := await t;` is **not** such a case: the discard is itself an owned-consuming position and disposes the result.

title: an async lambda may target a (string) -> Task<int> function type
rule: The function type of an async lambda has a `Task`, `Task<T>`, or `OwningTask<T>` return type. `Task<T>` for borrowing or value-typed results.

title: an ascribed async lambda may target OwningTask<T> for a fresh class result
rule: A **return-type ascription** names the wrapper: `async lambda(path): OwningTask<Widget> => ...` — Pattern B return; the lambda's state machine forwards the owned result through.

title: an async lambda may not target a function type with a ref slot
rule: The rule extends to conversions: an `async` lambda may not be assigned to a function type (§27.1) whose parameter list carries a `ref`/`out` slot.

title: await for consumes an async iterator's yielded values in order
rule: `await for` is valid only inside an async method or async lambda. It desugars analogously to `for`: it acquires an async enumerator with `await using`, calls `MoveNextAsync()` with `await` in a loop.

title: await for over IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T> yields an owned iteration variable
rule: Each iteration variable is owned; the §28.3 discharge rules apply on every exit edge of the loop body — the same rule as for synchronous `for` over `IOwningEnumerable<T>`.

title: with token passes a CancellationToken to GetAsyncEnumerator
rule: `await for` accepts an optional `with` clause to pass a `CancellationToken` to the async enumerator. The `with token` clause passes `token` as the argument to `GetAsyncEnumerator(token)`.

title: await for outside an async method is rejected
rule: `await for` is valid only inside an async method or async lambda.

title: await inside a source-written finally is rejected in an async iterator
rule: Inside an async iterator, `await` may not appear in a `finally` block — a compile error.

title: an await using var may not be live across a yield return
rule: An `await using var` whose static type is such a class (or is of **interface** static type) ... may not be **live across a `yield return`** in an async iterator: a compile error at the yield.

title: awaiting inside the token source's using var scope discharges the source-outlives obligation
rule: **The `CancellationTokenSource` must outlive the settlement of every task observing one of its tokens.** ... Awaiting the call inside the source's `using var` scope discharges the obligation.

title: IsCancellationRequested observes a Cancel() call on the source
rule: `CancellationToken` observes the source's state; when `Cancel()` is called on the source, all tokens derived from it report `IsCancellationRequested == true`.

title: an exception thrown after an await faults the task and is re-raised by the caller's await
rule: An exception thrown after an `await` faults the task. Awaiting a faulted task re-raises the exception with the original stack trace preserved.

title: an exception thrown in the synchronous prefix faults the returned task
rule: An exception thrown in the synchronous prefix of an async method (before any `await`) faults the returned task, not the immediate caller.

title: a catch guard may not contain await
rule: Catch **guards** are the one exception: a `when` guard on a catch arm is evaluated synchronously during exception dispatch and may not contain `await` (a compile error, in async and sync methods alike).

title: await is unrestricted inside catch and finally bodies
rule: `await` has no syntactic restrictions on its placement inside `try`/`catch`/`finally` *bodies*. The state machine handles suspension across exception-handling boundaries correctly.

title: Task.WhenAll completes only after every input task has settled
rule: `Task.WhenAll` (all input forms) completes only after **every** input has settled — it never abandons laggards. If every input succeeded it completes successfully.

title: Task.WhenAny yields the index of the settled task
rule: `Task.WhenAny(tasks: Array<Task>): Task<int>` — completes when the first task completes, yielding the **index** of the winner in `tasks`.

title: the owning WhenAll overload aggregates OwningTask<T> results
rule: `Task.WhenAll<T>(owned tasks: OwningArray<OwningTask<T>>): OwningTask<OwningArray<T>> where T: class` — the caller transfers ownership of the array (and its tasks); the result is an owned array of owned elements.

title: WhenAny of an empty array raises ArgumentException synchronously
rule: `WhenAny` of an **empty** array raises `ArgumentException` **synchronously at the call site**, not as a faulted task.

title: discarding a Task with the discard statement is rejected
rule: `Task.FireAndForget` is the only supported way to discard a `Task` value — the discard form `_ := someAsyncCall();` is rejected at compile time because abandoning a `Task` reference would skip its continuation cleanup.

title: the anonymous using-var binding of a Task is rejected
rule: The two legal patterns for "I don't want to await this task" are `Task.FireAndForget(call())` and a named `using var t := call();` — the anonymous `using var _ := call();` is rejected with the discard.

title: a named using-var binding is the legal unsupervised abandonment form
rule: A named `using var t := call();` is legal (unsupervised): the task is disposed at scope end without blocking, and any exceptions it raises are silently swallowed.

title: Task.FireAndForget accepts the task and relinquishes ownership
rule: `Task.FireAndForget(owned task: Task)` registers a continuation that logs or handles any exception the task produces, then disposes the task; the calling code relinquishes ownership.

title: WhenAll re-raises the first non-successful input in input order
rule: Awaiting a non-successful `Task.WhenAll` re-raises the exception of the **first non-successful input in input order**, per the first-fault-no-aggregation posture; the other inputs' faults remain observable on those tasks individually.

title: a cancelled input counts as OperationCanceledException for WhenAll
rule: Awaiting a non-successful `Task.WhenAll` re-raises the exception of the first non-successful input in input order — a cancelled input counting as `OperationCanceledException`.

title: Task.FromResult at a class-typed T is rejected
rule: `Task.FromResult<T>(value: T): Task<T>` is restricted to non-class T; calling FromResult with a class-typed T is a compile error pointing to the owned variant.

title: Task.FromOwnedResult transfers the value to the awaiting context
rule: `Task.FromOwnedResult<T>(owned value: T): OwningTask<T> where T: class` — the caller transfers ownership to the task; awaiters consume the task under Pattern B, the await appearing in an owned-consuming context to which ownership transfers.

title: TaskCompletionSource<T> completes a Task<T> imperatively for non-class T
rule: A `TaskCompletionSource<T>` produces a task whose state is controlled imperatively. For non-class T ... the produced `Task<T>` carries no ownership across the await boundary.

title: OwningTaskCompletionSource<T> transfers ownership of a class-typed result
rule: For class T ... the source takes ownership of the result on completion, and the eventual awaiter takes ownership through the `using var x := await ...` shape.

title: returning the source's Task property out of its own scope is a borrow escape
rule: The task never outlives its source, and there is no first-read ownership transfer ... returning `tcs.Task` *itself* out of the scope is the return of a borrow sourced at a local with no source that outlives the call — rejected by §28.3's borrowed-return rule.

title: Mutex.Acquire() lexically inside an async method is rejected
rule: The compiler rejects the blocking forms **lexically inside `async` methods and `async` lambdas** (there the async forms are strictly superior — `await m.AcquireAsync()`).

title: AcquireAsync is the admitted remedy for blocking acquisition inside async code
rule: The compiler rejects the blocking forms lexically inside `async` methods and `async` lambdas (there the async forms are strictly superior — `await m.AcquireAsync()`).

title: Domain.Spawn rejects a capturing lambda entry
rule: The compiler enforces at the call site: **the entry must be capture-free**: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference. A capturing lambda or an instance method reference is rejected — captures and receivers are borrows of the origin domain.

title: Domain.Spawn admits a non-capturing lambda entry
rule: The entry must be capture-free: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference.

title: Domain.Spawn admits a static method reference entry
rule: The entry must be capture-free: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference.

title: Domain.Spawn rejects a non-sendable class-typed argument
rule: **Argument and result types must be sendable**, per the rules above. A **class** type is sendable iff it is transfer-closed: the class must be `sealed` ... or `closed`. Open classes are not sendable.

title: Domain.Spawn admits a sealed class-typed argument
rule: A **class** type is sendable iff it is transfer-closed: the class is `sealed`; or it is `closed` and every class in its hierarchy is itself transfer-closed.

title: Channel<T> rejects a non-sendable class-typed element
rule: Channels are the only mutable objects reachable from more than one domain; they are compiler-known, internally synchronized, and their element type must be sendable (checked at instantiation per §3.6).

title: Send transfers ownership into the channel and Receive transfers it out
rule: A **channel** carries sendable values from one domain to another with ownership transfer at both ends: `Send` consumes the value in the sending domain; `Receive` produces it owned in the receiving domain.

title: a thrown owned exception is caught by a matching arm
rule: `throw expr` constructs and raises an exception; a thrown exception is caught by the first arm naming its class or a base of it.

title: throwing a primitive-typed operand is rejected
rule: `throw expr` requires `expr`'s static type, nullability not admitted, to be `Exception` or a class deriving from it; values of primitive type cannot be thrown — a compile error at the throw site.

title: throwing an Object-typed operand is rejected
rule: An `Object`-typed operand is likewise rejected (no interface derives from `Exception`, and an `Object` referent may be a boxed value); narrow to the exception class first.

title: throwing an interface-typed operand is rejected
rule: An interface-typed operand is likewise rejected — no interface derives from `Exception` — even when the runtime class implementing it does; narrow to the exception class first.

title: throwing the caught exception binding directly is rejected
rule: The throw operand is consumed as an owned value, so a borrowed class reference is not a valid operand; to re-raise the exception being handled, use the bare re-raise instead.

title: the bare re-raise is the admitted way to re-throw a caught exception
rule: To re-raise the exception being handled, use the bare re-raise (`throw`, valid only inside a catch arm body) rather than throwing the borrowed catch-arm binding.

title: the transfer marker at the marker-free throw position is rejected
rule: `throw` is a marker-free consuming position — `throw x;` — the keyword itself is the announcement, so `throw move x;` is rejected at the marker-free position, the same no-marker rule as an `owned` return.

title: throwing a named owned local is written unmarked
rule: `throw` is a marker-free consuming position: the correct spelling of a named owned binding as a throw operand is `throw x;`, with no `move`.

title: disposing the caught exception binding is rejected
rule: Inside a catch arm, the bound exception variable is a borrow of the in-flight exception; `Dispose()` requires an owning receiver, and a catch-arm binding is one of the borrow forms through which disposal is a compile error with no exception.

title: a closure over the caught exception assigned outside the arm is rejected
rule: A closure capturing the catch-arm binding may outlive the arm only when the closure's value can leave the arm; assigning it to a binding declared outside the arm is one such escape, and the counter-example is one assignment away from the confined-closure idiom.

title: a closure over the caught exception confined to the arm is admitted
rule: A closure over the catch-arm binding is confined to the arm — admitted, however many lambdas nest inside it — whenever its value stays inside the arm: bound to an arm-local and invoked there, nothing over the binding ever leaves.

title: a try statement with neither catch nor finally is rejected
rule: A `try` statement consists of a protected block, optionally followed by a `catch` block, optionally followed by a `finally` block. At least one of `catch` or `finally` must be present.

title: a try statement with only a finally is admitted
rule: If the `try` has only a `finally` (no `catch`), the catch block is omitted entirely, satisfying the at-least-one-of-catch-or-finally rule.

title: a broader arm listed first catches a more specific exception
rule: The arms are tried in order; the first arm whose pattern matches the thrown exception is selected, its body runs, and exception handling completes. Arms after the matched one are not considered.

title: a more specific arm listed first catches its own type
rule: The arms are tried in order; the first arm whose pattern matches the thrown exception is selected. Reordering the arms of s31_2_0003 so the more specific type is first changes which arm is selected.

title: finally runs when the protected block completes normally
rule: `finally` runs whether the protected block completed normally, was exited by an exception (caught or uncaught), or was exited by `return`.

title: finally runs when the protected block exits by return
rule: `finally` runs whether the protected block completed normally, was exited by an exception, or was exited by `return`.

title: return inside a finally block is rejected
rule: `return` inside a `finally` block is a compile error (§21.5, §21.7).

title: break inside a finally whose target loop encloses it is rejected
rule: Neither may exit a `finally` block: inside a `finally`, a `break` or `continue` — labeled or unlabeled — whose target loop lies outside the `finally` is a compile error, the same rule as `return` in a `finally`.

title: continue inside a finally whose target loop encloses it is rejected
rule: Neither may exit a `finally` block: inside a `finally`, a `break` or `continue` whose target loop lies outside the `finally` is a compile error — on the exception edge such a jump would silently discard the in-flight exception.

title: an owned local of the protected block is disposed before finally runs
rule: The `finally` is established at entry to the protected block: on the single establishment-ordered cleanup stack it ranks before anything the block itself establishes, so an owned local or `using var` declared inside the protected block is disposed before the `finally` runs on every exit edge.

title: a throw escaping a finally supersedes the in-flight exception
rule: A throw escaping a `finally` supersedes the in-flight exception: when a `finally` entered during exception propagation itself completes by throwing, the new exception replaces the one being handled, and the superseding exception propagates from the `try` statement as usual.

title: the superseding exception's SupersededChain records the lost exception
rule: At the instant of supersession, and before the superseded exception is disposed, the runtime appends to the superseding exception's `SupersededChain` an `ExceptionInfo` snapshot of the superseded exception itself — its type name, `Message`, and `StackTrace`.

title: a bare type arm matches without binding
rule: A catch arm's pattern may be a bare type, `IOException`: it matches any thrown exception that is an instance of the type, without binding.

title: a false guard skips the arm and falls through to the next
rule: Each pattern may be followed by an optional `when Expression` guard. The guard is evaluated only if the pattern matches; if the guard returns `false`, the arm is skipped and the next arm is considered.

title: a multi-type binding types at the nearest common base
rule: When binding, `name` has the static type of the nearest common base of the listed types — the most specific class that is a base of every listed type.

title: a binding over unrelated types types at Exception, not either listed type
rule: For alternatives sharing nothing more specific, the nearest common base is `Exception`; every listed type is `Exception`-derived, so the binding's static type is never narrower than that.

title: a catch arm naming a non-Exception-derived class is rejected
rule: With every throwable `Exception`-derived and inheritance single, an arm naming any other class type is provably dead — no thrown instance can ever match — and is a compile error naming this rule.

title: a catch arm naming Object is rejected
rule: `Object` itself is rejected by the same rule for the opposite reason — as the universal root it matches every throwable, and the spelling for that is the bare `Exception` arm; the remedy is to delete the arm or fix the type.

title: an interface-typed catch arm matches an implementing exception
rule: An interface-typed arm remains admissible — no interface derives from `Exception`, but an `Exception`-derived class may implement one, so the arm matches exactly the throwables whose class implements the interface.

title: an unconstrained generic parameter used as a catch-arm type is rejected
rule: A generic type parameter used as a catch arm's type must carry an `Exception`-derived class bound; a parameter that is unconstrained is a compile error at the arm, checked at the generic declaration.

title: a generic type parameter bounded by Exception matches the substituted type
rule: A generic type parameter is admissible as an arm's type when it carries an `Exception`-derived class bound; it matches exactly as the substituted type argument would.

title: an expression-form catch arm body discards its result
rule: A catch arm's body may be an expression: `=> SomeMethod(args)`; the expression's result is discarded.

title: a single-statement catch arm body ends with the statement's semicolon
rule: A catch arm's body may be a single statement: `=> Log(ex);` ends with the statement's `;` — the convenient form for a one-line arm body that is a statement.

title: a do...end block catch arm body holds several statements
rule: A catch arm's body may be a `do ... end` block: `=> do statements end`, used when the body contains multiple statements.

title: a specific arm before the catch-all handles its own type
rule: Arms are tried in order; the first match wins. The most specific exception types should appear first, ahead of a bare `Exception` catch-all.

title: a bare Exception arm at the end is the catch-all
rule: A bare `Exception` arm at the end is the catch-all: every throwable derives from `Exception`, so such an arm captures any thrown exception.

title: a non-exhaustive catch block draws no diagnostic
rule: A `catch` block need not be exhaustive. Exceptions not matched by any arm propagate to the enclosing handler. The compiler does not warn on non-exhaustive `catch` blocks — non-exhaustiveness is the normal case.

title: the bare re-raise expression re-throws with the stack trace preserved
rule: The bare re-raise re-throws the currently-handled exception with its stack trace preserved. As an expression: `throw` (without a semicolon) — the natural form for an arm body that does nothing but re-raise.

title: the bare re-raise statement re-throws after other statements in the arm
rule: As a statement: `throw;` (with the trailing semicolon), equivalent to the expression form followed by `;`, used inside `do ... end` blocks where the re-raise is one statement among several.

title: a bare re-raise outside a catch arm body is rejected
